## Research Report

### Research Questions Investigated

| Tier | Sub-question |
|------|-------------|
| Tier 1 | How is formative assessment defined in the literature, and what core components distinguish it from summative assessment, diagnostic assessment, feedback, and classroom assessment in K-12 or postsecondary settings? |
| Tier 1 | Which student learning outcomes are most commonly associated with formative assessment research, and how are those outcomes operationalized across subjects, grade levels, and contexts? |
| Tier 1 | What populations and instructional contexts are most often studied in formative assessment research, and how do these settings shape the interpretation of student learning outcomes? |
| Tier 2 | How are the target learning outcomes typically developed through standard instruction, assessment, and feedback practices when formative assessment is not used systematically in K-12 or postsecondary classrooms? |
| Tier 2 | What alternative approaches—such as summative assessment, teacher questioning, quizzes, feedback-only interventions, or progress monitoring—serve as common comparators for formative assessment studies? |
| Tier 2 | What are the usual baseline conditions for student learning in studies of formative assessment, and how do these counterfactuals differ across subjects, grade levels, and educational settings? |
| Tier 3 | How is formative assessment implemented in practice in K-12 or postsecondary classrooms, including methods such as exit tickets, hinge questions, quizzes, rubrics, peer assessment, and teacher feedback cycles? |
| Tier 3 | What instructional mechanisms are proposed to explain how formative assessment may influence student learning outcomes for specific populations, such as through timely feedback, adaptation of instruction, metacognition, or self-regulation? |
| Tier 3 | How do implementation features such as frequency, timing, teacher training, subject area, and use of digital tools affect the delivery of formative assessment in different contexts? |
| Tier 4 | What is the evidence that formative assessment improves student learning outcomes relative to standard instruction or other baseline conditions in K-12 and postsecondary education? |
| Tier 4 | Do effects of formative assessment vary by student population, grade level, subject area, or instructional context, and what limitations or heterogeneity are reported in the literature? |
| Tier 4 | How does the effectiveness of formative assessment compare with adjacent practices such as feedback, low-stakes quizzing, progress monitoring, or adaptive instruction when direct evidence is limited? |
| Tier 4 | What tradeoffs, implementation barriers, or dependency on teacher capacity affect the magnitude or reliability of formative assessment effects on student learning outcomes? |

### Synthesis and Implications

Across the corpus, formative assessment is best understood as a process rather than a single tool. The defining feature is not whether an activity is a quiz, peer review, rubric, or teacher question; rather, it is whether evidence of student understanding is elicited and then used to modify teaching and learning in real time (Black and Wiliam, 2009; Andrade et al., 2021; Rashid and Jaidin, 2014). That distinction matters because many ostensibly “formative” studies are actually about feedback, low-stakes testing, or self-regulated learning supports, and the same instrument can be formative or summative depending on how the information is used (McCarthy et al., 2025; Chen, 2020; Palabıyık and Daloglu, 2025).

The outcome literature is broader than the intervention literature. Achievement is the most commonly measured endpoint, but the studies retrieved here repeatedly extend to motivation, self-regulation, metacognition, engagement, and relatedness, especially in EFL and blended-learning settings (Ismail et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). Where the evidence is strongest, formative assessment appears to improve learning most when it is embedded in an instructional cycle that includes actionable feedback and visible pedagogical response, rather than being used as a standalone scoring mechanism (Karaman, 2021; Xuan et al., 2022; Beekman et al., 2021).

The practical implication for schools and instructors is that simply adding more quizzes, rubrics, or digital tools is unlikely to reproduce the effect unless the assessment information is actively used to change instruction. Several studies and reviews emphasize teacher capacity, differentiated instruction, and student participation as important conditions for success, which suggests that professional development and feedback literacy are central implementation levers (Wenzel et al., 2023; Xuan et al., 2022; Andrade et al., 2021). The evidence also suggests that formative assessment is most promising when it supports learner agency, because the strongest subgroup effects in the meta-analysis were linked to student-initiated or jointly enacted feedback processes (Karaman, 2021; Xuan et al., 2022).

The evidence base is not equally mature across sectors. K-12 reading and broad K-12 meta-analyses are the best synthesized areas, while postsecondary evidence is thinner, more heterogeneous, and more likely to be dominated by quasi-experimental, qualitative, or tool-specific studies rather than large randomized trials (Xuan et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2024; Sortwell et al., 2024). Subject coverage is also uneven: literacy, EFL/writing, mathematics, and science are better represented than social studies, arts, vocational education, and many graduate or professional domains. For policy and practice, this means formative assessment should be treated as a design principle that must be adapted locally rather than as a universal package with a stable effect size.

### Limitations and Research Gaps

The largest limitation is construct instability. The literature repeatedly uses formative assessment to refer to feedback, quizzes, peer assessment, self-assessment, progress monitoring, adaptive instruction, and classroom assessment more broadly, often without demonstrating that evidence was actually used to adapt teaching (Andrade et al., 2021; McCarthy et al., 2025; Chen, 2020). This makes it difficult to determine whether positive findings reflect formative assessment proper or adjacent practices that are only partially formative.

The second limitation is baseline ambiguity. Many studies compare formative assessment to “conventional teaching,” “standard instruction,” or “summative assessment,” but the comparator is often not described with enough precision to know whether the control condition already contained informal formative elements (Rashid and Jaidin, 2014; Palabıyık and Daloglu, 2025). That contamination likely attenuates estimated effects and makes cross-study comparison difficult.

A third gap is uneven causal rigor. Although there are useful meta-analyses and some quasi-experiments, the number of clean, well-powered randomized trials remains limited, especially in postsecondary education and in subjects outside literacy and EFL (Karaman, 2021; Xuan et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023). Many studies also use short follow-up windows, weak reporting of implementation fidelity, or self-report outcomes that are more vulnerable to expectancy and social desirability bias than achievement tests.

Equity and subgroup evidence remain underdeveloped. The best-synthesized K-12 reading meta-analysis found no significant differences by grade band or mainstream versus at-risk status and no digital-technology moderation, but the overall literature still provides little direct evidence for effects by disability status, multilingual learner status, socioeconomic background, race/ethnicity, or prior attainment across subjects (Xuan et al., 2022; Sortwell et al., 2024). The field therefore cannot yet support strong claims about who benefits most, under what conditions, or whether formative assessment reduces or reproduces existing inequities.

Finally, durability is still a weak point. Retention, transfer, and long-term self-regulation are frequently invoked as important outcomes, but only a minority of studies measure them directly, and fewer still do so with delayed post-tests or longitudinal designs (Beekman et al., 2021; Ryan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025). The clearest next step is more rigorous trials that specify the comparator, document instructional adaptation, and track not only immediate achievement but also retention, transfer, motivation, and self-regulated learning over meaningful time spans.

No sources cited.

## Body of Evidence Maturity: LIMITED
Justification: The evidence base is conceptually well developed and includes several meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and a smaller set of quasi-experimental studies, but clean randomized evidence is limited and the construct is inconsistently operationalized across studies. Coverage is strongest in K-12 literacy and broad classroom assessment, while postsecondary, equity-relevant subgroup, and long-term outcome evidence remains comparatively thin.

paper_profiles.title: Student engagement with teacher and automated feedback on L2 writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This naturalistic case study examines how two Chinese university students engaged with two sources of formative feedback on L2 writing: teacher written feedback and automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback. The paper asks how these feedback sources differed, how students responded to them behaviorally, affectively, and cognitively, and what factors shaped their engagement.

The study followed two third-year English majors over a 16-week semester in two EAP courses. In one assignment, students drafted an essay, submitted it to the Pigai AWE system, and revised multiple times before final submission; in another, they completed a teacher-reviewed essay without mandatory AWE use. Data included drafts, feedback records, submission logs, interviews, and course documents. The authors analyzed feedback types, revision operations, and student reports of emotions, strategy use, and time-on-task.

The main conclusion is that engagement strongly mediates the usefulness of formative feedback. The more engaged student showed sustained revision, multiple resubmissions, and deeper cognitive processing, and improved more; the less engaged student made mostly surface-level changes and benefited less. Teacher feedback was perceived as more comprehensive but less flexible, while AWE enabled autonomy, immediate feedback, and multiple drafting. The authors argue that both feedback source and learner factors such as proficiency, motivation, and strategy repertoire shape how students use feedback in writing development.

finding.finding_summary: Both students improved their writing after feedback, but the highly engaged learner (Flora) made substantially more and deeper revisions than the moderately engaged learner (David). Flora resubmitted her AWE essay 13 times and increased her AWE score from 79 to 90, while David resubmitted once and showed only a negligible score increase; the paper reports that Flora outperformed David in writing improvement, but does not provide standardized effect sizes.
finding.measure: L2 writing revision quality, number/type of revision operations, and AWE/teacher essay scores

finding.finding_summary: Engagement with feedback was strongly shaped by affective responses such as motivation, frustration, embarrassment, anxiety, and confidence. Flora reported motivation and positive emotional investment after teacher and AWE feedback, whereas David reported being overwhelmed, disappointed, and embarrassed by the AWE score, which reduced his willingness to revise.
finding.measure: Interview-based affective responses and observed engagement with feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally analyzes metacognition, self-regulation, planning, monitoring, evaluating, and strategy use in revision. Flora demonstrated extensive cognitive and metacognitive engagement (planning, goal-setting, monitoring, evaluating, rewriting, and reorganization), while David showed limited deep processing and mainly surface-level deletion/correction; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Revision operations, time-on-task, and interview evidence of planning/monitoring/evaluating/self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: AWE feedback enabled rapid, repeated drafting and individualized pacing, which the authors frame as an efficiency/autonomy advantage over teacher-only feedback. Flora used the system to revise over two days and 13 resubmissions, while David completed only one resubmission in less than 14 minutes; however, the paper is qualitative and does not report comparative efficiency effect sizes.
finding.measure: Submission timestamps, number of resubmissions, and time spent revising

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing the Integration of Financial Literacy in the Accountancy, Business, and Management Curriculum
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of financial literacy integration in the Philippine Accountancy, Business, and Management (ABM) senior high school curriculum and argues that students are not being adequately prepared for real-world financial decision-making. The study aims to assess the current status of financial literacy concepts in the curriculum, identify gaps and needs, and gauge the financial literacy competencies of ABM teachers, administrators, and students in Albay Division.

Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, the researcher surveyed 160 ABM students, 12 ABM teachers, and 6 administrators from six public schools, then followed up with interviews. The study focused on financial knowledge, skills, and attitudes, along with curriculum needs and possible instructional activities for integration into existing finance-related subjects. It emphasized experiential, localized, and practical learning approaches, including simulations, case studies, digital financial tools, and real-life financial scenarios.

The paper concludes that financial literacy is currently insufficiently embedded in the ABM curriculum and that there is strong demand for more practical, real-world, and future-ready instruction. It recommends continuous professional development, teacher training, and the use of assessment strategies and digital tools to strengthen delivery. The study is primarily descriptive and needs-focused rather than an impact evaluation, but it provides a curriculum design rationale for improving financial literacy education in senior high school ABM programs.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that financial literacy is not sufficiently integrated into the ABM curriculum and that respondents saw a strong need for deeper content, better resources, and more real-world application. The paper did not report an experimental effect size; instead, it used surveys and interviews with 178 respondents (160 students, 12 teachers, 6 administrators) to describe gaps and propose instructional activities for integration.
finding.measure: Survey ratings and interview responses on financial literacy curriculum status, needs, gaps, and competencies

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that stronger curriculum integration, teacher professional development, and instructional redesign are needed to improve institutional delivery of financial literacy in ABM programs. It identifies system-level gaps such as lack of standardized integration, insufficient teacher training, and limited resources, and recommends curriculum revision and capacity-building at the school/division level.
finding.measure: Institutional perceptions of curriculum needs, gaps, and implementation constraints

finding.finding_summary: The study frames financial literacy integration as a way to strengthen students' practical decision-making, critical thinking, and problem-solving in real-world financial scenarios. Respondents favored experiential activities, simulations, and case studies as mechanisms for building these durable skills, but no numeric effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Survey and interview indicators related to experiential learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving in financial contexts

paper_profiles.title: Stealth Assessment: Measuring and Supporting Learning in Video Games
paper_profiles.venue: The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Reports on Digital Media and Learning / MIT Press
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12 and Postsecondary; examples include middle school, high school, undergraduate, and ages 13-29 cancer patients)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report argues that traditional assessments are often detached from learning, limited in validity, and poorly suited to measuring twenty-first-century competencies such as persistence, creativity, collaboration, and conceptual understanding. The authors propose stealth assessment: embedded, unobtrusive, real-time assessment within digital games that both measures and supports learning through adaptive feedback and task selection.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and methodological report rather than a single empirical study. It reviews prior evidence that digital games can support learning and then explains how evidence-centered design can be used to build valid game-based assessments. The report also discusses implementation challenges, including construct-irrelevant demands, working-memory load, accessibility, tutorial needs, feedback design, and dependencies among in-game actions.

To illustrate the approach, the authors describe an application in Newton’s Playground, where stealth assessments are being developed to measure creativity, conscientiousness, and conceptual physics. They also summarize related studies showing that feedback-enhanced assessment systems can improve learning, and that educational games such as NIU-Torcs, Re-Mission, and Taiga Park have produced positive learning outcomes in prior controlled studies. Overall, the report concludes that stealth assessment is promising for formative assessment and personalized support, but that more research is needed to validate measures and understand tradeoffs in real classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The report cites a controlled experiment on Taiga Park showing that middle-school students using the game scored significantly higher than a classroom condition on posttest knowledge of core science concepts (e.g., erosion and eutrophication) and on a delayed posttest measuring retention and transfer in a novel task. Exact effect sizes were not reported in the report excerpt, but the differences were statistically significant at p < 0.01 for the immediate posttest and p < 0.001 for the delayed posttest.
finding.measure: Posttest and delayed posttest of science content knowledge and retention/transfer (water quality, erosion, eutrophication)

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the report is that stealth assessment can measure and support competencies such as conscientiousness, persistence, and self-efficacy, and that game-based feedback may strengthen these attributes. The report cites an adaptive assessment study (ACED) with 268 high-school students in which elaborated feedback improved learning, and it argues that game difficulty and repeated failure/retry cycles can foster persistence, although the persistence-improvement claim is largely theoretical in this report.
finding.measure: Learning gains on geometric sequences; inferred persistence/conscientiousness indicators during gameplay
finding.study_size: n=268 for ACED study; not_reported for persistence claim

finding.finding_summary: The report directly focuses on durable skills including creativity, conscientiousness/persistence, problem solving, and collaboration as target competencies for stealth assessment. It provides examples of in-game indicators that can be used to infer these skills (e.g., retries, time on difficult problems) and cites prior work showing that NIU-Torcs, Re-Mission, and Taiga Park were associated with deeper understanding or improved outcomes, but the main evidence for durable skills in this paper is conceptual rather than a new effect estimate.
finding.measure: In-game indicators and concept-map/deep understanding outcomes; no direct standardized durable-skill test reported in the report excerpt

finding.finding_summary: The report cites an undergraduate engineering study of NIU-Torcs in which students using the game-based instructional approach (n=38) outperformed students in four control classrooms (n=48) on a concept map assessment of programming/engineering understanding. Gains were reported specifically for deeper levels of understanding, including hierarchy depth and connections among branches, indicating improved conceptual learning in a vocational/engineering context.
finding.measure: Concept map assessment of programming and engineering understanding

finding.finding_summary: The report cites the Re-Mission trial as showing significant improvements in self-efficacy among young cancer patients who played the game compared with a control game. The intervention group included 197 participants and the control group 178; self-efficacy was one of several outcomes that improved, while stress, control, and quality of life did not.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy; also stress, control, quality of life, adherence, and cancer-related knowledge

finding.finding_summary: The report cites the Re-Mission study as showing significantly greater cancer-related knowledge in the intervention group than in the control group, alongside better adherence and self-efficacy. The trial involved 375 cancer patients aged 13-29 randomized to Re-Mission or an active control game, with outcomes measured at one and three months after pretest; exact effect sizes are not reported in the report excerpt.
finding.measure: Cancer-related knowledge and treatment adherence

paper_profiles.title: Learning and Satisfaction in Webinar, Online, and Face-to-Face Instruction: A Meta-Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether synchronous online instruction delivered via webinars improves learning and satisfaction relative to asynchronous online instruction and traditional face-to-face instruction. The authors frame the work around Kirkpatrick’s four-level training evaluation model, which assumes that learner satisfaction should be positively associated with learning, and they test that assumption using randomized controlled trials only.

The review included five studies (10 effect sizes; total N=381) drawn from higher education and professional training settings, mostly with medical, nursing, and health-care participants. Outcomes were objective post-test knowledge measures and satisfaction scales; self-report learning measures were excluded. Across comparisons, webinars were slightly more effective than asynchronous online instruction for learning (Hedges’ g=0.29, 95% CI 0.05–0.53) and roughly equivalent to face-to-face instruction (g=0.06, 95% CI −0.37–0.49), but these learning effects were negligible and statistically insignificant overall.

For satisfaction, webinars were slightly higher than asynchronous online instruction (g=0.12, 95% CI −0.11–0.36) and lower than face-to-face instruction (g=−0.33, 95% CI −1.87–1.21), again with negligible and statistically insignificant differences. Correlation and regression analyses found a negative, non-significant association between satisfaction and learning, providing no support for Kirkpatrick’s proposed positive relationship. The authors conclude that webinars are a reasonable flexible alternative to face-to-face instruction, but they do not appear to produce meaningfully better learning or satisfaction outcomes than other modalities.

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found webinars produced slightly higher post-test knowledge than asynchronous online instruction (Hedges’ g=0.29, 95% CI 0.05–0.53) and nearly identical outcomes relative to face-to-face instruction (g=0.06, 95% CI −0.37–0.49). Across all five RCTs (total N=381), these differences were described as negligible and not statistically significant overall, suggesting webinars are roughly comparable to baseline instruction for knowledge acquisition.
finding.measure: Objective post-test knowledge tests / course knowledge outcomes
finding.effect_size: g=0.29 vs asynchronous online; g=0.06 vs face-to-face

finding.finding_summary: Satisfaction was slightly higher in webinars than asynchronous online instruction (Hedges’ g=0.12, 95% CI −0.11–0.36) but lower than face-to-face instruction (g=−0.33, 95% CI −1.87–1.21). The review reports that all satisfaction effects were negligible and statistically insignificant, indicating no meaningful advantage for webinars on participant reaction outcomes.
finding.measure: Learner satisfaction scales
finding.effect_size: g=0.12 vs asynchronous online; g=−0.33 vs face-to-face

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines the role of formative assessment in improving student learning and describes an e-learning implementation using the Blackboard Learning System at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). The authors frame formative assessment as a way to provide ongoing feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment and arguing that frequent low-stakes assessments can support better learning and preparation for end-of-semester exams.

The implementation described uses weekly or fortnightly online tests in Blackboard, with immediate score reporting and detailed feedback. The paper reports a survey of university students (including Business, Engineering, and IT streams) about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the Blackboard test option. Students generally favored the online formative approach because it broke content into smaller units, provided immediate feedback, and was more flexible than classroom testing; Engineering students were especially supportive. The paper also notes tradeoffs, including concern that too many tests may create stress and overemphasize learning processes at the expense of grades.

Overall, the paper is primarily a descriptive and perception-based study rather than an outcome study of achievement gains. It draws on prior formative-assessment literature and meta-analyses to argue that formative assessment can improve learning, but its own empirical evidence is limited to student attitudes, with no direct pre/post learning outcome comparison reported.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments and immediate feedback were helpful, mainly because they could monitor strengths and weaknesses, stay on track, and correct mistakes without delay. However, some students also reported stress/pressure from too many tests, indicating mixed affective reactions to the implementation.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation (questionnaire and open-ended responses)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students reflect on feedback, understand errors, and track whether they are on course. In the survey, students similarly said the approach helped them learn topics progressively and keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester, but no direct skill outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reflection, self-monitoring, and progressive learning via formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on subject-course learning in a university setting rather than a specific domain like literacy or math. Students favored splitting coursework into 10-12 weekly Blackboard assessments, citing easier study of small topics and better preparation for the semester examination, but the paper does not report direct achievement scores or compare them to a baseline.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of frequent topic-based assessments for course learning and preparation for summative exams

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide about how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback practices. The paper is organized around a classic formative assessment framework—clarifying where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward—and maps possible LLM uses onto each component.

The authors focus on practical classroom applications rather than testing a single intervention. Examples include rewriting formal learning objectives into student-friendly language, generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work at different quality levels, automating diagnostic questions and multiple-choice items, and producing process-level feedback. The intended context spans K-12 and postsecondary education, with illustrative examples drawn largely from high school biology, undergraduate functional MRI, and general classroom settings.

The paper argues that LLMs can scale some aspects of formative assessment and reduce teacher workload, but they should augment rather than replace expert pedagogy. It repeatedly cautions that current benchmarks for LLM outputs often miss formative-assessment quality criteria, that outputs vary and require educator judgment, and that there are risks of over-reliance, inaccuracy, and weak contextual fit across subjects and settings. Overall, the article is a conceptual and practitioner-oriented synthesis that recommends careful, pedagogy-first adoption and future research on better evaluation metrics and classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce educator time and effort by automating or supporting tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating questions, creating exemplars, and producing feedback. No empirical effect estimate is reported because this is a narrative review rather than an outcome study.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time savings / task efficiency (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment may foster metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by helping learners monitor progress, co-construct success criteria, and critically evaluate AI-generated exemplars. These claims are theoretical and illustrative, not based on a direct empirical test in this paper.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM uses for writing-related formative assessment, including generating and revising learning objectives, sample essays, and methods sections. It cites prior work suggesting LLMs can produce student-friendly text and sample writing, but this article itself does not present original quantitative evidence of improved literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing quality / text simplification / exemplar generation (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: Scientific-learning examples are used to illustrate how LLMs could support formative assessment in biology and fMRI courses, such as clarifying objectives and generating sample methods sections. The paper argues these uses may support deeper understanding of scientific tasks, but it does not report direct empirical effects on scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Scientific understanding / methods-writing / task comprehension (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
paper_profiles.venue: American Journal of Physics (conference paper / proceedings-style manuscript)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports initial findings from the Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study, which examines how course, instructor, and student features are associated with learning outcomes in undergraduate STEM courses using Learning Assistants (LAs). The motivating problem is that LA programs have spread rapidly across institutions, but there is limited cross-institutional evidence about which implementation features are linked to better outcomes and whether those effects vary by context.

The study draws on data from 4,500+ students and 17 instructors across 13 LA Alliance institutions in the first semester of a multi-year project. Students completed pre/post online concept inventories in biology, chemistry, and physics; faculty also reported how LAs were used, course characteristics, and their experience with LAs. The authors analyzed pre-to-post change using hierarchical linear models, nesting student data within courses to estimate associations between student learning gains and factors such as gender, race, time spent interacting with LAs, student-to-LA ratio, faculty meeting time with LAs, and instructor experience teaching with LAs.

Overall, the paper reports mixed but generally positive associations between LA use and student learning gains, with an average pre/post effect size of d=0.845 across usable student pairs. Larger gains were associated with more student interaction time with LAs, with the strongest gains at 16-30 minutes per week, and with greater instructor experience using LAs in the course. At the same time, the study finds persistent demographic disparities: male students showed higher gains than female students, and racial differences varied by group. The authors emphasize that these findings are correlational, preliminary, and intended to establish a baseline for future analyses of specific LA practices and contextual variation.

finding.finding_summary: Students in LA-supported undergraduate STEM courses showed substantial pre-to-post gains on discipline concept inventories, with an unconditional mean effect size of d=0.845 across 3,315 usable pre/post pairs. Gains varied by concept inventory, ranging from d=0.052 on the CCI to d=1.248 on CINS and d=1.230 on FMCE, indicating that learning outcomes were generally positive but heterogeneous across subject/instrument and course context.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory scores in undergraduate biology, chemistry, and physics (e.g., FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, GCIICS)
finding.study_size: n=3315 usable pre/post pairs (4,500+ students overall)
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 (grand mean); inventory-specific d ranged from 0.052 to 1.248

finding.finding_summary: Students who spent more time interacting with LAs tended to show larger learning gains, suggesting an engagement-related relationship between LA contact and performance. Effect sizes rose from d=0.369 for 0 min/week to d=0.873 for 16-30 min/week, with the 16-30 min/week group significantly outperforming the 0 min/week group; the 30+ min/week category did not continue the increase, consistent with a possible selection effect among students needing extra help.
finding.measure: Weekly student interaction time with Learning Assistants and associated pre/post concept inventory gain
finding.study_size: n=1,284 in interaction-time categories (280, 299, 318, 184, 203 across bins)
finding.effect_size: d=0.873 for 16-30 min/week vs d=0.369 for 0 min/week; model slope not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Course-level implementation features were associated with better student outcomes, especially instructor experience using LAs. In the continuous models, each additional term an instructor had taught the course with LAs was associated with a +0.154 increase in student effect size (p<0.05), while more faculty meeting time with LAs was also positive though not statistically significant (+0.004 per additional minute/week).
finding.measure: Instructor experience teaching with LAs; faculty meeting/co-planning time with LAs; student-to-LA ratio
finding.effect_size: +0.154 per additional term taught with LAs; +0.004 per additional faculty minute/week with LAs; -0.005 per additional student per LA

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that LA programs may function as platforms for institutional and pedagogical transformation, but the evidence here is preliminary and correlational. The observed positive associations with instructor experience and co-planning support the idea that LA implementation matures over time, yet the paper does not directly test institutional change outcomes and therefore offers indirect evidence only.
finding.measure: Cross-course variation in student effect sizes related to instructor experience with LAs and LA implementation features
finding.effect_size: d=0.154 increase in student effect size per additional term taught with LAs

paper_profiles.title: The impact of learning assistants on inequities in physics student outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Learning Assistants (LAs) are associated with changes in inequities in student learning outcomes in introductory university physics. The authors address a gap in prior discipline-based education research by focusing not only on average gains, but on whether those gains differ for students from dominant versus non-dominant populations.

The study uses pre- and post-test concept inventory data from 2,868 students in 67 classes across 16 LA Alliance institutions. Three concept inventories were analyzed: the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), and Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM). The analysis compares normalized learning gains/effect sizes between demographic groups and uses multiple linear regression to examine associations among student status, assessment used, and classroom features in LA-supported courses.

The main finding is that LA-supported classes were associated with reduced or reversed learning gaps: non-dominant students performed better than dominant peers on the FCI and FMCE, and showed no significant gap on the CSEM. The authors conclude that the presence of LAs is strongly associated with the removal of traditional inequities in introductory physics, though they caution that the study is observational and that effects vary by assessment instrument and classroom context.

finding.finding_summary: Across 2,868 matched pre-post responses from 67 introductory physics classes, Learning Assistant (LA)-supported courses were associated with stronger conceptual learning outcomes for non-dominant students relative to dominant students. The learning gap was significantly negative without LAs and significantly positive with LAs on the overall pooled analysis, with similar reversals on the FCI and FMCE; on the CSEM, no significant learning gap was detected in LA-supported classes.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory scores and Cohen's d learning gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), and Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM)

paper_profiles.title: Student Explanation Strategies in Postsecondary Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines how student explanation strategies are used in postsecondary mathematics and statistics education and how the literature can be organized into coherent categories. The authors reviewed 46 peer-reviewed studies published from 2014 to 2024 and grouped student explanations into three forms: self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others.

The review is not an experiment; it synthesizes prior work to describe patterns, theoretical foundations, and implementation differences. Across the reviewed studies, student explanation strategies were generally associated with improved learning-related outcomes, especially when they promoted retrieval practice, generative learning, and social presence. However, the authors emphasize that effects vary by implementation, duration, context, and prior knowledge, and that peer explanation can introduce tradeoffs such as domination by more knowledgeable students or reinforcement of misconceptions.

The paper focuses on undergraduate and college mathematics, statistics, and related STEM contexts. It notes that self-explanation and explaining to fictitious others tend to support individual cognitive processing, while peer explanation adds collaborative benefits but can also create implementation challenges. The review concludes that these strategies are promising for improving postsecondary learning, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and would benefit from more systematic comparisons across conditions and stronger synthesis of outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across 46 postsecondary studies, student explanation strategies in mathematics and statistics were generally associated with improved learning, conceptual understanding, proof comprehension, and problem-solving. The review highlights that self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others can support mathematics learning, but the magnitude of benefits varies by implementation, duration, and context; no single pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics and statistics learning outcomes, including conceptual learning, proof comprehension, academic achievement, and problem-solving performance
finding.study_size: n=46 studies (reviewed); study-level sample sizes not consistently reported

finding.finding_summary: Peer explanation was linked in the reviewed literature to improved motivation and self-efficacy, and the review also notes findings on engagement and arousal in explanation-based activities. These effects are described as context-dependent and sometimes mixed, especially when peer dynamics reduce participation or when more knowledgeable students dominate discussion.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, engagement, and arousal measures reported in underlying studies

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that explanation strategies support durable learning processes such as metacognition, generative thinking, and collaboration. Self-explanation and explanation to fictitious others are described as fostering individual cognitive processing, while peer explanation adds collaborative learning and dialogue, though these benefits depend on explanation quality and structure.
finding.measure: Metacognition, generative thinking, collaboration, and explanatory quality

paper_profiles.title: Visual Analytics of Student Learning Behaviors on K-12 Mathematics E-learning Platforms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This poster paper addresses the problem of how to make sense of rich student interaction logs from K-12 mathematics e-learning platforms. The authors argue that while online learning systems record grades, login times, mouse trajectories, and other fine-grained behaviors, educators often lack tools for interpreting these data in ways that can improve the design of learning materials and reveal students’ problem-solving strategies.

To address this, the paper proposes a visual analytics system with multiple views, including an overview of performance, a heat map of interaction density, a transition map of mouse-movement sequences, and a correlation analysis view. The system is demonstrated on real log data from a K-12 math e-learning platform and through three case studies. These case studies suggest the tool can help instructors identify potentially miscalibrated question difficulty labels, distinguish different thinking patterns (e.g., additive vs. subtractive strategies), and infer problem-solving steps for questions with unique answers.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not test whether the analytics system improves student learning relative to a baseline instructional condition. Instead, it is primarily a visualization and exploratory analytics contribution aimed at supporting educator interpretation of learning behavior data and informing the design of future learning resources. The authors note future work on performance prediction and more comprehensive analysis of fine-grained problem-solving behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The paper analyzes real log data from K-12 mathematics e-learning activities and reports that the visual analytics system can reveal mismatches between designer-labeled difficulty and observed student performance, as well as distinct problem-solving strategies on math tasks. For example, some questions labeled “easy” had lower mean scores than expected, and the system helped distinguish additive versus subtractive solution patterns and different step sequences for correct versus incorrect answers.
finding.measure: Mean scores on math questions; mouse-movement logs and problem-solving interaction patterns

paper_profiles.title: AI Instructional Agent Improves Student’s Perceived Learner Control and Learning Outcome: Empirical Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an AI instructional agent can improve university students’ perceived learner control and academic performance compared with standard instructional baselines. The authors frame the study around a broader question in AI education: whether AI can do more than automate content delivery and instead function as a pedagogically integrated instructor that supports autonomy, pacing, and interaction.

The intervention was an AI instructional agent embedded in the MAIC platform that delivered lecture content in real time and answered student questions during the lesson. It was compared against two baselines: a traditional human-led in-person lecture and a self-paced MOOC-style video course with chatbot support. The study was conducted with 140 Beijing university undergraduates enrolled in a general education course on artificial intelligence; 125 valid responses were analyzed after exclusions.

Results showed that the AI instructional agent group reported significantly higher perceived learner control than both the human-teacher and MOOC groups. The AI group also completed the learning task more efficiently, interacted with the system more often, and scored higher on the post-test than both comparison groups. Perceived learner control was positively associated with post-test performance in correlation and regression analyses, suggesting that the autonomy supported by the AI system may be one mechanism through which learning improved. The authors conclude that AI instructional agents may enhance learning when they combine structured lecture delivery with real-time, learner-initiated interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught by the AI instructional agent scored significantly higher on the post-test than those taught by the human teacher and those in the MOOC condition. In the main ANOVA, post-test scores differed by group, F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01; Tukey comparisons showed AI-human mean difference = 0.128 (p<.01) and AI-MOOC mean difference = 0.112 (p<.01). The outcome was an immediate content knowledge post-test with 16 multiple-choice items retained after item-response analysis.
finding.measure: Post-test score on 16-item multiple-choice content assessment

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent significantly increased students’ perceived learner control relative to both comparison groups. Group differences were significant, F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001, with AI-human mean difference = 0.732 (p<.001) and AI-MOOC mean difference = 0.416 (p<.05). Perceived learner control was also positively correlated with post-test performance (r=0.23, p<.01), indicating that students who felt more autonomous tended to learn more.
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale (4-item scale; Cronbach’s alpha=0.823)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that perceived learner control and related self-directed behaviors were associated with better performance. PLC was negatively correlated with learning duration (r=-0.30, p<.001), and behavioral engagement was positively correlated with post-test scores (r=0.34, p<.001). In regression, PLC significantly predicted post-test performance (β=0.055, p<.05) after controlling for gender, age, self-regulated learning, and pre-test score, suggesting a relationship with self-management and efficient time use.
finding.measure: Perceived learner control, learning duration, feedback frequency, behavioral engagement, and regression-predicted post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent led students to complete the task more efficiently than the human-teacher condition. Learning duration differed strongly across groups, F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001, with both AI and MOOC groups spending approximately 30 minutes less than the human-teacher group; the AI-human mean difference was -1.860 (p<.001). The AI group also showed substantially higher interaction frequency than both comparison groups, F(2,122)=21.755, p<.001, with AI-human mean difference = 5.410 and AI-MOOC mean difference = 7.015.
finding.measure: Learning duration and feedback/interaction frequency

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students and, importantly, under what conditions those effects are larger or smaller. It also examines whether study design features linked to internal validity and moderators in the MUTOS framework explain heterogeneity in the effects of ITS.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies (77 effect sizes) covering 11 ITS used in elementary, middle, and high school settings in the United States. The included systems varied widely in subject area and support features, including feedback/explanations, hints, worked-out examples, reading materials, and video sequences. The review focused on studies meeting What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations or with reservations, though in the final sample all included studies were experimental and no quasi-experimental study met criteria.

Overall, ITS had a statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes (Hedges’ g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Effects were similar across elementary and middle school and across several student subgroups, but were lower in rural settings and in longer-duration interventions. MetaForest analysis suggested that worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators. The paper concludes that ITS can improve K-12 learning, but implementation details and context matter, and some support types appear more beneficial than others.

finding.finding_summary: Intelligent tutoring systems produced positive reading and writing outcomes in the meta-analysis. Across 55 effect sizes, the pooled effect for reading and writing outcomes was g=0.323 (SE=0.039, 95% CI [0.218, 0.428], p<0.001).
finding.measure: Reading and writing learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: ITS improved mathematics outcomes overall, though the effect was smaller than for reading/writing. Across 22 effect sizes, the pooled effect was g=0.253 (SE=0.007, 95% CI [0.224, 0.281], p<0.001). The paper also reports larger math-related effects for some support features and contexts, with standardized tests yielding g=0.200.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively reviews ITS features that directly support motivation and engagement, and it reports a positive pooled effect for motivation support. Across 23 effect sizes, motivation support had g=0.265 (SE=0.027, 95% CI [0.102, 0.428], p=0.024).
finding.measure: Motivation support within ITS; related learning/engagement-support outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review includes support types and moderation analyses tied to student-directed help-seeking and structured problem solving, especially worked-out examples and hints, which are relevant to metacognition and self-regulation. Worked-out examples showed a positive pooled effect of g=0.324 (SE=0.020, 95% CI [0.176, 0.472], p=0.018), and on-demand hints also showed a positive effect of g=0.316 (SE=0.041, 95% CI [0.085, 0.547], p=0.031).
finding.measure: Worked-out examples and on-demand hints as ITS supports; proxy for metacognitive/self-regulated learning support
finding.study_size: n=59 effect sizes for worked-out examples; n=37 for on-demand hints

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether student-produced videos can function as a formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that traditional tests and questionnaires capture only a narrow slice of understanding, while video production can reveal conceptual misconceptions, reasoning quality, planning processes, and collaborative skills during and after instruction.

The approach was implemented in a Brazilian high school (Colégio Pedro II) with students from grades equivalent to ages 14-17 across three school years. After regular physics instruction, 232 students working in self-selected groups produced 55 short videos on topics such as mechanics, optics, heat, electricity, waves, and sound, plus a short explanatory paper; teachers then reviewed, discussed, and graded the products as a small part of the term grade. The paper reports descriptive analysis of the videos' content and format, including the proportion that were conceptually correct, partially correct, or incorrect, and notes that many videos revealed misunderstandings not visible in formal assessments.

The main conclusion is that video production can serve as a useful and reliable formative assessment in high school physics because it exposes student thinking, supports classroom discussion, and gives teachers feedback in time to adjust instruction. The authors also report a strong correlation between technical video quality and conceptual accuracy, suggesting that planning and production quality were associated with stronger physics explanations. However, the study is descriptive and does not compare learning gains against a control condition, so it provides evidence of feasibility and assessment value rather than causal effects on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Student-produced videos were described as an effective formative assessment for physics understanding because they revealed misconceptions, clarity of explanation, and correctness of scientific content. Across 55 videos from 232 high school students, 35% were fully correct and 45% partially correct; the authors argue that the task helped identify where learning succeeded or failed, but no learning gain versus a baseline was reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy and clarity of physics content in student-produced videos; qualitative review of scientific explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames video production as requiring planning, replanning, collaborative work, and metacognitive reflection. The authors report that students did not simply choose quick productions; many selected more demanding formats, and the technical quality of the video was strongly correlated with the quality of the physics argumentation.
finding.measure: Observed planning/production choices, collaboration, and argument quality in student videos and associated written descriptions

finding.finding_summary: The activity was reported to support student engagement and active participation, with students discussing their videos in class and using age-appropriate, playful language. The authors suggest the format promoted motivation and involvement, but they did not use a formal engagement or motivation scale.
finding.measure: Observed student participation and discussion during video production and classroom presentation

paper_profiles.title: Randomized co-training: from cortical neurons to machine learning and back again
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a biologically plausible learning principle—randomized co-training—can explain how neurons exploit large amounts of unlabeled data to learn from sparse reward signals. The author connects ideas from cortical neuroscience (AMPA/NMDA synapses, spike-timing dependent plasticity, selectivity, and multiview learning) to semi-supervised machine learning algorithms that use two correlated views of the data.

The main technical contribution is a proposed semi-supervised method, Correlated Nystr�f6m Views (XNV), which constructs random feature views using the Nystr�f6m method and then applies a co-regularized regression objective. The paper reports that XNV outperforms a randomized semi-supervised baseline and kernel ridge regression on 18 benchmark datasets, with roughly 11% to 16% lower error than the randomized SSSL variant and about 30% less variance; it is also substantially faster at scale. The neuroscience portion is theoretical and speculative, sketching how a similar mechanism might operate in cortex, but it does not test educational interventions or student learning.

paper_profiles.title: Student-Teacher Curriculum Learning via Reinforcement Learning: Predicting Hospital Inpatient Admission Location
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2020)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting where emergency department patients will be admitted within a hospital, with the goal of improving bed allocation, patient flow, and resource planning. The authors frame the task as a multi-class classification problem for hospital admission location, and use this application as a testbed for a novel training framework rather than as an educational study.

The proposed method is a student-teacher curriculum learning approach in which a teacher network, trained with reinforcement learning, selects training batches for a student network based on the student’s current weights/state. Training data are ordered by a curriculum proxy (Mahalanobis distance for tabular data and cosine similarity for CIFAR-10), and the teacher learns policies that choose which batches to present and how large those batches should be. The paper evaluates the approach on hospital ward-admission data, MIMIC-III mortality prediction, and CIFAR-10, comparing against batch training, fixed curriculum training, prior teacher-student curriculum methods, and state-of-the-art baselines.

Across the reported experiments, the DDPG-based student-teacher method generally outperforms simple batchwise training and fixed curriculum learning on the hospital datasets, and performs competitively on CIFAR-10. The paper also analyzes learned curricula, showing that teachers often use low-entropy-to-high-entropy or entropy-spiking strategies, and reports that policies remain stable under noise and can transfer across tasks to some extent. The main contribution is methodological: demonstrating that a teacher network can learn a curriculum conditioned on a student’s state to improve classification performance, with implications for automated training schedules rather than educational instruction per se.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether the proposed student-teacher curriculum learning method improves prediction performance and training behavior in a hospital operations context. On the Ward Admission dataset (n=14,324), the DDPG student-teacher model achieved 0.62 accuracy (SD=0.02) versus 0.45 (SD=0.01) for batchwise training and 0.48 (SD=0.02) for fixed curriculum training, suggesting better operational prediction for ward allocation. On MIMIC-III mortality prediction (n=8,806), it achieved 0.70 accuracy (SD=0.01) versus 0.63 (SD=0.01) for both batchwise and fixed curriculum baselines.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy for ward admission prediction and mortality prediction

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that improved predictions could help hospitals allocate beds and resources more effectively, reduce emergency department crowding, and reduce patient waiting times. These institutional benefits are inferred from the improved predictive models rather than directly measured as downstream operational outcomes.
finding.measure: Predicted ward allocation usefulness for hospital resource planning

paper_profiles.title: AI-Mediated Feedback Improves Student Revisions: A Randomized Trial with FeedbackWriter in a Large Undergraduate Course
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-mediated formative feedback can improve student writing revisions and learning compared with standard human-only feedback. The authors argue that while LLMs can generate comments at scale, they may be inaccurate or misaligned with instructional goals; their alternative is a human-in-the-loop workflow where teaching assistants receive AI suggestions while authoring feedback, with full control to adopt, edit, or dismiss suggestions.

The intervention is FeedbackWriter, a system that aligns AI suggestions with TA feedback workflows for knowledge-intensive essays. In a randomized trial in a large introductory economics course at a public R1 university, 354 undergraduates and 11 TAs were assigned across two writing assignments so that each section experienced both AI-mediated feedback and a visually matched baseline without AI suggestions. Students wrote an initial draft, received formative feedback, revised, and then completed a post-test on assignment content.

Results show that AI-mediated feedback improved final draft quality relative to human-only feedback, with a reported effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.50. The gain was larger when TAs adopted more AI-suggested constructive feedback. However, the post-test measure of learning did not differ significantly between conditions. The paper also finds that AI-mediated feedback was more actionable and more supportive of independent learning, and that TAs found the system useful for spotting missed issues and clarifying rubrics, though grading time did not decrease.

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated feedback produced significantly higher-quality revised drafts than human-only feedback in a randomized trial with n=354 undergraduates across 1,366 graded essays. The main revision-quality outcome improved by Cohen’s d = 0.50, with the authors describing this as roughly equivalent to moving a student from the 50th to the 70th percentile; the model controlled for first-draft quality, assignment, and random effects for student and TA.
finding.measure: Final draft quality on rubric-based essay revisions

finding.finding_summary: Although better revised drafts were associated with higher learning, the study found no statistically significant difference between AI-mediated feedback and human-only feedback on the post-test. Learning was measured with an optional extra-credit quiz administered after the revision, and the paper reports that condition did not significantly predict post-test scores.
finding.measure: Post-test quiz on knowledge components covered in the writing assignment
finding.study_size: n=262 post-test completers for Assignment 1; n=305 for Assignment 2

finding.finding_summary: The system did not reduce TA grading time, despite providing AI suggestions during feedback authoring. The paper explicitly notes that TAs spent comparable time grading in both conditions, indicating no measurable efficiency gain in workflow duration for this deployment.
finding.measure: Per-essay grading time / elapsed time from first to last action while grading essays

finding.finding_summary: The AI-mediated condition produced feedback with more desirable properties associated with independent learning and actionable revision, compared with human-only feedback. Automated analysis found significantly greater actionability and stronger promotion of independent learning in the AI-mediated condition, suggesting stronger support for self-directed revision processes.
finding.measure: Automated feedback-quality ratings for actionability and promotion of independent learning
finding.study_size: 50 paired feedback samples analyzed qualitatively; full essay feedback corpus in the trial

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.population: Middle School; K-12 students with hearing impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible computer science learning resources for Deaf/Hard of Hearing (D/HH) K-12 students, especially those who use American Sign Language (ASL) as their primary language. The authors argue that captions alone are often insufficient because of language mismatch, inaccurate captions, and low literacy levels among some D/HH learners, creating a need for instruction delivered directly in ASL and designed for visual learners.

The paper presents an early-stage project concept rather than results from an evaluation study. The approach combines ASL video explanations of core computer science concepts with an accessible block-based coding web application and robot programming activities. The design incorporates accessibility features such as captioning, adjustable video speed, sign-language tooltips, visual feedback, and simplified interface design, guided by Deaf web usability heuristics (HE4DWUX).

The target context is middle school and broader K-12 computing education for D/HH students, with attention to both pre-lingual and post-lingual deaf learners. The paper does not report student outcome data; instead, it outlines planned implementation and future research, including an upcoming study to examine the impact of ASL videos on learning CS. Its main conclusion is that ASL-based, multimodal, visually grounded instruction may improve access, engagement, and inclusion for D/HH students, but this claim remains prospective and untested in the paper itself.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical learning outcome was reported in this paper. The article proposes an accessible computer science curriculum and ASL video resources for D/HH K-12 students, but it does not present measured effects on computer science achievement, coding performance, or other academic outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper hypothesizes that ASL-based, visually accessible instruction may increase pre-lingual deaf students' excitement about computer science and their sense of inclusion. However, these are design goals and expectations rather than measured outcomes, so no empirical effect size is available.
finding.measure: sense of inclusion; excitement/motivation toward CS

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the learning gains produced by a classroom model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment vary by student learning style. The authors studied an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory course in which students used simulation-based activities and responded to open-format formative prompts through InkSurvey on pen-enabled mobile devices. They then correlated learning gains on five simulation-based content topics with scores on the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles.

The paper’s main purpose is not to compare the coupled model against a control group, but to test whether the model is especially effective for students with particular learning-style profiles. Learning gains were measured with pre-tests and end-of-semester summative assessments, and the authors report statistically significant gains across all five simulations. Correlations between learning gains and the four learning-style dimensions were near zero and not statistically significant, suggesting no meaningful variation in effectiveness by learning style in this sample.

The study was conducted in two sections of an advanced physics laboratory course for engineering physics juniors at Colorado School of Mines. The context is undergraduate STEM instruction using simulations, scaffolded questioning, and immediate feedback. The authors conclude that the coupled model appears broadly effective across learning styles, though the evidence is limited to a small, non-randomized sample and does not isolate the effect of formative assessment from the simulation-based instructional package.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed large and statistically significant learning gains on five simulation-based science/engineering topics when interactive simulations were coupled with real-time formative assessment. Class average normalized gains were 63% (circuits, n=41), 67% (Fourier, n=41), 60% (diffraction, n=30), 75% (standard deviation mean, n=40), and 61% (least squares, n=33); all paired tests were reported as p < 0.001.
finding.measure: Pre-test to summative assessment learning gains on physics/statistics simulation topics
finding.study_size: n=41 total across two sections; topic-level n ranged from 30 to 41
finding.confidence_interval: Correlation confidence ranges reported for learning-style analyses only; not reported for learning gains
finding.std_deviation: Inter-rater reliability SD=0.12 for assessment scoring; topic-level gain SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Learning gains were not meaningfully related to any of the four learning-style dimensions, indicating no evidence that the coupled model preferentially benefited particular cognitive style profiles. Pearson correlations between gain and ACT-REF, SEN-INT, VIS-VRB, and SEQ-GLO were all near zero (e.g., circuits r=0.02, 0.02, -0.04, -0.12; Fourier r=0.03, -0.004, -0.06, -0.05).
finding.measure: Correlation of learning gains with Index of Learning Styles scores
finding.confidence_interval: Reported 95% confidence ranges for correlations, e.g. circuits ACT-REF -0.28 to 0.32; other dimensions similarly included zero

paper_profiles.title: Optimal designs for active controlled dose finding trials with efficacy-toxicity outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical design problem in clinical dose-finding trials with bivariate outcomes: efficacy and toxicity. The authors derive locally optimal approximate experimental designs for active-controlled trials, where patients receive either multiple doses of a new drug or an active control, under several nonlinear regression models (linear, quadratic, Michaelis-Menten, and Emax combinations). The goal is to reduce the number of doses and allocations that need to be considered while still obtaining efficient estimation of dose-response relationships for both outcomes.

The paper develops general theoretical results that bound the number of support points needed for admissible and optimal designs, using Tchebycheff system arguments and equivalence theorems. It also characterizes minimally supported D-optimal designs and shows that, in some cases, these designs do not depend on the correlation between efficacy and toxicity. For active-controlled trials, the authors show how optimal designs for the new drug can be transformed into optimal designs that include the active control arm.

The paper is methodological rather than an intervention study and is illustrated with numerical examples from pharmaceutical dose-finding, including Emax and quadratic or Michaelis-Menten models. The main conclusion is that efficient active-controlled dose-finding trials with joint efficacy-toxicity outcomes can often be run with a small number of dose levels, but minimally supported designs may be less efficient when the correlation between outcomes is strong. The paper does not study educational populations or formative assessment, so it does not provide evidence relevant to K-12 or postsecondary learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Identifying At-Risk K-12 Students in Multimodal Online Environments: A Machine Learning Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying K-12 students who are at risk of dropping out of online tutoring courses. The authors argue that K-12 online learning differs from MOOC dropout prediction because it involves richer multimodal interactions, paid-service out-of-class activities, and a lower but still important dropout rate; they therefore develop a specialized early warning framework for this setting.

The proposed approach extracts three broad feature sets from a third-party K-12 online education platform: in-class multimodal features from classroom audio/video and transcripts (prosodic, linguistic, and interaction features), out-of-class features from pre-class and post-class service interactions, and time-variant features summarizing lookback-window activity and teacher history. To handle class imbalance and recency effects, the authors create time-aware pseudo-positive examples through data augmentation and train a gradient boosting decision tree model.

The study uses data from 3,922 registered middle and high school students enrolled between August 2018 and February 2019, with 634 dropouts (16.16%) and 338,428 observation-time pairs. Offline experiments show the model outperforms logistic regression, decision trees, and random forests on AUC across multi-step-ahead prediction horizons (e.g., next-day AUC 0.8262; next-two-week AUC 0.7430), and the online deployment reportedly detects more than 70% of dropout students when flagging the top 30% highest-risk students. The strongest feature set comes from out-of-class variables, and the authors conclude that K-12 online dropout prediction depends heavily on service/context factors beyond classroom interaction alone.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central outcome is dropout risk/retention, which is an indicator of persistence rather than academic achievement. In offline testing on 3,922 middle and high school students (634 dropouts), the proposed model improved AUC over baseline classifiers, reaching 0.8262 for next-day prediction and 0.7430 for next-two-week prediction; in production, the system detected more than 70% of dropout students among the top 30% highest-risk cases.
finding.measure: Dropout prediction / retention risk; AUC; online detection rate of dropout students

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed as an operational early warning tool for K-12 online tutoring platforms, aiming to support timely intervention and reduce manual monitoring burden. In a two-month production deployment, ranking students by predicted risk and flagging the top 30% resulted in more than 70% of actual dropout students being detected, suggesting practical utility for platform operations.
finding.measure: Top-30% risk flagging overlap with actual daily dropouts; production deployment detection rate

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a deployed early warning system in a real third-party K-12 online tutoring platform, showing that a machine-learning warning framework can be integrated into live service operations. The reported result that more than 70% of dropouts were detected in production suggests institutional-level benefit for retention monitoring and intervention planning.
finding.measure: Real-world platform deployment performance; detection of dropout students

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Student Expectations and Confidence in Learning Analytics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students perceive the use of learning analytics (LA) in higher education, with a focus on their expectations and confidence about how their data will be used. The authors frame LA as a tool for optimizing learning and retention, but note that its implementation raises important privacy and data protection concerns. The central question is not whether LA improves learning outcomes directly, but how students evaluate the desirability and feasibility of LA features related to data protection, progress feedback, personalized support, and lecturer use of analytics.

To study this, the authors administered an anonymous adapted version of the 12-item Student Expectations of Learning Analytics Questionnaire (SELAQ) to 553 students at a university in Germany across multiple faculties and degree programs, mainly in STEM but also sustainability, architecture, business, and other engineering fields. Responses were analyzed descriptively and then clustered using K-means into four student profiles: Enthusiasts, Realists, Cautious, and Indifferent. A decision tree was then used to make the cluster structure more interpretable and to relate cluster membership to broad rating thresholds and disciplinary differences.

The main findings are that students generally expressed high desire for both data protection and learning analytics features, but expected actual implementation to be lower, especially for lecturer-related support actions. Cluster patterns differed by discipline: Sustainability students were more enthusiastic, Architecture students more skeptical, and Business students more indifferent, while Computer Science and engineering students were split between enthusiasm and realism. The paper concludes that successful adoption of learning analytics in universities depends on transparent communication, strong privacy protections, and tailored implementation strategies by student subgroup and discipline. It does not provide evidence that formative assessment improves student learning outcomes relative to baseline instruction; rather, it studies student attitudes toward analytics-enabled feedback and support.

finding.finding_summary: The study found broad student acceptance of learning analytics in principle, but lower confidence that universities and lecturers will implement it effectively, especially for support-oriented lecturer actions. In a survey of n=553 students, average ratings were high for desired data protection (DP desire=5.91) and learning analytics (LA desire=5.33), but lower for expectations that these would actually occur (DP expectation=5.39; LA expectation=4.51), with the lowest expectation on lecturer obligation to act when students are at risk of failing. The authors interpret this as an institutional implementation challenge rather than an effectiveness effect.
finding.measure: Student expectations and confidence regarding university learning analytics, privacy, and lecturer support practices (SELAQ ratings; cluster analysis)

paper_profiles.title: Student Evaluations of Teaching Fail to Predict Learning: Meta-Analysis of Bias, Grade Inflation, and Incentive Distortion in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: Open Journal of Transformative Education & LifeLong Learning (OJ-TELL)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether end-of-course student evaluations of teaching (SETs) are valid indicators of genuine instructional effectiveness in higher education, especially whether they predict longer-term student learning and external success.
