It also asks whether making SET scores high-stakes in personnel decisions changes instructor behavior in ways that reduce rigor and encourage grade inflation.

The authors synthesize five strands of secondary evidence: a PRISMA-registered meta-analysis of 89 studies (about 5.4 million students), re-analyses of quasi-experimental datasets with random instructor assignment, psychometric audits of SET instruments, text mining of open-ended comments, and linkage of department-level SET averages to alumni and employer outcomes. Across the evidence base, the pooled correlation between SETs and subsequent student performance was near zero and slightly negative after grade controls, with substantial heterogeneity. The paper argues that SETs capture short-term satisfaction more than durable learning, and that high-stakes use of SETs encourages leniency, grade inflation, and curriculum softening.

In addition to questioning validity, the paper highlights equity and measurement concerns. Differential item functioning appeared for some items against female and racially minoritized faculty, and high-SET programs did not show advantages in alumni career readiness or employer satisfaction. The authors conclude that universities should treat SETs as formative feedback rather than as punitive accountability tools, and should use multi-measure systems anchored in stakeholder and learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across 89 studies covering approximately 5.4 million students, the pooled random-effects correlation between SET scores and subsequent academic performance was r = 0.04 (95% CI -0.03, 0.10), and the association became slightly negative after grade controls. The paper concludes that higher SET ratings do not predict better learning outcomes in follow-on courses, standardized exams, or licensure outcomes.
finding.measure: Subsequent course performance, standardized/ licensure exam performance, cumulative GPA, and related post-course academic outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that more engaging, fluent, or charismatic instruction can raise students' perceived learning and satisfaction, but these gains do not correspond to improved objective learning. In text analysis, high-rated courses were often described as 'fun,' 'clear,' or 'not too heavy,' suggesting SETs are more sensitive to short-term enjoyment than to persistence or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Student evaluations, perceived learning, qualitative comments about course enjoyment and difficulty

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds no evidence that higher SETs correspond to better development of durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, or transferable competence. Programs with high SET averages showed no advantage in alumni career readiness, and employer surveys did not favor high-SET programs on competencies like communication, teamwork, professionalism, leadership, or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Alumni career readiness, employer-rated competency outcomes, and program-level stakeholder feedback

finding.finding_summary: When departments tied contract renewal or promotion to SET thresholds, average grades rose by about 0.27 GPA points relative to matched controls, indicating grade inflation rather than improved teaching effectiveness. The paper also reports that 38% of professors in one survey admitted making courses easier in response to student evaluations, including reducing workload and softening feedback standards.
finding.measure: Course GPA, grade distributions, faculty self-reports of leniency and course easing

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that high-stakes SET use distorts institutional decision-making and undermines measurement fairness. Differential item functioning against female and racially minoritized faculty appeared in 9 of 23 common items, and programs that relied heavily on SETs showed no benefit in external stakeholder outcomes, suggesting institutional misuse of the metric creates equity harms and weak governance signals.
finding.measure: Measurement invariance / differential item functioning, policy use of SETs in hiring/promotion/contract renewal, alumni and employer outcome linkages
finding.study_size: n=14 institutional SET instruments; 23 common items; 89 studies in the meta-analysis

paper_profiles.title: Technology-Enhanced Writing Pedagogy for EFL Learners: A Multi-Study Dissertation on Practice, Effectiveness, and Teacher Perceptions
paper_profiles.venue: University of California, Irvine Electronic Theses and Dissertations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines how digital tools shape English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction in Chinese higher education. It addresses a broader problem in the literature: although many tools are used in writing instruction, evidence about their effectiveness, genre-specific benefits, and implementation conditions remains fragmented, especially in EFL university contexts.

The dissertation contains three studies. Study 1 is a classroom experiment with 111 Chinese undergraduates comparing infographic-based prewriting against traditional outlining for summary and opinion writing. Study 2 is a meta-analysis of 17 experimental and quasi-experimental studies (N=1,085) on web-based collaborative writing (WBCW) versus non-technological collaborative writing among EFL college learners. Study 3 is a qualitative interview study of seven Chinese university writing instructors about technology integration since the pandemic and their views on future hybrid and AI-supported instruction.

Across the studies, the dissertation finds that technology is most effective when aligned with genre and task demands and supported by scaffolding, training, and institutional context. Infographic planning improved source-based summary writing and writing self-efficacy but not opinion writing. WBCW showed a moderate positive overall effect on writing quality (Hedges’ g = 0.51), with training emerging as an important moderator. Teacher interviews further suggest that implementation is constrained by access, policy, and concerns about academic integrity, especially around generative AI. The overall conclusion is that technology can improve EFL writing outcomes, but only when pedagogically and institutionally well aligned.

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation directly studies writing outcomes in EFL higher education. In Study 1, infographic-based prewriting improved summary-writing quality relative to outlining (n=111; treatment n=72, control n=39), including better use of source content, integration, and elaboration, but it did not improve opinion writing. In Study 2, web-based collaborative writing also improved writing quality over non-technological collaborative writing across 17 studies (N=1,085; Hedges’ g = 0.51), indicating a moderate positive effect on writing performance.
finding.measure: Writing quality, summary writing quality, opinion writing quality, source use in writing
finding.std_deviation: Study 1 summary writing SDs reported in table; Study 2 not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether pre-existing social relationships among students bias peer assessment in an e-learning course, and whether those biases meaningfully affect the quality of peer grading. The authors focus on a Moodle-based peer assessment workflow in a Master's-level multimedia course, asking two questions: whether relationships affect peer assessment quality and whether students perceive relationship bias in the process.

The intervention/approach is a custom Moodle plugin, PeerForum, that supports peer assessment with relationship-aware reviewer assignment. Students self-reported liked/disliked peers at the start of the semester, completed rubric-based training before assessing, and each post was assigned to five peer graders using a weighted selection process that incorporated nominations while keeping grading single-anonymous. The study analyzed 2681 peer assessments from 64 students (after exclusions), comparing peer grades to professor grades and examining whether like/dislike/neutral relationships changed grading patterns.

Results show that peer assessment was generally reliable and accurate when posts had at least three peer assessments. Average peer grades correlated moderately with professor ratings (Spearman rs=.56 for average peer grades across 588 posts with at least three peer assessments), and inter-rater reliability improved notably with three graders relative to two. Relationship bias was detectable: students who liked the author tended to grade higher, while students who disliked the author tended to grade lower, but these differences were small and had little effect on the final aggregated peer grade in this context. Students also reported generally positive perceptions of peer assessment, including usefulness and fairness, though the study notes limitations such as a small sample, a single Master's course, a 6-point scale, and the unusual fully online pandemic context.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment reduced reliance on instructor grading while remaining usable as a course assessment workflow in a Moodle-based e-learning environment. The paper argues that peer assessment can replace traditional evaluation for this Master's course, and notes that peer assessment was scalable enough to support 863 posts with peer review, though it required rubric training and at least three peer assessments for acceptable reliability.
finding.measure: Peer assessment workflow feasibility and scalability; professor grading workload reduction (qualitative course implementation evidence)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported improved perceptions of peer assessment usefulness and fairness over the semester, and many indicated that assessing peers helped them complete the course skills and stay engaged. On the end-of-course questionnaire (53 students analyzed), 54.7% agreed peer assessment was helpful after the course versus 43.4% before, and 52.8% agreed it was fair after the course versus 24.5% who disagreed that it was fair before.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of usefulness, fairness, difficulty, and engagement on Likert-scale questionnaire
finding.study_size: n=53 questionnaire respondents who had peer-graded
finding.std_deviation: Cronbach's alpha=0.958 for the questionnaire scale

finding.finding_summary: The peer assessment process was associated with learning-oriented behaviors such as giving feedback, reflecting on criteria, and improving submissions, but these were measured mainly through self-report rather than direct skill assessment. Students reported that peer grading helped them learn what teachers expected, improve their work, and provide useful feedback to colleagues; several open-ended responses highlighted collaboration and engagement benefits.
finding.measure: Self-reported learning, feedback quality, and perceived help for completing skills
finding.study_size: n=53 questionnaire respondents; qualitative comments from open-text responses

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment grades were reasonably aligned with instructor grades, indicating that students could evaluate the multimedia-content tasks similarly to faculty when three or more peer assessments were aggregated. Across 588 posts with at least three peer assessments, the Spearman correlation between professor ratings and final peer grades was rs=.49 (p<.001) and rs=.56 (p<.001) when using the average peer grade without rounding; the authors also report that students' grades were slightly higher on average than professors' (mean 3.58 vs 3.16).
finding.measure: Professor rating vs final peer grade / average peer grade on 6-point scale for multimedia content production skills
finding.std_deviation: Professor rating SD=.92; final peer grade SD=.61; average peer grades SD=.57

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that peer assessment can be implemented institutionally as a replacement for traditional evaluation in a higher-education e-learning course, but only under certain conditions: at least three peer assessments, rubric training, and careful reviewer assignment to balance relationship bias. The authors also caution that the approach may not generalize to high-stakes assessment or to other contexts without similar course structure and student familiarity.
finding.measure: Institutional feasibility of replacing traditional evaluation with peer assessment under a Moodle plugin and relationship-aware reviewer assignment
finding.study_size: n=64 students; one Master's course; one semester

paper_profiles.title: Higher education assessment practice in the era of generative AI tools
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard/Gemini perform when used to answer assessment tasks in higher education. The authors are motivated by concerns that GenAI may undermine authentic assessment, academic integrity, and student learning, while also acknowledging that these tools might support teaching and learning if used carefully.

The study uses three case-study assessment instruments drawn from data science, data analytics, and construction management at the master’s degree level. The authors asked ChatGPT-4 and Bard to complete the assessments, then graded and moderated the outputs using criterion-referenced assessment and a standard A–G scale. The assessments were designed to probe subject knowledge, problem-solving, analysis, critical thinking, and presentation. The paper reports that both tools produced coherent and often strong responses in data science/data analytics, but performed less well on the more project-specific construction management task, suggesting discipline-dependent variation.

The main conclusion is that GenAI tools can generate content that appears to demonstrate several high-level skills, but this may mask weaknesses and can limit student learning if used unethically. The authors argue that assessment design should be redesigned to account for AI capabilities, and they recommend contextualized authentic assessment, reflective tasks, presentations, and formative uses of GenAI such as question banks and comparison exercises. The paper is primarily an exploratory assessment of AI-generated work rather than a study of student learning outcomes from an instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Across three master’s-level assessment case studies, ChatGPT-4 and Bard/Gemini were judged to exhibit subject knowledge, problem-solving, analytical skills, critical thinking, and presentation skills in two of the three tasks. Performance was stronger in data analytics/data science than in construction management, indicating discipline-dependent variation and limits in complex thinking for project-based work. No standardized effect sizes were reported; findings were based on qualitative grading of AI-generated solutions by authors and subject-area tutors.
finding.measure: Criterion-referenced grading of AI-generated assessment solutions for comprehension, analysis, accuracy, discussion, and presentation
finding.study_size: n=3 assessment case studies; 2 GenAI tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can streamline parts of teaching and learning by generating assessment responses, examples, and questions, and by supporting rapid critique and comparison activities. However, it also emphasizes tradeoffs: unregulated use may reduce learning, increase cheating risk, and require instructors to redesign assessments and add supervision. No quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Observed capability of GenAI tools to produce assessment solutions and support formative classroom activities

finding.finding_summary: The authors recommend institutional changes including redesigning assessments, integrating AI-content detectors with plagiarism tools, training tutors, and revising curricula and policy to reflect GenAI capabilities. They also note that AI detector tools remain unreliable and that discipline-specific differences complicate general policy. The study provides no effect sizes because it is an exploratory assessment-practice paper, not an outcomes trial.
finding.measure: Assessment-policy and assessment-design implications derived from case-study analysis

paper_profiles.title: Student Explanation Strategies in Postsecondary Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines research on student explanation strategies in postsecondary mathematics and statistics education. The authors synthesize 46 peer-reviewed articles published from 2014 to 2024 and organize the literature into three categories: self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others. The review is focused on how these explanation strategies are implemented, what theoretical mechanisms may explain their effects, and what patterns emerge across contexts, durations, and learner prior knowledge.

Across the reviewed studies, the paper concludes that self-explanation and explaining to fictitious others generally support individual generative learning processes, while peer explanation can add collaborative benefits but also introduces tradeoffs such as dominance by more knowledgeable students, propagation of misconceptions, and variable explanation quality. The review emphasizes that outcomes vary by implementation details, timing, and context, and that peer explanation may help bridge differences in prior knowledge when well structured. Because this is a scoping review rather than a quantitative meta-analysis, it does not report pooled effect sizes; instead it summarizes the range of findings and limitations in the literature.

The paper is situated entirely in undergraduate and postsecondary mathematics/statistics/STEM settings, including self-explanation tasks, peer-led or peer-instruction formats, and explaining to imagined or fictitious others via written, oral, or video modalities. It highlights that student explanation is linked to learning outcomes, conceptual understanding, problem solving, motivation, self-efficacy, and anxiety, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and the authors call for more systematic synthesis to compare the relative impact of these approaches.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes 46 postsecondary studies and finds that student explanation strategies are often associated with improved mathematics learning, conceptual understanding, proof comprehension, and problem-solving performance, but results vary by implementation, duration, and context. The paper reports no pooled effect size; instead it notes that self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others can support learning, with peer explanation sometimes producing negative tradeoffs when misconceptions or dominance dynamics emerge.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes, proof comprehension, problem-solving performance, academic achievement in mathematics/statistics

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies examined motivation, self-efficacy, anxiety, and related affective outcomes in postsecondary mathematics/STEM settings. The review concludes that peer explanation and peer-led learning can increase motivation and self-efficacy, though some studies also report negative affect in certain peer-tutoring contexts; the review itself does not pool effect sizes.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, anxiety, affective engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights durable-skill outcomes such as metacognition, generative thinking, collaboration, and explanation quality as central mechanisms and targets of the literature. Across the reviewed studies, student explanation is described as fostering cognitive processing, organization, integration, and collaborative discussion, although peer settings can also reduce quality when stronger students dominate or when misconceptions spread.
finding.measure: Metacognition, collaboration, generative thinking, explanation quality

paper_profiles.title: Assessment Formats and Student Learning Performance: What is the Relation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether different assessment formats are associated with differences in student learning performance in an undergraduate computer networking course. The authors argue that prior work on assessment and learning often lacks demographic comparisons, sufficient sample size, and comparable course structures, and they attempt to address these issues by analyzing student outcomes across multiple sections of the same course.

The study was conducted in four sections of IT 341 at George Mason University: three face-to-face sections and one distance-learning section, all taught in Fall 2016. Students completed similar home/lab assignments and shared comparable course content, but the final exam formats differed by section (essay-only, MCQ+essay, MCQ+essay+fill-in-the-blank+numerical problem, and MCQ-only). Using LMS data and Pearson correlations, the authors compared assessment components with final course grades and concluded that mixed assessment formats were associated with better performance than single-format exams, while essay-only finals corresponded to the lowest section performance.

The paper’s main claim is that combining multiple assessment question types may better allow students to demonstrate knowledge and is linked to higher final grades in this setting. The analysis is correlational rather than causal, and the authors note that students tended to prefer objective questions and combined assessment techniques. The work is limited to one undergraduate IT course at a single institution, so its findings are suggestive rather than definitive evidence that formative assessment improves learning outcomes relative to standard instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In an undergraduate computer networking course (n=115 across four sections), sections with mixed final-exam formats had higher course grades than the section using essay-only finals. The section with the most varied format (MCQ, essay, fill-in-the-blank, and numerical problem) had the highest median final exam score and overall course performance, while the essay-only section had the lowest performance.
finding.measure: Final exam score and overall course grade

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret higher performance with mixed assessment formats as evidence that students were better able to demonstrate knowledge through multiple question types, including problem solving and objective items. Correlation analysis showed the strongest association between essay questions and final exam score (r=0.920, p=2.2e-16), but the paper does not estimate a causal effect on critical thinking or metacognition.
finding.measure: Correlation between question-type scores and final exam score
finding.effect_size: r=0.920 for essays vs final score; r=0.869 MCQs; r=0.830 fill-in-the-blank; r=0.430 numerical problem

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concept of formative assessment and argues for its use in higher education, with particular attention to implementing it through the Blackboard e-learning system. The authors motivate the study by describing formative assessment as a way to provide ongoing feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment and citing prior literature and meta-analyses that suggest benefits for learning, motivation, and classroom climate.

The paper proposes weekly or fortnightly online tests in Blackboard, including multiple-choice and other item types, with immediate detailed feedback to students. It then reports a student survey conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported frequent low-stakes assessments and immediate feedback, and responses varied somewhat by stream (Business, Engineering, IT), with Engineering students more strongly favoring the approach.

The study’s evidence is primarily perception-based rather than outcome-based: students believed the approach would help them learn topics progressively, stay engaged throughout the semester, and improve performance on end-of-semester exams. The authors conclude that formative assessment, especially when supported by e-learning tools and timely feedback, may improve learning and summative grades, but they also note tradeoffs such as stress from too many tests and the need to balance learning with grading pressures.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments with immediate feedback helped them stay in touch with the subject, check their strengths and weaknesses, and feel more confident about whether they were on track. However, some students also reported stress/pressure from too many tests, so the perceived effect was positive overall but with notable tradeoffs.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of continuous assessment, need for teacher feedback, and attitudes toward Blackboard online tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognition and self-monitoring as intended benefits of formative assessment, and students reported that the frequent assessments and feedback would help them understand mistakes, reflect on performance, and track their learning progress. This is a perceived rather than directly measured effect.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of feedback usefulness for self-checking, reflection, and progressive topic learning

finding.finding_summary: Students generally believed the Blackboard-based formative assessments would improve learning across course topics and help them perform better on the summative semester examination. The paper does not report achievement gains from a controlled comparison; instead it reports favorable perceptions of small-topic assessments, immediate feedback, and preparation for end-of-semester tests.
finding.measure: Student survey and open-ended responses about learning progress and perceived preparation for semester examination

paper_profiles.title: Visual Analytics of Student Learning Behaviors on K-12 Mathematics E-learning Platforms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This poster presents a visual analytics system for examining detailed student learning logs from a K-12 mathematics e-learning platform. The authors argue that while online systems collect rich behavioral data such as grades, login time, and mouse trajectories, educators need better tools to interpret these data and use them to improve learning materials and instruction.

The proposed system combines overview dashboards, heat maps, transition maps, and correlation analysis to reveal how students interact with math questions and where they struggle. The paper reports three case studies on real platform log data showing that the system can help identify potentially miscalibrated item difficulty labels, uncover different problem-solving/thinking patterns, and reveal step-by-step solution processes for students with correct versus incorrect answers.

The work is primarily a descriptive visualization and learning analytics paper rather than an intervention study. It does not test whether formative assessment improves student outcomes relative to standard instruction; instead, it suggests that the analytics could support educators in revising learning resources and better understanding student behavior. The main conclusion is that fine-grained interaction logs can be useful for diagnosing problem design issues and interpreting student problem-solving styles on K-12 mathematics platforms.

finding.finding_summary: The system was applied to real K-12 mathematics platform logs to analyze student performance on question sets. In one case study, some questions labeled “easy” by the designer had lower mean scores than expected, suggesting miscalibrated difficulty labels; in another, the system differentiated correct vs incorrect problem-solving paths. No causal effect on learning was tested, but the analysis showed that log data can reveal item difficulty and solution behavior patterns.
finding.measure: Mean scores on math questions; correctness/full marks; problem-solving interaction logs

finding.finding_summary: The visual analytics tool was intended to help instructors quickly identify flaws in learning material design, including which question difficulty levels should be revised. The paper reports that the system can facilitate rapid interpretation of student behaviors and guide optimization of teaching materials, indicating potential efficiency gains for educators rather than direct learner performance gains.
finding.measure: Instructor interpretation of question difficulty and problem-solving logs; design feedback utility

paper_profiles.title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports initial findings from the Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study, a multi-institution effort examining how features of courses, instructors, and students relate to learning in undergraduate STEM classes using Learning Assistants (LAs). The authors frame the study as part of a broader effort to identify context-specific best practices for LA programs and to understand which aspects of LA use are associated with stronger student learning outcomes.

The study uses pre/post concept inventories administered in LA-supported courses across 13 institutions, with over 4,500 participating students and 17 instructors in the pilot semester. Disciplines included physics, biology, and chemistry, and the analysis focused on student-level change scores (Cohen's d) modeled with hierarchical linear models that nested students within courses. The paper examines associations between outcomes and student demographics, time spent interacting with LAs, student-to-LA ratios, faculty meeting time with LAs, and instructor experience teaching the course with LAs.

Overall, the findings are mixed. Students on average showed positive pre-to-post gains, and stronger gains were associated with more interaction with LAs up to 16-30 minutes per week, lower student-to-LA ratios, more faculty co-planning time with LAs, and more prior instructor experience teaching with LAs. However, the paper also reports gender and racial differences in effect sizes, indicating inequities in outcomes across student groups. Because the design is correlational and the authors emphasize that the first semester of a multi-year study is preliminary, the results are best interpreted as descriptive associations rather than causal evidence that LAs themselves produced the gains.

finding.finding_summary: Across 3,315 usable pre-post pairs, students' average effect size on concept inventories was 0.845 standard deviations. Effects varied by discipline/instrument, with physics inventories showing the largest average gains (FMCE d=1.230, n=5; BEMA d=1.130, n=5) and chemistry inventories the smallest (CCI d=0.052, n=2).
finding.measure: Pre/post science concept inventory scores (FMCE, BEMA, IMCA, GCIICS, GCA, CINS, CCI) analyzed as Cohen's d
finding.study_size: n=3,315 usable pre-post pairs (17 courses, 13 institutions)
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 overall; by inventory ranged from d=0.052 to d=1.248

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure motivation or engagement with a validated survey, but it does analyze students' time spent interacting with LAs as an engagement-related implementation variable. Students who spent 16-30 minutes/week with LAs had the highest average effect size (d=0.873), while those reporting 0 minutes/week had lower gains (d=0.369); students spending 30+ minutes/week did not outperform the 0-minute group.
finding.measure: Self-reported weekly time interacting with Learning Assistants
finding.study_size: n=1,284 in the interaction-time model (category totals reported: 0 min n=280; 1-5 min n=299; 6-15 min n=318; 16-30 min n=184; 30+ min n=203)

finding.finding_summary: Instructor-side implementation features were associated with stronger student outcomes. Students in courses where faculty had taught the course with LAs more often showed higher gains, with each additional term of prior LA-supported teaching associated with a 0.154 increase in effect size (p<0.05). More faculty meeting time with LAs was also positively associated with gains (+0.004 per additional minute/week), although this estimate was not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Student pre/post concept inventory effect sizes predicted by faculty LA experience and faculty meeting time with LAs
finding.study_size: n=17 courses for continuous course-level models
finding.effect_size: 0.154 per additional prior term taught with LAs; 0.004 per additional faculty meeting minute/week

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests institutional and classroom implementation conditions matter for LA-supported outcomes across sites. Lower student-to-LA ratios were associated with higher gains (effect size slope -0.005 per additional student per LA), and the authors argue that LA programs may function as platforms for sustaining faculty and institutional transformation over time.
finding.measure: Student pre/post concept inventory effect sizes modeled against course-level student-to-LA ratio and instructor LA experience
finding.study_size: n=17 courses for continuous course-level models

paper_profiles.title: The impact of learning assistants on inequities in physics student outcomes
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Physics Education Research Conference (PERC 2016)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Learning Assistants (LAs) are associated with changes in inequities in introductory university physics learning outcomes. The authors focus on the longstanding achievement gaps between dominant and non-dominant student populations and ask whether LA-supported instruction is linked to different pre-to-post learning gains on physics concept inventories.

The study uses paired pre/post concept inventory data from 2,868 students in 67 introductory physics classes across 16 institutions in the LA Alliance. Outcomes were measured with the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), and Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM), and analyzed using Cohen’s d and regression models. The paper reports that LA-supported classes were associated with reduced or reversed learning gaps: non-dominant students outperformed dominant students on the FCI and FMCE and showed no significant gap on the CSEM. The authors also found that outcomes varied by assessment instrument, indicating heterogeneity across course contexts and measures.

finding.finding_summary: Across 2,868 paired pre/post responses from 67 introductory physics classes, Learning Assistant-supported courses were associated with improved learning outcomes for non-dominant students relative to dominant students. The overall learning gap was significantly negative without LAs (dominant students outperformed non-dominant students; t597.6=3.67, p<0.005) and significantly positive with LAs (non-dominant students outperformed dominant students; t2068.2=-2.63, p<0.025), indicating a reversal of inequity in concept-inventory learning gains.
finding.measure: Pre/post physics concept inventory scores and Cohen's d learning gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), and Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that course-level implementation features, especially the presence of Learning Assistants and differences among assessment instruments, are associated with institutional variation in student inequities. In regression models restricted to LA-supported courses, non-dominant status predicted higher mean effect sizes by 0.262, and the FMCE was associated with effect sizes 0.200 lower than the FCI, suggesting that institutional/classroom structures and assessment choice shape observed outcomes.
finding.measure: Regression model of student effect size as a function of dominance status and concept inventory in LA-supported classes

paper_profiles.title: Research on Education Big Data for Student’s Academic Performance Analysis based on Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educational big data and machine learning can be used to analyze and predict student academic performance. The authors frame the problem as one of helping schools identify students at risk of poor outcomes, dropout, or academic difficulty by leveraging large-scale behavioral and administrative data generated through learning platforms and campus systems.

The study proposes an LSTM-based model for student performance prediction using the EdNet-KT1 dataset, which contains large-scale online learning interaction records. The paper describes preprocessing, model specification, dynamic adjustment, and cross-validation, and it compares the proposed deep learning approach with other prediction methods such as KNN, DTW, and regression-based approaches discussed in related work. The experimental results are presented primarily in terms of predictive accuracy, F1 score, and cross-validation stability rather than causal effects on learning.

Overall, the paper concludes that the LSTM-based approach can more accurately predict student performance than simpler or baseline methods, supporting the use of big data and machine learning for personalized education and early intervention. However, it does not evaluate a formative assessment intervention against standard instruction, nor does it report direct learning gains attributable to a teaching practice. Its contribution is therefore predictive and descriptive rather than causal or intervention-focused.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed LSTM-based model predicted student academic performance more accurately than comparison methods in the paper's experimental analysis. The authors report higher accuracy and F1 scores for their approach, and note that K-fold cross-validation showed better stability and reliability, but no causal improvement in actual learning outcomes was tested.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score on student performance prediction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that educational big data and machine learning can improve the efficiency of identifying at-risk students and supporting early intervention. This is presented as a decision-support and monitoring use case, with the model intended to help educators manage large-scale student data more effectively.
finding.measure: Model-based student performance prediction for early identification and decision support

paper_profiles.title: On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies contrastive learning from a theoretical perspective, asking how the cosine similarities of learned embeddings behave under different contrastive loss formulations and training regimes. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention, it analyzes the geometry of representations produced by contrastive models, focusing on the similarities of positive pairs and negative pairs in full-batch versus mini-batch optimization.

The paper develops a unified framework covering common losses such as InfoNCE, SimCLR, DCL, DHEL, SigLIP, and spectral contrastive loss. The authors prove that in full-batch settings, optimal embeddings fully align positive pairs and separate negative pairs to a uniform cosine similarity of -1/(n-1), but some loss forms can over-separate negatives and prevent perfect positive alignment. In mini-batch settings, they show that smaller batch sizes increase the variance of negative-pair similarities, which may degrade representation quality. They propose an auxiliary variance-reduction loss that encourages negative similarities to stay near the full-batch optimum, and their experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show reduced variance and improved downstream classification accuracy, especially for smaller batch sizes.

The empirical section is limited to computer vision pretraining and linear/evaluation-style classification experiments, not educational populations or formative assessment contexts. The paper's conclusions are about representation learning optimization and batch-size tradeoffs, with performance gains from the auxiliary loss but no direct evidence about student learning outcomes or instructional interventions.

paper_profiles.title: Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the peer-grading literature to understand how different peer-assessment designs affect grading accuracy, fairness, learning, and scalability. The authors frame peer grading as an increasingly important response to large classes and online courses, where instructor-only grading is difficult to sustain, and they ask how peer-grading systems can minimize staff effort while maximizing learning gains for students.

Using PRISMA procedures, the review synthesizes 122 peer-reviewed studies published between 1981 and 2024. The paper develops a taxonomy with two main dimensions: evaluation approach (summative rating, ranking, categorization, and formative feedback) and reviewer weighting strategy (calibration, back-evaluation, consensus, reputation, and related hybrids). Across the literature, the authors conclude that no single peer-grading strategy is universally optimal: numeric ratings are often noisy and biased, ranking can reduce cognitive load and improve reliability, formative feedback supports learning and fairness but is harder to evaluate at scale, and weighting methods such as calibration, consensus, reputation, and back-evaluation can improve accuracy under different conditions.

The review is primarily situated in postsecondary and online learning contexts, especially MOOCs, computer science, engineering, pharmacy, and writing-related courses. Its main contribution is conceptual and synthesis-based rather than estimating an overall causal effect of peer grading on student outcomes. The authors emphasize trade-offs among accuracy, fairness, transparency, scalability, and student workload, and recommend hybrid, staged systems that combine calibration, accountability mechanisms, consensus filtering, and reputation when historical data are available.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, peer grading is presented as a scalable alternative to instructor-only grading, especially in large and online courses. The review synthesizes evidence that systems using ranking, consensus weighting, calibration, and reputation can reduce instructor workload and make grading manageable at scale, though some approaches require initial setup or instructor-graded calibration items.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, scalability of grading systems, need for manual calibration or intervention

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that peer grading and especially formative feedback can increase student engagement, motivation, and perceived accountability. Reported studies suggest that being aware reviews will be evaluated, receiving peer-score transparency, and giving feedback can motivate students to write more useful reviews and participate more seriously in the assessment process.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, attitudes toward reviewing, perceived accountability

finding.finding_summary: Peer grading is repeatedly linked to gains in critical thinking, reasoning, and metacognitive judgment, especially when students compare work, justify scores, or provide formative comments. The review highlights studies showing that ranking and pairwise comparison can foster deeper critical engagement, and that calibration/training can improve graders’ evaluation skills over time.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, evaluation skill, metacognitive judgment, writing of justifications and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies in writing, essay, and clinical writing contexts suggest that formative peer feedback can improve writing-related learning and the quality of submissions. The review notes that actionable comments and justifications can support authors’ revision and that peer assessment can also improve graders’ own writing skills, although detailed writing feedback is more demanding than numeric scoring.
finding.measure: Writing skill, essay quality, quality of written submissions, peer commentary quality

paper_profiles.title: Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic literature review of educational recommender systems (ERS), asking how such systems measure and optimize learning, what target metrics they use, what evaluation methods they employ, and whether they implement outcome-based assessment. The authors frame the central issue as a mismatch between standard recommender-system metrics such as user ratings or relevance and the pedagogical goal of improving learning outcomes.

The review screened 1,395 papers from IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and SpringerLink and retained 28 journal papers for detailed analysis. The reviewed systems span formal education, informal learning, and lifelong learning, with the largest share in higher education and the main end-user being learners; most systems recommend resources, exercises, or feedback using knowledge-based, collaborative-filtering, machine-learning, or hybrid methods.

The main conclusion is that most ERS still optimize relevance or other user-centric proxies, while only 12 of 28 papers explicitly optimize learning-centered metrics such as academic performance or probability of learning. Outcome-based assessment is used in only about a third of the papers, and it is most feasible in formal university or professional-training contexts where outcomes and assessments already exist. The authors argue that the field lacks comprehensive evaluation criteria that prioritize learning, and they highlight the need for better outcome-based assessment methods, especially for informal learning settings.

finding.finding_summary: This review does not test an intervention directly; it synthesizes 28 ERS papers and finds that only 12/28 papers optimized learning-centered metrics such as academic performance or probability of learning, while many more optimized relevance or user rating. For the subset that did use academic-performance-oriented evaluation, the papers typically relied on formal course assessment in higher education or controlled experiments, but the review reports no pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Academic performance / formal course assessment
finding.study_size: n=28 studies reviewed; learning-centered metrics in 12/28

paper_profiles.title: Randomized co-training: from cortical neurons to machine learning and back again
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how neural systems might use large amounts of unlabeled data to speed learning from sparse reward signals, and how that insight can be translated into machine learning. The author proposes randomized co-training as a biologically plausible meta-algorithm for semi-supervised learning, motivated by cortical anatomy and synaptic dynamics, and argues that randomizing feature views can make co-training broadly applicable even when natural multi-view structure is absent.

The paper develops a theoretical link from discretized neuronal models and spike-timing dependent plasticity to selective linear regression and then to a two-view co-training/co-regularization formulation. It then introduces Correlated Nystr�m Views (XNV), a semi-supervised learning algorithm that uses random Nystr�m features, canonical correlation analysis, and unlabeled data. The empirical evidence reported is on 18 machine-learning benchmark datasets, where XNV is said to outperform a randomized semi-supervised baseline and kernel ridge regression while running much faster, but this is not an education study.

Because the paper is about machine learning and computational neuroscience rather than learners or instructional practice, it does not provide evidence about formative assessment or student learning outcomes in K-12 or postsecondary education. Its main contribution is methodological: showing how randomized co-training can improve semi-supervised learning efficiency and error rates in benchmark tasks, with a discussion of possible cortical analogues.

paper_profiles.title: Emotion in Reinforcement Learning Agents and Robots: A Survey
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (non-human AI/robot agents; no K-12 or postsecondary participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of computational models of emotion in reinforcement learning (RL) agents and robots. Its main purpose is to organize a fragmented literature that spans machine learning, affective computing, and human-robot interaction, and to propose a taxonomy for how emotions are elicited, what kinds of emotions are represented, and how emotions function within RL systems.

The survey reviews 52 papers and groups them into four emotion-elicitation families: homeostasis/extrinsic motivation, appraisal/intrinsic motivation, reward- or value-based elicitation, and hard-wired sensory mappings. It also compares categorical versus dimensional emotion representations and outlines how emotions can affect reward, state, learning (adaptive critic), and action selection. The paper is conceptual and synthetic rather than an intervention study; it does not evaluate educational outcomes or human learning.

The authors conclude that emotion modeling in RL can sometimes improve agent learning efficiency, support social interaction, and provide a testbed for affective theories, but they emphasize major heterogeneity in definitions, implementation choices, and evaluation criteria. They also note that many papers leave the mapping from computational variables to emotions underspecified, limiting reproducibility and cross-paper comparison. Overall, the work is a field survey and design guide for engineers, not evidence about formative assessment or student achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Peer Grading: A Systematic Literature Review of Reviewer Assignment Strategies and Quantity of Reviewers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how peer grading systems should assign reviewers and how many reviewers per submission are needed to optimize accuracy, fairness, and educational value. The authors conduct a systematic literature review of 87 studies published from 2010 to 2024, covering peer grading in traditional classrooms and MOOCs. The review focuses on reviewer-assignment strategies (random, competency-based, social-network-based, and bidding-based) and on review quantity.

The central finding is that random assignment is the most common approach but often creates fairness and accuracy problems, especially when reviewer quality varies widely. Competency-based assignment appears more promising for improving fairness and grading reliability, though direct comparative evidence remains limited. Social-network and bidding approaches are discussed as conceptually promising but under-studied.

Across studies, the review finds that three to five reviews per submission is the most common and often the most practical range, balancing grading accuracy, student workload, and learning/engagement. Accuracy generally improves as the number of reviewers increases, but gains diminish after roughly 5–6 reviewers. The paper concludes that peer assessment can support learning and efficiency, but optimal design depends on implementation trade-offs, and more rigorous empirical comparisons are needed, especially for hybrid or socially informed assignment strategies.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review finds that peer grading can reduce instructor grading burden and that reviewer-allocation design affects throughput, reliability, and student workload. Across the reviewed literature, three to five reviews per submission is presented as a practical balance between grading accuracy and efficiency, while requiring more than five reviews often increases student burden and can reduce participation.
finding.measure: Reviewer workload, grading efficiency, review completion rates, and perceived workload

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that peer assessment can improve student engagement and perceived educational value, but these benefits depend on how reviews are assigned and how many are required. More than five reviews per student can lead to disengagement or rushed, low-effort grading, whereas three to five reviews is repeatedly described as a workload-engagement balance that supports sustained participation.
finding.measure: Student engagement, attitudes toward peer review, and participation in reviewing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer grading can help students understand assignment expectations and alternative solutions, which supports learning through exposure to multiple perspectives. Competency-based reviewer assignment is described as especially helpful because it can provide complementary feedback from diverse reviewers, supporting metacognitive and collaborative learning benefits, although the evidence base is heterogeneous and often indirect.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, understanding of requirements, and quality/diversity of feedback perspectives

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that peer grading is educationally valuable across the reviewed higher-education and MOOC settings, with learning benefits linked to receiving and producing feedback. It cites multiple studies showing improved alignment with expert grading and suggests that diverse reviewer assignment can enrich the feedback students receive, though the paper is a synthesis rather than a primary effect study.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes from peer assessment and alignment with expert grading

paper_profiles.title: Alpha MAML: Adaptive Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning
paper_profiles.venue: 6th ICML Workshop on Automated Machine Learning
paper_profiles.population: Not education / machine learning research population (few-shot image recognition tasks on Omniglot)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine learning optimization problem rather than an education problem. The authors focus on Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), a method designed to learn an initialization that can adapt quickly to new tasks, and they identify a practical limitation: MAML is sensitive to learning-rate hyperparameters and often requires extensive tuning for stable training.

To address this, the paper proposes Alpha MAML, an extension that adapts both the inner learning rate (α) and the meta-learning rate (β) online using hypergradient descent. The method is evaluated on few-shot image classification using the Omniglot dataset, with experiments comparing convergence and training stability under tuned and untuned initial hyperparameters. The main conclusion is that Alpha MAML reduces sensitivity to hyperparameter choice, improves training stability, and often converges faster than standard MAML, especially when initial hyperparameters are poorly chosen.

The study is entirely in a computer vision/meta-learning context and does not investigate student learning, formative assessment, schooling, or postsecondary education. As a result, it does not provide evidence relevant to the educational effectiveness of formative assessment relative to standard instruction or other baseline conditions.

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines how instructional support can facilitate diagnostic competences in higher education, focusing on medical education and teacher education. The authors synthesize 35 empirical studies and ask whether problem-solving, examples, prompts, role assignment, and reflection improve learners’ ability to identify problems, analyze evidence, draw conclusions, and make diagnostic decisions.

A central aim is to determine whether effects differ by learners’ prior professional knowledge and by diagnostic context. The review distinguishes low- versus high-knowledge learners and compares scaffolding types ranging from more guided supports (e.g., worked examples, prompts, roles) to more self-regulated supports (e.g., reflection phases). It also codes context features such as document-based versus interaction-based diagnosis and individual versus collaborative processing.

Across studies, instructional support had a moderate positive overall effect on diagnostic competences (g = .39, 95% CI [.22, .56], n = 3472, k = 35). Effects were larger for learners with low prior knowledge (g = .48) than for those with high prior knowledge (g = .27), and the authors conclude that scaffolding should be matched to learners’ knowledge base and the diagnostic task context. The evidence suggests that guided problem-solving and appropriate scaffolding can improve diagnostic reasoning in postsecondary medical and teacher education, but the usefulness of specific supports varies by learner expertise and implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 35 empirical studies (n=3472), instructional support had a moderate positive effect on diagnostic competences, a set of skills including problem identification, hypothesis generation, evidence evaluation, and drawing conclusions. The random-effects meta-analysis yielded g = .39 with a 95% CI [.22, .56], indicating that scaffolding and guided problem-solving improved learners’ diagnostic reasoning overall.
finding.measure: Diagnostic competences / diagnostic quality / epistemic-diagnostic activities (e.g., identifying problems, questioning, generating hypotheses, evaluating evidence, drawing conclusions)

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis specifically focuses on diagnostic competences in medical and teacher education, which the authors frame as professional higher-education learning outcomes rather than literacy, numeracy, or language. The pooled effect for instructional support was positive (g = .39, 95% CI [.22, .56]) across studies assessing medical clinical reasoning, teacher professional vision, and related domain-specific diagnostic tasks.
finding.measure: Professional diagnostic competence in medical and teacher education

paper_profiles.title: Assessment as a positive influence on 21st century teaching and learning: A systems approach to progress
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (policy/theoretical paper; no specific study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues that assessment, when properly designed and used, can positively support teaching and learning in the 21st century. Rather than reporting results from an intervention study, the paper synthesizes assessment theory and prior research to explain how classroom and large-scale assessments should be designed to support deeper learning, transferable skills, and coherent educational systems.

The paper centers on three conceptual frameworks: assessment as evidentiary reasoning, learning progressions, and evidence-centered design. It discusses how classroom formative assessment and large-scale summative assessment should be aligned with cognitive models of learning, with tasks that directly elicit evidence of important competencies rather than narrow proxies. The author also emphasizes the need for balanced assessment systems that are comprehensive, coherent, and continuous across instructional contexts.

The paper’s context is broad K-12 education, especially the U.S. standards-based reform environment and its implications for classroom, district, state, national, and international assessment systems. It does not study a specific sample, intervention, or counterfactual. Its main conclusion is normative and theoretical: assessment can improve learning if it is instructionally sensitive, grounded in learning theory, and integrated with curriculum and instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that coherent, theory-driven assessment systems can improve educational transformation by aligning classroom and large-scale measures with standards, curriculum, and instruction. It does not report a quantitative effect size or an empirical counterfactual; the claim is conceptual and policy-oriented rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Assessment system design principles and policy/implementation considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes the assessment of higher-order competencies such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, metacognition, strategy use, and knowledge organization. These are discussed as desired learning outcomes that well-designed assessments should capture, but the article does not provide outcome data from a study.
finding.measure: Conceptual coverage of higher-order competencies in assessment design

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses assessment design across school subjects and standards, including English language arts, mathematics, and science, with an emphasis on deeper learning and performance assessment. It does not present subject-specific empirical results, but it argues that assessments should measure complex disciplinary performances directly.
finding.measure: Cross-disciplinary assessment design principles and performance tasks

paper_profiles.title: Defining Active Learning: A Restricted Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how ‘active learning’ is defined and used across higher education research, because the term is widely invoked but inconsistently operationalized. The authors conducted a restricted systematic review of SCOPUS-indexed, peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2017 to 2022, focusing on higher education and excluding K–12, computer science/AI, and non-English records.

The review identified 547 articles that explicitly used the term active learning. The authors extracted whether each article defined active learning, which authors were cited in those definitions, and which instructional strategies were linked to active learning. They found that most articles did not define the term at all, while the most common definitions traced back to a small set of canonical sources (especially Bonwell and Eison, Prince, and Freeman et al.).

Qualitatively, the paper synthesizes the literature into three main themes: active learning as grounded in constructivist, student-centered theory; active learning as a way to promote higher-order thinking and deep learning; and active learning as an instructional strategy characterized by participation, engagement, and activity rather than passive lecture. The paper’s main contribution is definitional and conceptual rather than causal: it proposes a representative definition of active learning and maps the instructional strategies most often associated with the term across higher education research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test an intervention effect, but it synthesizes how higher education literature defines active learning as fostering higher-order thinking, critical thinking, problem solving, decision making, and metacognition/reflective thinking. Across 547 articles, the most frequently cited strategies included problem-based learning/problem solving (64 mentions), flipped classroom (53), small groups/group work/jigsaw (36), and team-based learning (36), indicating that durable skills are a central theoretical and conceptual focus of the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Definitions and instructional-strategy coding from reviewed articles
finding.study_size: n=547 articles reviewed; n=161 definitions; n=675 strategy mentions

paper_profiles.title: Describing undergraduate STEM teaching practices: a comparison of instructor self-report instruments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement problem in undergraduate STEM education: researchers and faculty developers need better ways to describe what instructional practices instructors actually use, but available self-report surveys vary widely in scope, quality, and content. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors compare existing instructor self-report instruments to identify what they measure, how they were developed, and where the instrumentation literature is weak.

The study reviews 12 postsecondary teaching-practice instruments, including surveys designed for all postsecondary instructors and discipline-specific instruments for physics, engineering, chemistry/biology, geoscience, statistics, and science/mathematics. The authors qualitatively analyze instrument development features (e.g., intended population, reliability/validity evidence, response scales, scoring conventions) and code 320 teaching-practice items into autonomous categories such as instructional format, assessment, and reflective practice.

The paper concludes that most existing instruments emphasize instructional format and summative assessment, while formative assessment, laboratory instruction, online teaching, and inclusive/universal-design practices are underrepresented. It also finds that many instruments lack transparent development documentation, strong reliability evidence, and construct-validity testing. The authors recommend using complete, validated instruments when possible and call for new or revised tools that better capture missing dimensions of postsecondary teaching practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not estimate student-outcome effects; instead, it finds that the field lacks standardized, well-documented instruments for characterizing postsecondary teaching practices. Among 12 surveys, many had incomplete development records, limited reliability evidence, and weak construct-validity testing, indicating an important measurement gap for institutional research and improvement efforts.
finding.measure: Review of instructional-practice survey instruments; documentation of development, reliability, validity, scoring, and item content

paper_profiles.title: Design Patterns for Learning and Assessment: Facilitating the Introduction of a Complex Simulation-Based Learning Environment into a Community of Instructors
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and deployment of Packet Tracer, a simulation-based learning and assessment environment used in the Cisco Networking Academy. The central problem is not whether simulation can support learning in general, but how to make a complex simulator usable by a distributed community of instructors so that it supports instruction, formative assessment, and assessment authoring at scale. The authors frame this as a design and implementation challenge involving representational fidelity, scaffolding, reusability, and communication around task patterns.

The approach is a layered architecture built on top of a network simulator. The paper explains how Packet Tracer supports logical and physical network views, real-time and simulation modes, event tracing, authoring of troubleshooting and design tasks, and assessment tools that create initial networks, answer networks, grading trees, and dynamic variables. It also describes four activity patterns—concept builders, skill builders, design challenges, and troubleshooting scenarios—and additional supports for localization and instructor training.

The context is a large postsecondary and professional-education network: Cisco Networking Academies in more than 9,000 institutions across 160 countries, where students learn computer networking skills and prepare for the CCNA exam. The paper emphasizes instructor enablement and local customization rather than testing a single treatment effect. It presents the system’s design rationale and gives illustrative examples of use, but it does not report a causal evaluation, comparison group, or quantitative learning outcomes. The main conclusion is that a design-pattern approach and layered tooling can make simulation-based learning and assessment more scalable, extensible, and communicable across a global instructor community.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Packet Tracer improves instructor productivity and assessment-authoring efficiency by enabling reusable activity templates, answer networks, grading trees, and dynamic variables. It reports that these features allow instructors to create numerous complex variants and isomorphs from a master network with relatively little work, but it does not provide quantitative effect sizes or a controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Assessment authoring workflow efficiency; reuse and generation of variant activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes Packet Tracer as a support framework for a distributed, global Cisco Networking Academy community of over 9,000 institutions in 160 countries. It argues that the system improves shared communication, instructor training, localization, and the ability to distribute common assessment and instructional patterns across institutions, but these claims are descriptive rather than experimentally evaluated.
finding.measure: Global instructor-community support, localization, and dissemination of assessment/instructional patterns

paper_profiles.title: The impact of self-assessment, planning and goal setting, and reflection before and after revision on student self-efficacy and writing performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether adding a student-facing revision planner to a writing intervention improves sixth-grade students’ writing self-efficacy and analytical writing performance. The core question is whether having students self-assess their draft, set revision goals, and reflect after revising produces benefits beyond the teacher instruction and trained-reader feedback already provided to all students.

The study was conducted in a large, urban California school district with predominantly Hispanic and predominantly Redesignated English Learner sixth graders. All participating teachers received extensive professional development in a cognitive-strategies writing intervention, including instruction on planning, revising, and evaluating analytical essays. Students in the treatment condition, in addition, completed a Pre-Test Essay Revision Planner and a post-revision reflection form; comparison students revised their drafts with teacher instruction and reader comments but without the planner.

Using a sequential mixed-methods design, the authors analyzed pre/post self-efficacy surveys, pre/post on-demand writing assessments, and student interviews. Quantitatively, treatment students showed significantly greater gains in writing performance than comparison students, and there were small positive changes in self-efficacy overall, especially in the revision subscale. Qualitative interview data suggested that students found the planner helpful as a roadmap for revision, but they most often credited teacher instruction and feedback as the main support for improving their drafts. The paper concludes that planned self-assessment and reflection can support revision and writing outcomes when embedded within a broader teacher-led intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Treatment students produced greater gains on the Academic Writing Assessment than comparison students after the revision-planner intervention. Treatment students improved by 1.90 points and control students by 1.33 points from pre to post; the difference-in-differences was statistically significant (Δ=0.57, p<.001).
finding.measure: Academic Writing Assessment (timed on-demand analytical essay score, 2-12 scale)

finding.finding_summary: The treatment group showed a small improvement in overall writing self-efficacy relative to comparison peers. Post-survey mean self-efficacy increased to 3.63 for treatment students and decreased to 3.47 for comparison students, with a marginally significant difference-in-differences (Δ=0.11, p<.10).
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy in Writing Scale (SEW)

finding.finding_summary: The self-efficacy subscale most directly tied to revision showed a positive treatment effect. Treatment students increased on the Revision factor by 0.12 points (3.59 to 3.71), while comparison students decreased by 0.08 points (3.58 to 3.50), yielding a statistically significant difference (t(212)=2.201, p=.029).
finding.measure: SEW Revision composite (factor analysis of survey items about revising introductions, conclusions, and claims)

finding.finding_summary: Volition self-efficacy declined in both groups, though the decline was smaller for treatment students. Comparison students dropped from 3.53 to 3.24, while treatment students dropped from 3.47 to 3.41; the difference was statistically significant (t(212)=2.240, p=.026), but the paper interprets this as a weaker decline rather than a strong positive effect.
finding.measure: SEW Volition composite (persistence/focus while writing)

paper_profiles.title: Critical Components of Formative Assessment in Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning for Online Labs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be adapted for online, lab-based undergraduate instruction using Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning (POGIL). The authors are motivated by the challenge that online virtual labs make it harder to monitor student understanding and provide timely feedback, especially in hands-on, team-based courses where traditional instructor-led formative assessment is difficult to deliver.

To address this, the authors designed and implemented a Student Team Learning Monitor (STLM) module within the OpenMRS electronic health record system and used it in two undergraduate Health Information Management courses (M200 and M220) at IUPUI. The study used iterative Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles over two years, with groups of 3-4 students, discussion forums, quizzes, assignments, and peer comparison of task performance to support POGIL activities in online labs. The paper is primarily descriptive and implementation-focused: it identifies critical components for a workable "Cyber POGIL" model, such as the role of monitoring tools, group structure, limited active tutoring, and student-generated questions/tasks.

The main conclusion is that POGIL can be translated into online lab settings, but the implementation requires modifications from traditional in-person POGIL, especially to accommodate asynchronous communication and monitoring through a custom tool. The authors report improved learning and knowledge reconstruction through peer comparison and repeated task attempts, but the paper does not provide a controlled causal estimate isolating formative assessment from adjacent instructional features. It therefore serves as an early implementation account and conceptual analysis rather than high-quality causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Across two undergraduate Health Information Management courses implemented over three PDSA iterations, the authors report that integrating POGIL activities and the STLM monitoring tool supported student learning of course-specific concepts such as patient identifiers, forms, and distinguishing data, information, and knowledge. The paper states that repeated attempts and comparison of work across peers led to improved learning and knowledge reconstruction, but it does not report a controlled effect size, confidence interval, or standardized outcome score.
finding.measure: Course assessment grades, quizzes, assignments, and performance on POGIL tasks in online labs

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes improved student engagement in online labs and uses the STLM tool to monitor participation and peer interaction. The authors also report a 10-item survey and volunteer interviews intended to assess usability and students' perceptions of the tool, but no numerical engagement effect or psychometric results are reported in the text provided.
finding.measure: Student engagement observations, forum participation, survey responses, and interviews

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that Cyber POGIL promotes process skills, critical thinking, and collaborative knowledge construction in an online lab environment. The authors describe students learning to compare approaches, generate questions, and solve tasks independently and in groups; however, the paper provides no formal effect size or counterfactual estimate for critical thinking or collaboration outcomes.
finding.measure: Performance on POGIL process tasks, peer comparison of task completion, and instructor/researcher observation of group work

finding.finding_summary: The STLM tool was designed to monitor student activity, support formative feedback, and help students complete lab tasks more efficiently in an online EHR environment. The authors describe the tool as improving the efficiency of task completion and reducing the burden of direct instructor intervention, but they do not provide quantitative productivity metrics, time-on-task data, or workload estimates.
finding.measure: Task completion process, tool usability, and perceived efficiency of completing lab activities

paper_profiles.title: The Pathway to Academic Success: Scaling Up a Text-Based Analytical Writing Intervention for Latinos and English Learners in Secondary School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a previously successful professional development intervention for secondary English language arts teachers could be scaled up across multiple sites and still improve student writing outcomes. The Pathway to Academic Success Project was created to help Latinos and mainstreamed English learners in high-need middle and high school classrooms meet rigorous English language arts standards through explicit cognitive-strategy instruction for text-based analytical writing.

The intervention provided teachers with 46 hours of professional development delivered across six full-day and five after-school sessions. Teachers learned how to teach reading and writing strategies, use on-demand writing assessments formatively, and guide students through planning, drafting, revising, and analyzing nonfiction texts. The study used a multisite cluster randomized controlled trial in four National Writing Project sites in southern California, with 230 secondary teachers randomly assigned to treatment or delayed-treatment control conditions.

The main student outcome was performance on an on-demand analytical writing assessment.
