In the cognition-focused studies, assessment practices such as self-assessment, rubrics, post-exam wrappers, and reflective diaries were associated with improved metacognitive awareness and strategic task selection, though results for self-assessment accuracy were mixed.
finding.measure: Metacognitive awareness, self-regulated learning behaviors, planning/monitoring/revision activities, rubric use, reflection, and strategy selection
finding.study_size: varied across studies; cognition collection n=60 studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies focused on writing and reading outcomes, and these generally showed benefits from assessment-supported regulation. Reported outcomes included improved writing skill, writing quality, and reading comprehension, often when feedback, self-assessment, or peer assessment was used to scaffold revision and strategy use; the review does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Writing skill, writing revision/quality, and reading comprehension
finding.study_size: varied across literacy-related studies; not_reported for a single pooled sample

finding.finding_summary: Some studies in the review examined science learning and scientific reasoning-related outcomes, including performance on science exams and science-topic motivation. These studies generally found that formative assessment, self-evaluation, and feedback scaffolding were associated with better science learning and engagement, but the review does not provide pooled effect sizes for science outcomes.
finding.measure: Science exam performance and science-topic learning outcomes
finding.study_size: varied across studies; not_reported for a single pooled sample

finding.finding_summary: The review also included studies in other academic domains such as mathematics, language learning, project management, and visual arts. In these domain-specific studies, assessment practices such as portfolios, reflective assessment, and feedback were generally associated with better task performance and learning processes, but the paper does not report a common effect size across domains.
finding.measure: Domain-specific performance measures across mathematics, language learning, project management, and visual arts
finding.study_size: varied across studies; not_reported for a single pooled sample

finding.finding_summary: A smaller set of studies addressed behaviors tied to efficiency and task management, such as revision, information seeking, help seeking, time management, and using supplementary exercises or study strategies. The review notes that peer review and feedback sometimes improved these behaviors or related self-discipline, although one study found little draft-to-final-paper revision despite perceived usefulness.
finding.measure: Revision behavior, help seeking, information seeking, study strategy use, and time-management/self-discipline indicators
finding.study_size: varied across behavior-related studies; n=15 studies coded as behavior

finding.finding_summary: This review does not directly evaluate policy or institutional outcomes, but it does argue that assessment practices shape classroom culture and instructional response. The main evidence is indirect: teachers sometimes adjusted instruction in response to student feedback and reflection, suggesting institutional-level implications for classroom assessment design, but no direct effect sizes or institutional measures were reported.
finding.measure: Classroom instructional adjustment, assessment culture, and teacher responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review on trends in using Moodle for teaching and learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how Moodle has been used in teaching and learning research across disciplines, with a focus on identifying adoption patterns, research gaps, and effective ways to improve online teaching and learning. The authors searched Scopus and Web of Science and screened 155 journal articles published from January 2015 to June 2021, then combined bibliometric analysis with thematic analysis.

The review finds that Moodle is used most heavily in university STEM contexts, especially at the undergraduate level, and is commonly associated with improvements in student performance, satisfaction, and engagement. Thematic findings show that Moodle is widely used for course design, quizzes, workshops/peer assessment, forums, adaptive learning, formative and summative assessment, analytics, and software extensions. The paper concludes that Moodle is increasingly being adapted for adaptive and collaborative learning and for online assessment, but more qualitative research—especially on educators’ perspectives—and more theory-driven research are needed.

finding.finding_summary: Across 155 reviewed journal articles, Moodle was reported to improve student performance in university STEM settings, with the review characterizing the overall evidence as showing positive effects on performance, satisfaction, and engagement. The paper does not synthesize a single pooled effect size, but it consistently reports Moodle as an effective platform for teaching and learning in higher education, especially for online assessments and course delivery.
finding.measure: Student performance / grades / course outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that Moodle use is associated with improved student satisfaction and engagement, based on findings across the included studies. These outcomes are discussed as recurring student success indicators, but the article does not report a pooled effect size or a common standardized measure across studies.
finding.measure: Student engagement and satisfaction indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies Moodle activities and tools that support collaborative learning, peer review, critical reflection, and problem/project-based work. Evidence is mixed because several studies report benefits for metacognition and collaboration, while others note that peer assessment tools can be time-consuming, perceived as unfair or unprofessional, and may not reduce teacher workload.
finding.measure: Peer assessment, collaboration, critical reflection, and project-based learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A major theme in the review is that Moodle tools can streamline assessment, marking, and feedback processes for teachers. The paper reports that online marking systems can lower long-term costs, increase feedback speed, improve flexibility, and reduce the space required to manage assessment, although some peer-assessment tools may still be time-consuming to administer.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, marking speed, feedback efficiency, assessment process management

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that Moodle is being adopted broadly across countries, journals, and institutions, particularly in university STEM education, and that software developers are increasingly extending the platform with analytics, AI, security, and assessment-related plug-ins. These patterns suggest institutional-level uptake and adaptation, but the review does not estimate a pooled institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Adoption trends, institutional use, software adaptation, and analytics integration

paper_profiles.title: The Future of Feedback: Integrating Peer and Generative AI Reviews to Support Student Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI reviews can function as a useful complement to peer feedback in formative assessment, and whether students perceive AI-generated feedback as quality feedback that is useful and actionable. The authors situate the study in broader debates about formative assessment, arguing that assessment is only truly formative when feedback leads to instructional or learner revision, and they contrast this with “pseudo-formative” uses of quizzes, automated grading, and other assessment tools that may not meaningfully shape learning.

The study was conducted in online graduate courses in the College of Education at a US Mid-Western university during Spring, Summer, and Fall 2023. A total of 295 adult participants, mostly master’s and doctoral students who were also working educators, completed post-course surveys after receiving both blind peer reviews and AI reviews on extended multimodal projects. The intervention used CGScholar/CGMap and OpenAI’s ChatGPT-3.5 API to generate AI feedback based on a shared rubric derived from the Learning by Design framework; students then revised their work across multiple iterations, received peer and AI feedback, and made final revisions before publication.

Using a convergent mixed-methods design, the authors analyzed Likert-scale survey responses with descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, and regressions, and analyzed open-ended responses thematically. Across the three feedback dimensions of quality, usefulness, and actionability, students rated peer reviews slightly higher than AI reviews, though both were seen as beneficial. Qualitative findings suggested that peer feedback was valued for human judgment, empathy, and contextual nuance, while AI feedback was valued for speed, consistency, and scalability. The paper concludes that peer and AI feedback can be complementary in a blended formative feedback ecosystem, but that AI should be used critically because it may be less nuanced, less context-sensitive, and not always sufficiently reliable or explainable.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived AI reviews as faster, more scalable, and more consistent than peer reviews, suggesting an efficiency advantage for feedback provision in large or time-constrained courses. The paper does not report a single pooled effect size for efficiency outcomes, but it repeatedly emphasizes that AI reduced turnaround time and could provide timely feedback to every student.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of usefulness, actionability, and qualitative reports about speed/efficiency of AI feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined perceived actionability of peer and AI feedback, which is closely tied to students' ability to revise work, reflect on feedback, and exercise judgment about improvements. Students generally found both forms of feedback actionable, but peer reviews were rated slightly higher overall, indicating that AI feedback supported revision yet did not fully match human feedback on perceived usefulness for higher-order improvement.
finding.measure: Perceived actionability ratings and open-ended survey responses about revising work based on feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on feedback for extended multimodal course projects in a graduate education program, not on a specific literacy, math, or science achievement test. Students revised their project work after receiving peer and AI feedback, and the study suggests that both feedback sources supported improvement in the quality of the final multimodal work, although peer feedback was preferred slightly over AI on all measured dimensions.
finding.measure: Post-course perceptions of feedback quality/usefulness/actionability for multimodal project work

finding.finding_summary: Students' feelings toward AI were examined as a predictor of perceived feedback quality, usefulness, and actionability, making affective response a central part of the study. The qualitative findings suggest peer review offered emotional support and human connection, whereas AI review was valued less for interpersonal support but more for functional feedback; overall, emotional responses appeared to shape how students received AI feedback.
finding.measure: Survey items on feelings toward AI and perceived quality/usefulness/actionability of AI feedback; open-ended comments about advantages and drawbacks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating peer and GenAI feedback can inform instructional design, educational policy, and platform development for formative assessment at scale. It reports that institutions can use blended human-AI feedback to support course workflows and larger learning systems, though the paper does not report a direct institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Interpretive findings about pedagogical, instructional design, and policy implications of blending peer and AI feedback

paper_profiles.title: Educational Data Analytics for Teachers and School Leaders
paper_profiles.venue: Springer (Advances in Analytics for Learning and Teaching series)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education professionals (teachers, school leaders, instructional designers, e-tutors, and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book introduces educational data analytics and educational data literacy as core competences for educators working in online, blended, and data-rich learning environments. Its central question is how teachers, instructional designers, tutors, and school leaders can identify, collect, interpret, and act on educational data to improve teaching, learning, assessment, and institutional decision making.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the book is a practice-oriented, open-access professional text that synthesizes concepts, frameworks, and examples. It explains how educational data supports data-driven decision making, personalized learning, instructional design (especially the ADDIE process), learning analytics, teaching analytics, ethics/privacy, and school self-evaluation. Throughout the chapters, the emphasis is on how data can inform adaptive action—e.g., redesigning courses, adjusting tutoring, tailoring support, and using evidence-based run-time revisions—rather than on a specific experimental intervention.

The intended audience includes K-12 teachers and school leaders, e-learning professionals, instructional designers, tutors, and higher-education students. The book argues that educational data is most useful when it is part of a continuous cycle of collection, analysis, interpretation, action, and reevaluation. It also highlights ethical considerations, data quality, and the need for educational data literacy as prerequisites for effective use of analytics in education.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that educational data analytics can improve efficiency in instructional design and teaching by enabling educators to make evidence-based, run-time adaptations and revisions. In the ADDIE framework, monitoring learner and teacher actions is described as supporting continuous improvement of delivery and reducing time/cost inefficiencies, but no quantitative effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Use of educational data for evidence-based adaptations, monitoring, and decision making in instructional design and teaching processes

finding.finding_summary: The text presents educational data analytics and data-driven decision making as tools for improving courses, curricula, school self-evaluation, and institutional decision making. It describes how schools and universities can use analytics to identify areas for improvement, set policies, measure results, and support student experience, but it does not report a controlled evaluation with numerical outcomes.
finding.measure: Institutional decision making, course/curriculum redesign, school self-evaluation, and policy/quality improvement processes

finding.finding_summary: The book claims that using learner-generated data can support personalized learning, increase engagement, and help students become self-directed, lifelong learners. These are conceptual/practice claims rather than experimentally measured results, and no sample sizes or effect sizes are provided.
finding.measure: Student engagement, self-directed learning, and personalized learning support

paper_profiles.title: Handbook of Educational Reform Through Blended Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This handbook chapter collection addresses the theory, design, and implementation of blended learning in higher education and related training contexts. The opening chapter lays out the rationale for blended learning as a response to digital transformation, arguing that emerging technologies, changing workforce needs, and learner diversity require more flexible learning systems than traditional face-to-face instruction alone.

The main approach studied is conceptual and theoretical rather than experimental: the chapter synthesizes psychology and pedagogy to explain why blended learning is needed, how it should be structured, and what learner characteristics it should accommodate. It argues that blended learning integrates online and offline environments, supports personalization, and can help develop twenty-first-century skills such as collaboration, communication, creativity, critical thinking, autonomy, and problem solving.

The population and context are broad, spanning learners across the lifespan but with a strong emphasis on higher education and institutional reform in China and internationally. The text discusses applications such as MOOCs, SPOCs, learning analytics, intelligent classrooms, and tools like Rain Classroom as examples of how blended learning can support teaching and learning processes.

Overall, the chapter concludes that blended learning is a necessary and increasingly common model for education in the information age because it better aligns instruction with common developmental patterns and individual differences. It emphasizes that effective blended learning requires coordinated online/offline design, diversified learning activities, hierarchical resources, and personalized guidance so that students' learning potential can be fully developed.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that blended learning can strengthen durable skills such as autonomy, collaboration, communication, creativity, critical thinking, and problem solving. It cites prior studies in which blended learning models on platforms such as Wisdom Tree/SPOC and MOOC improved students' autonomous learning ability, learning efficiency, language expression, teamwork, and teacher-student/student-student communication, but no original effect sizes are reported in this handbook chapter.
finding.measure: Autonomous learning ability, learning efficiency, teamwork, communication, critical thinking, problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes that blended learning can better accommodate learners' interests, needs, and pacing, thereby supporting motivation, engagement, and persistence. It cites the need for feedback, self-paced learning, and a more autonomous learning atmosphere, but does not report direct quantitative evidence in this chapter.
finding.measure: Learning interest, engagement, self-paced learning, autonomy

finding.finding_summary: The text argues that blended learning and associated digital tools can improve teaching and learning efficiency by providing data-driven feedback and by reducing the constraints of time, space, and class size. It specifically notes that intelligent learning analytics can offer timely and accurate feedback to optimize classroom learning and management, but it does not provide original effect estimates.
finding.measure: Teaching and learning efficiency, classroom management, feedback timeliness

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the handbook is that blended learning is a major direction for educational reform and digital transformation in higher education institutions. The chapter describes institutional adoption of online platforms, learning management systems, and multi-modal blended learning as part of broader system-level change, but it does not present a formal impact evaluation.
finding.measure: Institutional adoption of blended learning, digital transformation of higher education

paper_profiles.title: Performance-based assessment in virtual versus non-virtual classes: impacts on academic resilience, motivation, teacher support, and personal best goals
paper_profiles.venue: Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether performance-based assessment (PBA) functions differently in online versus traditional in-person classes, and whether it is associated with changes in students’ academic resilience, motivation, perceived teacher support, and personal best goals. The paper is motivated by a broader question relevant to formative assessment: whether assessment becomes consequential only when instruction adapts in response, and how assessment experiences differ across virtual and physical learning contexts.

Using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest comparison group design, the authors studied 84 learners divided into an online experimental group (n=41) and a physical-classroom control group (n=43). Both groups experienced PBA tasks embedded in instruction; the online group completed tasks through digital platforms and virtual simulations, while the control group completed in-person role plays, presentations, group discussions, and hands-on projects. Outcomes were measured with established questionnaires for academic resilience, motivation, teacher support, and personal best goals, and analyzed with chi-square tests.

The main finding is that online classes combined with PBA were associated with significantly higher posttest levels of academic resilience, motivation, perceived teacher support, and personal best goals than physical classes. Pretest differences were not significant, suggesting the groups were initially similar. The authors conclude that PBA in online settings may better support students’ psychosocial outcomes, likely through greater autonomy, flexibility, individualized feedback, and easier goal-tracking. The paper does not directly test whether instruction was changed in response to assessment in a formative-assessment sense; rather, it shows that assessment was embedded in instruction and that online delivery was linked to more favorable student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Online classes combined with PBA were associated with significantly higher academic resilience than physical classes at posttest. The study reports 29 resilient learners in the online group versus 16 in the control group (n=84 total), with a significant chi-square result and a moderate effect size (Phi Cramer’s V=0.336).
finding.measure: Academic resilience scale (ARS-30); resilient vs non-resilient classification

finding.finding_summary: Online classes with PBA significantly increased motivation relative to physical classes. At posttest, 34 learners in the experimental group and 20 in the control group were classified as motivated (n=84), with a significant chi-square result and a moderate effect size (Phi Cramer’s V=0.38).
finding.measure: Science Motivation Questionnaire II (SMQ-II); motivated vs unmotivated classification

finding.finding_summary: Perceived teacher support was higher in the online PBA condition at posttest, although the effect was smaller than for resilience and motivation. The online group had 24 students reporting teacher support versus 17 in the control group (n=84), with a statistically significant posttest difference and a small effect size (Phi Cramer’s V=0.19).
finding.measure: Teacher Support Scale (TTS); provided vs unprovided classification

finding.finding_summary: Personal best goals increased more in the online PBA group than in the physical-classroom group. At posttest, 35 learners in the online group and 26 in the control group reported set PBGs (n=84), with a significant chi-square result and an almost-moderate effect size (Phi Cramer’s V=0.279).
finding.measure: Personal Best Goals scale; set vs unset classification

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review on the formative assessment practice in teaching and learning in secondary school
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how formative assessment is being practiced in secondary school teaching and learning, and what themes emerge across recent empirical studies. The authors note a persistent problem in the literature and practice: many teachers use assessment activities, but formative assessment is not always well understood or implemented in ways that truly support ongoing learning. They therefore conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review to synthesize evidence on formative assessment practices in secondary schools.

The review searched Web of Science and Scopus and retained 19 empirical journal articles published from 2017 to 2021. The included studies covered multiple countries and subjects, with methods spanning qualitative, mixed-methods, and quantitative designs. Using thematic analysis, the authors identified three major themes: assessment diversity, assessment strategies, and student learning development.

Across the reviewed studies, formative assessment was shown to involve teachers, students, and peers in complementary roles. Reported practices included clarifying learning objectives, using feedback, questioning, self-assessment, peer assessment, quizzes, portfolios, rubrics, observation sheets, and learning analytics/data use. The review concludes that formative assessment is most effective when assessment information leads to instructional adjustment, when students actively participate, and when teachers use assessment to support both academic progress and social development. The paper also emphasizes professional development for teachers so formative assessment can be implemented more comprehensively.

finding.finding_summary: Across 19 studies (2017-2021), formative assessment practices were associated with improved student learning outcomes in secondary school, but the review does not report a pooled effect size. Evidence included improved academic performance, better concept understanding, and enhanced inquiry skills when teachers used assessment information to adjust instruction; however, some traditional or teacher-centered assessment practices showed no significant effect on inquiry skill development.
finding.measure: Academic performance, concept understanding, inquiry skills, and student learning development outcomes reported across the reviewed studies
finding.study_size: 19 studies (systematic review); individual study samples ranged from 4 teachers to 2,767 students

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that formative assessment was linked to positive student dispositions such as motivation to learn, self-confidence, independence, responsibility, discipline, and positive attitudes toward lessons. Individual studies in the review found these benefits in secondary school contexts, but no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Motivation, attitudes toward the lesson, self-regulation, self-efficacy, responsibility, confidence, and discipline
finding.study_size: 19 studies (systematic review); included studies such as n=45 students/teachers, n=234 students, n=2,767 students

finding.finding_summary: The review found that formative assessment supported durable skills including self-regulation, collaboration, and more active participation in learning. Teachers’ use of feedback, peer assessment, and group work was described as helping students become more independent and cooperative, though the review provides no effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, collaboration, active participation, and independent learning
finding.study_size: 19 studies (systematic review); individual studies included teacher, peer, and student reports

finding.finding_summary: In science-focused studies, formative assessment was associated with improved inquiry skills and better conceptual understanding. One included study reported that teacher-centered teaching and traditional assessment did not significantly improve inquiry skills, while formative assessment was described as a tool to enhance inquiry development; the review does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Inquiry skills and conceptual understanding in science education
finding.study_size: Included science studies within the 19-paper review; one cited study used 45 participants and another focused on two physics teachers

paper_profiles.title: Online and Blended Teaching and Learning Supported by Educational Data
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Analytics for Learning and Teaching
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and Higher Education educators in online and blended learning contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter introduces educational data as a key enabler of data-driven decision making in online and blended teaching and learning. Rather than testing a single intervention, it surveys how educational data and learning analytics can support instructional design, tutoring, school teaching, and continuous improvement through the Learn2Analyze educational data literacy framework.

The chapter argues that educational data should be used not simply for description, but for action: identifying problems, designing instruction, monitoring implementation, and revising teaching in response to evidence. It emphasizes personalization, flipped classroom implementation, formative and summative evaluation, and the need for educators to collect, manage, interpret, and ethically use data from multiple sources.

The context is primarily online and blended learning, with examples spanning instructional designers, e-tutors, and school teachers in K-12 settings. The main conclusion is that educational data only becomes useful when educators can convert it into decisions and adaptations; therefore, data literacy is a prerequisite for effective use of analytics in teaching and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that educational data and analytics improve the efficiency of teaching and course design by helping educators identify problems early, monitor implementation, and make evidence-based run-time adaptations. It frames data use as a continuous cycle of collection, analysis, reflection, and revision rather than a one-time assessment activity.
finding.measure: Descriptive discussion of data-driven decision making, monitoring, and instructional adaptation in online/blended courses

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents educational data literacy as an institutional competence needed for teachers, instructional designers, and school leaders to improve teaching and learning systems. It emphasizes policy, governance, evaluation, and continuous improvement processes, including data access, consent, privacy, and the use of school and district data sources.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of data literacy frameworks, school self-evaluation, and data governance/ethics

finding.finding_summary: The chapter links educational data use to student engagement, self-directed learning, and personalized support. It claims that when data are used well, learners can better understand their progress, make informed choices, and stay on track toward their goals, especially in blended and flipped classroom contexts.
finding.measure: Engagement, self-directed learning, and personalized learning outcomes discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes metacognition and reflective practice for educators, as well as learner awareness of progress and goal-setting. It also highlights critical interpretation of multiple data sources and translating data into actionable knowledge as core durable skills in educational data literacy.
finding.measure: Reflective practice, data interpretation, and goal-setting discussed in the Learn2Analyze framework

paper_profiles.title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines the rapidly growing literature on AI-enhanced learning and argues that claims about AI’s benefits are often overstated when they ignore instructional implementation, comparison conditions, and cognitive learning processes. Rather than presenting a primary empirical test of a specific AI intervention, the paper synthesizes prior empirical and theoretical work to clarify how AI may affect learning and to caution against conflating performance during AI-supported tasks with genuine learning gains.

A central contribution is the ISAR model, which distinguishes inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition effects of AI in education. The authors use examples from intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI, dashboards, AI-generated quizzes and feedback, and conversational agents to show that AI can either undermine deep learning through over-reliance, substitute for existing instructional functions without changing outcomes, augment instruction by adding feedback and scaffolding, or redefine tasks to support deeper constructive/interactive learning.

The paper does not study a single population or intervention; instead, it discusses students and teachers across educational contexts, with a particular emphasis on generative AI, LLMs, and other digital learning technologies. The main conclusion is that AI’s educational value depends on how it is implemented, what instructional function it serves, and whether it preserves or strengthens cognitive engagement. The authors emphasize the need for careful comparisons, human oversight, learner and teacher AI literacy, and rigorous validation of AI-supported instructional tools.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual reflection rather than a primary empirical study, so no direct effect estimates are reported for academic outcomes overall. The paper reviews prior evidence showing that AI tools can produce comparable performance to non-AI alternatives in some cases (e.g., AI-generated instructional videos or quizzes) but can also fail to improve or even reduce learning when overused or poorly implemented.
finding.measure: Review of prior studies on learning performance, knowledge gain, and instructional equivalence

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can both support and undermine learner engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning depending on implementation. It cites prior studies where support tools increased elaboration and organization during revision, but ChatGPT use was associated with lower metacognitive processing and potential 'metacognitive laziness'.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning behavior, metacognitive processing, engagement during revision

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and problem-solving, arguing that AI should support deep learning rather than replace these processes. It synthesizes prior studies showing that AI can foster reflection and collaboration in some settings, but over-reliance on generative AI may reduce cognitive processing depth and weaken critical thinking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive processing, collaboration, problem-solving in AI-supported learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights operational benefits of AI such as replacing teacher-created quizzes with AI-generated quiz questions and flashcards, providing instant responses to clarification questions, and reducing teacher workload through automated feedback and tutoring support. These are discussed as efficiency gains rather than direct learning gains.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, immediacy of responses, automation of feedback and quiz generation

paper_profiles.title: A Multilevel Framework and Method for Learning Analytics Integrated Learning Design
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) to High School to Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design problem in learning analytics: how to integrate analytics and feedback into learning design so that analytics are not added after the fact, but are built into the instructional sequence from the beginning. The authors argue that common analytics tools and learning design taxonomies are too coarse to support the nuanced decisions teachers make across course, curriculum-component, and task levels, especially when the goal is to “close the loop” by changing instruction in response to learner data.

To address this, the paper proposes a multilevel framework for learning-analytics-integrated learning design. The framework combines a learning design triangle, a multilevel learning analytics taxonomy, and the idea of Learning Analytics integrated Curriculum Component Design Patterns (LA-CCDP). The authors ground the framework in a review of prior literature and in analysis of 60 STEM curriculum units from authentic classrooms in a university-school partnership project focused on self-directed learning and inquiry-oriented STEM teaching.

The paper illustrates the framework using one Grade 8 unit, “The Science of Cooking,” showing how learning outcomes, disciplinary practice, pedagogical approach, curriculum components, task sequences, feedback, and analytics can be aligned across levels. The main conclusion is that learning analytics is truly formative only when it is tightly coupled to the instructional design and can support iterative redesign of tasks, feedback, and supports in response to evidence about student learning. The paper is primarily conceptual and framework-building rather than an empirical test of learner outcomes, but it identifies mechanisms of adaptation such as revising task sequences, interface supports, hints, rubrics, and feedback timing based on analytics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s applied framework work is centered on STEM inquiry and scientific investigation as a learning design context, but it does not report a controlled evaluation of learner outcomes. In the illustrated Grade 8 unit, scientific inquiry skills were part of the intended learning outcomes, and the authors argue that tightly integrated learning analytics can support those outcomes by informing redesign of inquiry tasks and feedback.
finding.measure: not_reported
finding.study_size: 60 STEM curriculum units reviewed; 1 Grade 8 unit illustrated

finding.finding_summary: The paper also substantively focuses on curricular and genre-specific writing/assessment design as examples of learning-analytics-integrated curriculum components, but these are used as illustrative cases rather than as outcome evaluations. The authors highlight that analytics can be used to support rubric-based revision, assessment design, and task sequencing in authentic learning contexts.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is on self-directed learning and related metacognitive processes such as goal setting, self-planning, self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and revision. The framework is designed to help teachers structure tasks and analytics so that they can support these durable skills through evidence-informed adaptation of instructional sequences and feedback.
finding.measure: Framework analysis of self-directed learning stages in curriculum design
finding.study_size: 60 STEM curriculum units reviewed; 1 Grade 8 unit illustrated

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that an LA-integrated design framework can improve the efficiency and usability of learning design by providing teachers with explicit support for planning, documenting, and iterating curriculum components. However, it does not provide quantitative evidence of reduced workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Design framework and process support for teachers

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogical Applications of Generative AI in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of the Field
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how generative AI (GenAI) has been used pedagogically in higher education during the first two years after ChatGPT’s release. The paper is motivated by a gap in the literature: prior reviews had addressed AI broadly or student/faculty perceptions, but few had focused specifically on direct teaching-and-learning applications of GenAI in peer-reviewed empirical studies from 2023–2024.

The review screened 262 records from ERIC, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect and included 37 empirical journal articles. Using grounded coding and thematic analysis, the author organized GenAI uses into three major pedagogical themes: automated feedback and assessment, learning support, and development of critical skills. Across these studies, GenAI was used for tasks such as generating formative feedback, creating assessments, answering student questions, supporting lesson planning and writing, and fostering creativity, critical thinking, learner autonomy, and prompt literacy.

The paper concludes that GenAI is currently being used mainly to automate conventional instructional tasks, especially in text-centric contexts like writing, English language learning, and computer science. While these applications can improve efficiency and provide timely support, the review also finds recurring concerns about inaccurate outputs, bias, academic integrity, and student dependency. The author argues that future work should move beyond automation toward more meaningful teacher-student-AI collaboration and multimodal applications.

finding.finding_summary: Across 37 empirical studies, GenAI was repeatedly used to streamline instructional work through automated feedback, assessment generation, lesson planning, and rapid Q&A support. The review does not report a pooled effect size, but it consistently characterizes these uses as reducing instructor workload and improving the speed of response (e.g., immediate feedback, automated assessment, and task generation).
finding.measure: Instructor workload, turnaround time for feedback/assessment, and task automation in teaching support

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that GenAI is used to support and develop higher-order skills such as critical thinking, creativity, learner autonomy, and prompt literacy, but the evidence is mixed because benefits are accompanied by risks of overreliance and weakened independent thinking. The paper synthesizes 37 studies and reports no pooled effect size; instead, it notes that these skills are strengthened when students actively critique, refine, and strategically prompt AI outputs.
finding.measure: Critical thinking tasks, creative production, learner agency/autonomy, and prompt literacy activities

finding.finding_summary: GenAI was widely applied to academic writing and English language learning, including drafting support, feedback generation, grammar assistance, and idea development. The review synthesizes multiple studies showing that these tools can improve writing processes and language practice, but it does not provide a pooled quantitative estimate or a standardized effect size.
finding.measure: Writing quality/process, composition support, ESL/EFL practice, and language-learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: Some studies in the review describe GenAI as providing encouragement, patient interaction, and tailored support that can help students persist and work independently. The synthesis is largely qualitative and conceptual at the review level, and it also notes that these benefits can be offset by dependency and reduced motivation for some learners.
finding.measure: Learning autonomy, engagement, and supportive/encouraging interaction with GenAI tools

paper_profiles.title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design problem in self-paced online learning: many courses rely heavily on summative assessment and do not generate enough meaningful data for learning analytics (LA) to support timely awareness, prediction, and intervention. The authors argue that learning analytics is most useful when it is intentionally built into the course design loop, rather than applied only after the fact to whatever logs happen to exist.

The paper proposes a Learning Design-Analytic (LDA) model for STEM courses in self-paced online learning, emphasizing that learning activities should be designed to create useful learner and learning data. The model recommends adding diagnostic tests, learner profile surveys, repeated formative assessments, auto-graded quizzes, immediate feedback, and adaptive mechanisms such as item response theory for initial diagnostics and multi-armed bandit methods for unit-level formative quizzes. It also discusses using dashboards and predictive models to increase learner awareness, identify struggling students, and support instructor intervention.

The context is an undergraduate computer science course at Athabasca University (COMP272: Data Structures and Algorithms), where the authors describe a work-in-progress redesign using design-based research. The paper does not report completed outcome data from the redesigned course; instead, it presents the rationale, proposed design strategies, example implementation plans, and future evaluation plans. Its main conclusion is that formative assessment in online courses becomes more powerful when paired with adaptive assessment and when instruction is redesigned to collect pedagogically useful data that can drive feedback and intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedding auto-graded formative quizzes and adaptive mechanisms can reduce instructor marking workload and make assessment more efficient. However, this is a design claim rather than a tested outcome; no post-intervention workload data are reported.
finding.measure: Instructor marking workload; assessment efficiency (proposed, not empirically evaluated)

finding.finding_summary: The proposed design is intended to improve students’ learning awareness, self-regulation, help-seeking, and motivation through repeated formative assessment, feedback, dashboards, and gamified quizzes. The paper describes these as expected benefits and cites prior literature, but it does not present direct empirical estimates from this study.
finding.measure: Self-awareness, self-regulation, help-seeking behavior, motivation (proposed/evaluative plan)

finding.finding_summary: The formative assessment design is meant to support learners’ reflection on knowledge gaps and higher-level skills such as reasoning and problem-solving, especially through auto-graded items and algorithm visualization tasks. The article is primarily conceptual, so no direct measured effect sizes or completed study outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Reasoning, problem-solving, reflection, self-assessment (proposed)

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically targets STEM learning and states that the formative assessments will test high-level cognitive skills such as sense-making, reasoning, and problem-solving in computer science. These are design intentions within a course redesign case study; the paper does not yet report results on scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: High-level STEM cognitive skills; reasoning/problem-solving performance (proposed)

finding.finding_summary: At the course level, the paper proposes a redesign process intended to improve institutional course success by increasing pass rates and enabling more actionable learning analytics. It notes that the existing COMP272 course had a 79% pass rate versus an 89% program average, but the redesigned course had not yet been evaluated, so institutional impact remains proposed rather than demonstrated.
finding.measure: Course pass rate; implementation of a course-level learning design-analytics model

paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Learning Pathways: Personalized Learning and Dynamic Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-powered personalized learning pathways and dynamic assessments can improve learning efficiency, performance, and engagement compared with traditional instruction. The authors frame the problem as one of conventional teaching being too rigid to respond to diverse learner needs in real time, and argue that AI can support continuous adaptation through data-driven feedback loops, individualized content delivery, and assessment that changes difficulty based on student responses.

The proposed system combines learning analytics, adaptive content sequencing, real-time feedback, and dynamic assessments. In the study, 100 students in a mathematics course over six weeks were divided into an experimental group using the AI-based system and a control group using traditional methods. The experiment used pre-tests, post-tests, continuous assessment, task timing, and engagement measures. The experimental group outperformed the control group on post-test gains (25% vs. 14%), completed tasks faster (30 vs. 40 minutes per task), and showed higher engagement (15% increase), suggesting that AI-driven adaptation can improve both academic outcomes and learning efficiency.

The paper’s main conclusion is that dynamic, AI-mediated adjustment of difficulty, pacing, and feedback can make learning more effective than fixed curriculum delivery. It also argues that the system’s responsiveness—such as increasing difficulty after correct answers, providing scaffolds after errors, and tailoring content to learning preferences—creates a more engaging and efficient learning experience. However, the evidence is short-term and limited to a small quasi-experimental study, so the authors call for larger-scale and longer-term research.

finding.finding_summary: In a 6-week mathematics course with 100 students, the AI-powered learning group improved from 55% to 80% on post-tests, a 25% gain, compared with a 14% gain for the control group (54% to 68%). This indicates a substantial positive effect on math learning outcomes, although no inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics pre-test and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group showed a 15% increase in engagement relative to the control group, with higher average weekly sessions (4 vs. 3) and longer session duration (52 vs. 45 minutes). The paper interprets this as evidence that personalized challenges and dynamic feedback increased student motivation and engagement.
finding.measure: Engagement metrics and self-reported/behavioral engagement indicators

finding.finding_summary: Students using the AI system completed learning tasks in 30 minutes on average versus 40 minutes for the control group, a 25% reduction in time per task. The authors attribute this efficiency gain to real-time adaptation of content difficulty and the system’s ability to focus students on areas needing improvement.
finding.measure: Average time spent on learning tasks

paper_profiles.title: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Measurement: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper examines how artificial intelligence is being used across educational measurement and what ethical challenges arise from these uses. Rather than testing a single intervention, it surveys current and emerging applications of AI in item generation, scoring, proctoring, and feedback, with particular attention to validity, fairness, transparency, bias, privacy, and human oversight.

The paper discusses how AI tools such as large language models, automated scoring systems, learning analytics, and automated writing evaluation can speed scoring, generate items, and personalize feedback. It also argues that these systems must be embedded in human-in-the-loop workflows and supported by documentation, bias checks, and psychometric validation. The authors use illustrative examples from AP Chinese scoring and NAEP scoring challenges to show how AI can match human agreement overall while still producing subgroup differences or differing scoring rationales.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI can improve efficiency and feedback timeliness, but educational measurement use should remain tightly governed by ethical and validity considerations. It emphasizes that feedback and assessment are only beneficial when they are interpretable, fair, and aligned with instructional purposes, and that teachers and measurement specialists must remain involved in design, interpretation, and correction of AI outputs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can automate scoring, content analysis, item generation, and feedback, reducing educator workload and accelerating turnaround time. It gives illustrative examples showing that automated scoring and NLP-based feedback can provide faster, more consistent outputs than human-only processes, but it does not report a single experimental effect size.
finding.measure: teacher workload; scoring turnaround time; automation of feedback and item generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a governance-oriented analysis of AI in educational measurement, focusing on validity, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and human oversight. It synthesizes examples and standards rather than reporting a single empirical estimate, concluding that AI systems can support educational measurement only if institutions implement ethical guidelines, bias checks, and documentation.
finding.measure: ethical governance considerations; validity/fairness standards; institutional AI use guidelines

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses automated writing evaluation and automated essay scoring as AI-supported literacy tools that can improve writing quality and provide feedback on grammar, organization, development, and revision. It cites prior studies reporting effect sizes ranging from 0.38 to 0.98 in tertiary and L2 settings, but those results are summarized from the literature rather than newly estimated in this paper.
finding.measure: writing quality; automated writing evaluation feedback; essay scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AWE can sometimes increase motivation and self-efficacy, but effects are inconsistent and may be negative for some high-achieving students who perceive automated feedback as less affirming than teacher feedback. These claims are based on cited prior studies, not new data from the paper itself.
finding.measure: motivation; self-efficacy; writing-related beliefs and affect

paper_profiles.title: Intentionality and Players of Effective Online Courses in Mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether online mathematics courses at the University of the South Pacific were effective in promoting student engagement and achievement, and whether the structure of assessments mattered for those outcomes. The core question is whether common online activities and assessments—such as quizzes, assignments, forums, and learning resources—were associated with stronger performance, and whether courses with more frequent, interactive assessment were more successful than courses relying mainly on end-of-semester assessment.

The authors analyzed two mathematics courses (MA111 and MA112) and two information systems courses (IS121 and IS122) offered through Moodle. They extracted class lists, final grades, and Moodle log data, then used normality tests and Spearman correlations to relate student interactions in activities to assessment marks and final grades. The mathematics courses had relatively few assessment opportunities and showed only weak positive associations between interaction and performance, whereas the information systems courses used more frequent weekly assessments and showed stronger correlations between activity engagement and achievement.

The main conclusion is that online mathematics courses in this setting were less interactive and less engaging than the comparison information systems courses, and that limited formative/continuous assessment likely contributed to lower success rates. The paper recommends more frequent quizzes, discussion forums, peer evaluation, self-assessment, and immediate feedback, arguing that these mechanisms can better support active learning, community, and student success in online mathematics courses. Although the paper is about course design and engagement rather than AI specifically, it is directly relevant to the role of learning analytics and embedded assessment in formative adaptation of instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across the mathematics courses, stronger participation in online activities was associated with higher assessment marks, but the relationships were generally weak. In MA111 and MA112, Spearman correlations between activity interaction and performance were mostly below +0.5, while the strongest association in mathematics was for collective course work and final performance (e.g., r_s=0.904 in MA111 Sem 2, 2017; r_s=0.877 in MA111 Sem 1, 2018; r_s=0.605 in MA112 Sem 1, 2016; r_s=0.904 in MA112 Sem 2, 2017).
finding.measure: Spearman correlation between online activity interactions, course work, and final course marks in mathematics courses
finding.study_size: MA111 n=75 and n=116; MA112 n=33 and n=72

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that more interactive and frequent online assessments were linked to greater student engagement in the mathematics and comparison information systems courses. In mathematics, interaction-performance links were weak, and the authors interpret this as reflecting limited engagement and presence in the online learning space; in information systems, weekly assessments and forum use were associated with stronger engagement and achievement, suggesting that frequent formative activities help sustain motivation and participation.
finding.measure: Interaction counts in Moodle logs, engagement/presence in activities, and their correlation with marks
finding.study_size: MA111 n=75 and n=116; MA112 n=33 and n=72; IS121 n=72 and n=126; IS122 n=32 and n=50

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that interactive assessments such as quizzes, forum discussions, peer evaluations, and self-assessments support collaboration, higher-order thinking, and active learning. Empirically, forum and quiz participation showed positive correlations with performance in several offerings, especially in the information systems courses, where weekly forum discussions and quizzes were moderately to strongly associated with achievement (e.g., rs values commonly >+0.5).
finding.measure: Moodle activity interactions tied to discussion forums, quizzes, homework, and assessed/nonassessed course performance
finding.study_size: MA111 n=75 and n=116; MA112 n=33 and n=72; IS121 n=72 and n=126; IS122 n=32 and n=50

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of a Mobile Web Application for Assessment Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a mobile web application for assessment feedback, called MyFeedBack, improves students’ experience of receiving feedback compared with the university’s existing Moodle system. The study is motivated by a common problem in higher education: feedback is often delivered in ways that are slow, impersonal, hard to access, and do not encourage two-way communication. The author asks whether a different delivery medium can increase acceptance, engagement, and dialogue around assessment feedback.

MyFeedBack was designed to let students access formative or summative feedback on any device, see feedback before grades, keep feedback private, and use a ‘Leave Feedback’ feature to reply to lecturers. The paper uses a sequential explanatory mixed-method design with 239 higher-education students in the UK, including a summative subgroup (n=65, with survey comparison across Moodle and MyFeedBack) and a formative subgroup (n=25 for the type-of-feedback comparison). Quantitative analyses found significantly higher system acceptance for MyFeedBack than Moodle (M=12.4 vs 11.0, t(229)=-2.43, p=.0156, Cohen’s d=0.30), while most other scales did not differ. Within MyFeedBack users, system functions were rated more positively for summative than formative feedback (Md=18 vs 14, U=565, p=.0389, r=-0.22). Qualitative findings showed that MyFeedBack supported faster access, privacy, personalization, and especially communication and dialogue for summative feedback, but the formative group did not meaningfully engage in dialogue. The paper concludes with design guidelines for feedback systems, emphasizing accessibility, feedback-first presentation, personalization, privacy, dialogue, monitoring, and optional peer-feedback tools.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported more positive attitudes toward MyFeedBack than Moodle, especially on system acceptance items related to engagement and motivation with feedback. Quantitatively, system acceptance was significantly higher for MyFeedBack (M=12.4, SD=4.00) than Moodle (M=11.0, SD=4.21), t(229)=-2.43, p=.0156, Cohen's d=0.30.
finding.measure: System Acceptance scale; student attitudes toward engagement/motivation/interaction with feedback

finding.finding_summary: The application was intended to increase communication, dialogue, and interaction about feedback, and qualitative evidence showed this happened strongly for summative feedback but not for formative feedback. In the summative group, 21% of 251 students used the Leave Feedback feature and lecturers replied to comments, but the formative group produced no comments and lower digital engagement.
finding.measure: Feedback dialogue / communication via Leave Feedback feature; qualitative interview and observation data
finding.study_size: summative digital footprints n=251; formative group not_reported; survey users n=90

finding.finding_summary: Students and the lecturer described MyFeedBack as faster and easier for retrieving and delivering feedback, and the study proposes it as a way to reduce the effort of personalized feedback delivery. The qualitative findings emphasize quicker turnaround, easier access, and less cumbersome communication than email or Moodle, but no direct workload metric was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of speed, ease of use, and convenience for feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that MyFeedBack offers design guidelines for institutions seeking to improve assessment feedback systems, including accessibility, privacy, personalization, dialogue, and monitoring. It also suggests that integrating such a system into institutional VLEs could support broader adoption, though the evidence is based on one institution and no policy-level outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Design guidelines for feedback systems; institutional adoption and integration implications

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing Education: The Impact of AI-Enhanced Teaching Strategies
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science & Engineering Technology (IJRASET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence can transform education through personalized learning, adaptive feedback, intelligent tutoring systems, and learning analytics. It frames AI as a way to move beyond one-size-fits-all instruction by using student performance data to tailor content, pacing, remediation, and support in real time.

The article is a broad conceptual review rather than an empirical evaluation. It describes example platforms such as Knewton, DreamBox, ALEKS, Carnegie Learning’s Cognitive Tutor, Duolingo, and Squirrel AI, and argues that AI can improve engagement, inclusivity, and instructional responsiveness. The paper also highlights how AI-driven analytics can identify learning gaps and support targeted interventions, but it does not report original data, sample characteristics, or effect estimates.

Because the paper is largely descriptive and synthesizes prior work at a high level, it offers general claims about benefits and implementation challenges rather than a test of a specific intervention in a defined population. Its main conclusion is that AI-enhanced teaching strategies can support more adaptive, student-centered education when used thoughtfully and ethically, though the article provides no direct empirical evidence for those claims.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-driven analytics and automated assessment can reduce teacher workload by providing immediate scoring, identifying learning gaps, and supporting data-informed instructional decisions. It claims these tools optimize instructional methods and enable targeted interventions, but it does not report original empirical evidence, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: teacher workload, automated assessment, instructional decision support

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI-enhanced personalization, adaptive challenge, and immediate feedback can increase student engagement, motivation, and participation. These effects are described qualitatively through examples such as gamified learning and real-time feedback loops, with no original measurement or numerical outcomes reported.
finding.measure: student engagement, motivation, participation

paper_profiles.title: From tests to tasks: how Vietnamese EFL teachers navigate washback through formative assessment practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Vietnamese EFL teachers respond to the strong washback of high-stakes, exam-oriented assessment by adopting formative assessment (FA) practices after participating in British Council professional development courses. The authors ask how teachers reframe the purpose of assessment, what tensions they face when trying to implement FA in test-driven schools, and how they adapt assessment practices in context-specific ways.

The study is based on 72 written reflective narratives from teachers working across primary, lower secondary, and upper secondary schools in Vietnam, including urban, rural, semi-boarding, and ethnic minority-focused settings. Using a thematic narrative analysis, the paper shows that teachers moved, to varying degrees, from score-focused routines toward more dialogic, student-centered, and responsive assessment practices, such as peer feedback, storytelling circles, rubric-based peer review, exit tickets, self-assessment checklists, and observation-based adjustments to instruction.

The main conclusion is that formative assessment is not simply a matter of using quizzes, rubrics, or feedback tools; it becomes meaningfully formative only when teachers use evidence from those activities to adjust teaching and involve students in the assessment process. The paper also identifies four enactment modes—strategic alignment, symbolic integration, hybrid blending, and pedagogical reframing—showing that teacher agency, institutional pressure, and local context shape whether FA is used instrumentally for test preparation or more fully as learning-oriented practice.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that formative assessment practices such as peer feedback, storytelling circles, oral questioning, and group discussion helped make student speaking and oral comprehension more visible and supported more dialogic participation. However, implementation was uneven: some students remained test-oriented, some peer feedback was superficial, and in some cases teachers found oral evidence hard to interpret or follow up on, limiting the formative value.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections describing oral tasks, speaking participation, peer feedback, and observation of student oral responses

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described using FA to support writing and vocabulary learning through rubrics, peer review, self-assessment checklists, drawing-based prompts, and replacing weekly quizzes with more process-oriented tasks. Reflections suggest these practices helped students revise writing more specifically and revealed vocabulary knowledge beyond rote memorization, although some enactments remained symbolic or instrumental rather than truly learning-centered.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on writing tasks, descriptive writing peer review, vocabulary quizzes, spelling tests, and written self-assessment

finding.finding_summary: Across reflections, teachers reported that FA reduced pressure and anxiety for some students and increased engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate in classroom activities. At the same time, some students were confused by non-test forms of assessment or continued to wait for the 'real test,' so the emotional and motivational effects were positive but not universal.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student anxiety, engagement, confidence, and participation during formative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that FA supported durable skills by fostering collaboration, reflection, self-assessment, and metacognitive adjustment. Teachers repeatedly described peer feedback, rubric use, self-assessment checklists, and responsive task redesign as ways students learned to think about quality, revise work, and participate in feedback loops, though the strength of enactment varied by context.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on peer review, self-assessment, collaboration, reflection, and responsive adjustment of learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that institutional and policy pressures strongly shaped whether FA could be enacted, with teachers negotiating exam demands, department heads, grading requirements, school ranking pressures, and local authority structures. The paper identifies four modes of enactment and concludes that FA reform is mediated by policy enactment, teacher agency, and school culture rather than simple PD uptake.
finding.measure: Teacher narratives about school policy, grading expectations, exam pressure, departmental oversight, and FA enactment modes

paper_profiles.title: State English Learner Education Policy: A Conceptual Framework to Guide Comprehensive Policy Action
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that U.S. states, as the primary governing level for public education, need a coherent way to organize English learner (EL) policy, yet existing research and policymaking are fragmented across classrooms, schools, and districts. The authors argue that EL policy should be driven by an equity-oriented conceptual framework that recognizes student diversity and aligns policy choices with EL students’ access to content, language development, and supportive systems.

The paper does not evaluate an intervention. Instead, it synthesizes decades of EL policy research and state policy examples to build a framework organized around three principles: understanding student needs and assets, providing accessible high-quality instruction, and supporting effective and aligned education systems. Within these principles, it outlines nine policy areas, including EL diversity, assessment, classification/reclassification, access to core content, English language development instruction, bilingual education, funding, teacher preparation, and pre-K through postsecondary alignment.

The population of focus is K-12 English learners in U.S. public schools, with special attention to subgroups such as English learners with disabilities, newcomers, and long-term English learners. The context is state policy in the U.S., and the intended users are policymakers and other state-level education administrators. The main conclusion is that states should adopt more comprehensive, differentiated, and coherent EL policy approaches rather than isolated or reactive policies, and that policy design should better align identification, instructional access, assessment, and reclassification with the varied needs of EL students.

finding.finding_summary: This conceptual policy paper synthesizes existing research to propose a state-level framework for EL education policy rather than testing a program or intervention. It argues that state policies should be organized around student needs and assets, high-quality instruction, and aligned systems, and identifies nine policy areas for action; no effect size or sample size is reported because the paper is not an empirical outcomes study.
finding.measure: State EL policy frameworks, policy areas, and policy implications synthesized from prior literature

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Equity and Inclusion in Online Learning Environments: Strategies for Ensuring Access and Success for All Students
paper_profiles.population: Not clearly specified; broad online learning population (students in online education settings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of inequitable access and exclusion in online learning environments. It argues that while online education can expand access, students still face barriers related to socioeconomic status, the digital divide, technological infrastructure, disability access, language and culture, and the lack of inclusive course design.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature, case studies, reports, and policy documents to identify strategies for more equitable and inclusive online learning. It discusses frameworks and practices such as Universal Design for Learning (UDL), personalized learning, multimodal course materials, clear communication, collaborative learning, assistive technologies, adaptive learning systems, and immersive technologies like VR/AR. The paper’s main conclusion is that institutions should combine accessible design, supportive technologies, and inclusive pedagogy to improve participation, engagement, and success for diverse learners.

The context is online learning broadly, with particular attention to students from marginalized or underrepresented groups, including students with disabilities, multilingual learners, and learners from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. The paper is conceptual/theoretical rather than empirical; it does not report original participant data or measure outcomes from an implemented intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions can improve equity and inclusion in online learning by adopting policies and practices such as UDL, accessibility standards, support services, and culturally responsive design. No original effect estimates are reported; the conclusions are based on a synthesis of prior literature and case examples.
finding.measure: Institutional policies, accessibility practices, and inclusive design strategies in online learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that inclusive online environments improve student engagement, motivation, belonging, perseverance, and satisfaction. These claims are supported conceptually through cited literature, but no original sample or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, belonging, motivation, perseverance, and satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses collaborative learning, critical thinking, and metacognitive skills as benefits of inclusive online instructional strategies, especially collaborative learning, personalized learning, and immersive technologies. The paper does not present new quantitative evidence.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, collaboration, metacognition, and communication skills

paper_profiles.title: Linguistically and Culturally Diverse Students: Their Language Development, Assessment, and Support in the Public Education System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines how linguistically and culturally diverse (LCD) students in Ontario’s K–12 public education system develop language and literacy, how fairly they are assessed, and how their heritage-language learning is supported. The work is motivated by concerns that education systems often privilege students who speak the dominant societal language, leaving multilingual, immigrant, and other LCD students vulnerable to lower achievement, biased assessment, and weak support for maintaining home languages.

The dissertation contains three empirical studies. Study 1 uses longitudinal cohort data from Ontario provincial assessments to examine changes in home language use from grades 3 to 10 and how different home-language shift patterns relate to English literacy growth; it also tests whether immigration status and ESL enrollment predict achievement patterns. Study 2 analyzes approximately 3,400 grade 3 students from a large-scale reading assessment using differential item functioning to determine whether culturally familiar or culturally sensitive items disadvantage students with different lengths of residence in Canada. Study 3 is a qualitative case study of Korean heritage language classes in Ontario’s International Languages Elementary Program, based on interviews with five teachers and nine parents, to understand assessment and reporting practices in a publicly funded heritage-language program.

Across the studies, the dissertation concludes that maintaining home languages is associated with stronger literacy performance, culturally loaded test items can disadvantage LCD students, and heritage-language programs need clearer, more supportive assessment practices. More broadly, the dissertation argues for policies and assessment systems that recognize the heterogeneity of LCD students, avoid deficit-oriented assumptions, and better support bilingual and multilingual development in public schools.

finding.finding_summary: Study 1 found that students who maintained multilingual home-language environments showed superior English literacy performance relative to students whose home language shifted toward English dominance, suggesting a positive association between sustained multilingualism and literacy outcomes. The study used provincial cohort data across grades 3 to 10 (home-language change sample n=89,609; analytic growth model subsample n=18,000), but the excerpt does not report standardized effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations.
finding.measure: English literacy performance / provincial literacy assessment scores; home language environment

finding.finding_summary: Study 2 found that reading test items with high cultural sensitivity functioned differentially across student groups, disadvantaging LCD students relative to Canadian-born English-first-language peers. The analysis used provincial reading assessment data (N=82,922 for descriptive/item analyses; the study sample for the DIF comparisons is described as approximately 3,400 grade 3 students in the dissertation overview), but the excerpt does not report a single overall effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Differential item functioning (DIF) on large-scale reading test items
finding.study_size: N=82,922 (test dataset); approximately n=3,400 grade 3 students in the study overview

paper_profiles.title: Assessment of Digital Literacy Skills on Autonomous Learning Practices among Undergraduate Students of Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, Kaduna State
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether and to what extent digital literacy skills are associated with autonomous learning practices among 100-level English as a Second Language (ESL) undergraduates at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. The paper is motivated by the growing role of digital tools in language learning and the view that digital literacy may help students become more self-directed learners.
