However, the authors also note that incremental/fixed mindset effects were small (ES=0.19), suggesting limited impact for changing mindset alone.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, task value, anxiety, attitude to content, mindset, motivation

finding.finding_summary: Durable-skills strategies showed positive effects, especially for metacognition, self-regulation, and transfer. The review reports strong effects for knowing success criteria (overall ES=0.54), acquiring deep learning (ES=0.57), consolidating deep learning (ES=0.53), and transfer strategies such as detecting similarities and differences (ES=1.32) and seeing patterns in new situations (ES=1.14).
finding.measure: Success criteria, metacognitive/self-regulation strategies, and transfer performance

finding.finding_summary: Several strategies aimed at improving study efficiency and task management showed positive associations, though generally smaller than content-focused strategies. The review reports effects for environmental structuring (ES=0.41), time management (ES=0.40), and student control over learning (ES=0.02), indicating that some efficiency-related supports help but are not among the strongest influences.
finding.measure: Environmental structuring, time management, student control over learning

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perception of Kahoot!’s influence on teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how university students perceived the use of Kahoot!, a game-based student response system, in a third-year Information Systems Strategy and Governance course. The authors were interested in whether Kahoot! influenced classroom dynamics, engagement, motivation, and learning, because prior research had largely relied on quantitative ratings and had left open questions about how students actually experienced the tool.

The intervention was embedded in seven lectures over a semester at a research-intensive university in New Zealand. Kahoot! was used in several ways: as a pre-lecture or in-lecture quiz to gauge understanding, as a post-lecture check on comprehension, as student-created quizzes, and occasionally for off-topic fun. Fourteen of 48 enrolled students participated in semi-structured interviews after the course, and the researchers conducted inductive content analysis of the transcripts.

Findings were uniformly positive for engagement and classroom dynamics, with students describing Kahoot! as capturing attention, creating breaks in long lectures, increasing interaction with peers and the lecturer, and motivating participation through competition and anonymity. Students also reported that Kahoot! supported revision, helped them remember and retain knowledge, and was most valuable when paired with post-quiz discussion and timely feedback. The study concludes that Kahoot! can enrich learning experiences in tertiary classrooms, but its educational value depends on balancing fun with subject relevance and on the quality of the follow-up discussion.

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported that Kahoot! increased attention, engagement, motivation, and enjoyment in class. All 14 participants said it positively impacted engagement, and the tool was described as helping maintain focus during long lectures, motivating preparation, and making participation feel safer through anonymity.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions of engagement, attention, motivation, and enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that Kahoot! supported deeper thinking, reflection, and knowledge checking, especially when combined with post-quiz discussion and feedback. However, some participants said competition and game-like elements could distract from learning, suggesting that metacognitive benefits depended on how the tool was used.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions of reflection, deeper understanding, and knowledge checking

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that students perceived Kahoot! as improving learning and knowledge retention in an undergraduate Information Systems course. Nine participants explicitly described improved learning and retention, 12 viewed it as useful for revision, and students said it helped them remember previously covered material and understand new perspectives.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions of learning, revision, and retention of course content

paper_profiles.title: Introductory programming: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.venue: ITiCSE 2018 Companion: Proceedings Companion of the 23rd Annual ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic literature review of introductory programming research published between 2003 and 2017. The authors ask what aspects of introductory programming have been studied, what developments occurred over time, and what evidence has been reported across those studies. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes the literature across four broad areas: the student, teaching, curriculum, and assessment.

The review follows a structured search-and-screen process across ACM, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Scopus, ultimately classifying 1,666 papers into topical categories. The authors emphasize that most work in the field focuses on teaching and students, with fewer studies on curriculum and assessment. Within student-focused work, they summarize findings on mental models, code literacy, behavior, ability, attitudes, engagement, student experience, and at-risk/underrepresented subgroups.

For the specific question of outcomes beyond immediate achievement, the review identifies research on motivation, self-regulated learning, engagement, and related attitudes, but it is itself a synthesis rather than an empirical intervention study. The paper concludes that the field has grown substantially, especially outside SIGCSE venues, and that stronger methodological rigor, better measurement, and more work on correlations between behavior and learning outcomes are needed. It also notes that many interventions report success, but effect sizes are often missing or hard to compare across studies.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes a large body of introductory programming research showing substantial attention to motivation, self-efficacy, engagement, and self-regulated learning, but the evidence is uneven. It notes that many interventions report success (e.g., peer instruction, flipped classrooms, journaling, gamification, mindset feedback), yet effect sizes are often not reported or not comparable, and some motivational findings are weak or context-dependent.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, self-efficacy/self-perception measures, engagement measures, self-regulated learning constructs, persistence/retention indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports research on code reading, code writing, debugging, and related cognitive processes such as mental models and reasoning about programs. The review concludes that code-reading skills underpin code-writing/problem-solving, but also notes that students can sometimes perform well on tasks despite holding non-viable mental models, implying that conventional assessments may miss some misconceptions.
finding.measure: Code-reading tasks, tracing tasks, code-writing/debugging performance, program comprehension tasks, assessments of mental models

finding.finding_summary: As a broad review of introductory programming, the paper documents evidence across programming-learning outcomes and course performance rather than a single subject area. It summarizes that students’ ability is commonly measured using exams, code assessment, knowledge tests, and learning analytics, with a general conclusion that performance can be predicted and measured in multiple ways but that richer, more reliable indicators are still needed.
finding.measure: Exams, code assessment, knowledge acquisition tests, self-report, learning analytics, course performance

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual perspective; no empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may reshape human learning, with attention to both opportunities and risks. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize literature from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI could scale personalized learning support, diversify learning resources, provide timely feedback, and enable more authentic and adaptive assessment.

The paper also highlights major challenges, including hallucinations, transparency, privacy, bias, equity, and the disruption of conventional assessment practices. A central argument is that GenAI should be used to support, not replace, human cognition and metacognition, and that AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor are necessary for responsible adoption.

Because the article is a conceptual review/perspective rather than an empirical study, it does not report primary data, participant samples, or effect sizes. Its main contribution is a research agenda: future studies should evaluate GenAI’s impact on cognition, metacognition, creativity, agency, and learning outcomes using rigorous designs such as longitudinal and randomized controlled studies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may improve learner engagement and motivation through timely feedback and personalized support, but also warns that overreliance can reduce agency and possibly undermine motivation. No primary study is reported; the paper synthesizes prior findings and explicitly notes that evidence on engagement and agency is currently mixed.
finding.measure: Learner engagement, agency, motivation (literature-synthesized outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, creativity, and self-regulation. It claims GenAI may support these skills when used as a guided tutor, but also emphasizes evidence that performance can improve while underlying skills do not, creating a 'performance paradox' and possible overdependence.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, problem-solving, creativity (conceptual/literature review)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can reduce educator workload and improve efficiency by generating learning resources and providing instant, scalable feedback. It presents this as a promise rather than a tested effect, and does not report primary quantitative evidence in this article.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, feedback efficiency, resource-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes broader institutional implications, including assessment redesign, AI literacy, ethical governance, privacy, equity, and methodological standards for GenAI research and deployment. It does not test policy outcomes empirically, but argues these systemic issues are central to responsible educational adoption of GenAI.
finding.measure: Assessment validity, AI literacy, ethics, equity, research rigor, institutional adoption

paper_profiles.title: Teaching in Blended Learning Environments: Creating and Sustaining Communities of Inquiry
paper_profiles.venue: au Press (book in the Issues in Distance Education series)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book addresses how to design, facilitate, direct, and assess blended learning in higher education so that it supports a Community of Inquiry (CoI) rather than merely adding online tools to conventional instruction. The central problem is that simply mixing face-to-face and online activities does not automatically improve learning; instead, the authors argue that teaching presence must be intentionally designed to support social presence, cognitive presence, and meaningful educational outcomes.

The approach is primarily conceptual and practice-oriented rather than empirical. Drawing on the CoI framework, the book lays out seven principles for blended teaching, organized around design, facilitation, direct instruction, and assessment. It emphasizes purposeful inquiry, open communication, cohesion, critical reflection, discourse, and assessment aligned with intended processes and outcomes.

The context is higher education, with examples, rubrics, and social media activities illustrating how instructors might structure blended courses. The book repeatedly argues that blended learning can improve engagement, reflection, and persistence when it is thoughtfully designed, but it does not present original experimental data or comparative outcome testing. Its conclusions are prescriptive: effective blended learning depends on coherent instructional design, sustained community, and assessment practices that support deep and meaningful learning.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that blended learning, when designed around a Community of Inquiry, supports higher-order thinking, critical reflection, discourse, metacognition, and collaboration. However, these claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than based on reported empirical effect sizes or original outcome data.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, reflection, discourse, and collaboration within blended learning designs

finding.finding_summary: The authors emphasize that well-designed blended learning can strengthen engagement, persistence, trust, open communication, and group cohesion. The text links social presence to perceived learning and persistence, but does not report original quantitative results for these outcomes.
finding.measure: Conceptual/practice-oriented discussion of engagement, persistence, trust, and group cohesion

finding.finding_summary: The book focuses on higher education teaching and learning processes, arguing that thoughtful blended design can improve the quality of the educational experience and support meaningful learning outcomes. These are design claims supported by cited literature and examples, not by new empirical evaluation in the book itself.
finding.measure: Quality of educational experience / meaningful learning outcomes in higher education

paper_profiles.title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether computer-based scaffolding improves learning in problem-based learning (PBL) settings for STEM education, and whether effects differ by scaffolding type, customization, delivery method, strategy, intended higher-order skill, and discipline. The authors use Bayesian meta-analysis to address limitations of traditional meta-analysis, including small-study effects and sparse subgroups.

The review includes 21 studies and 47 outcomes published between 1990 and 2015. It synthesizes evidence from STEM PBL interventions using conceptual, strategic, metacognitive, and motivational scaffolds, as well as different scaffolding strategies (feedback, question prompts, hints, expert modeling) and customization approaches (fading, adding, self-selection, performance-adaptation, fixed intervals). The analysis focuses on student cognitive learning outcomes and higher-order thinking skills rather than general classroom processes.

Overall, computer-based scaffolding produced a small-to-moderate positive effect on cognitive outcomes (g = 0.385, 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802). Effects were stronger for metacognitive and strategic scaffolding than for conceptual scaffolding, stronger when scaffolds were customized than when they were not, and strongest when students self-selected scaffolding changes. Among higher-order skills, scaffolding most strongly supported analysis (g = 0.537), while synthesis and evaluation effects were much smaller. Effects also varied by discipline, with larger effects in engineering, mathematics, and technology than in science, and a relatively smaller effect in integrated STEM.

finding.finding_summary: Computer-based scaffolding in STEM PBL had a positive overall effect on higher-order thinking outcomes (g = 0.385, 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802) across 21 studies and 47 outcomes. The strongest effect was for analysis skills (g = 0.537, 95% CrI 0.038 to 0.981), while synthesis (g = 0.156, 95% CrI 0.004 to 0.329) and evaluation (g = 0.147, 95% CrI 0.003 to 0.288) were much smaller.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills (analysis, synthesis, evaluation) in problem-based learning STEM outcomes
finding.effect_size: g=0.385 overall; g=0.537 analysis; g=0.156 synthesis; g=0.147 evaluation
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802 overall; analysis 0.038 to 0.981; synthesis 0.004 to 0.329; evaluation 0.003 to 0.288

paper_profiles.title: Online Instruction in Higher Education: Promising, Research-based, and Evidence-based Practices
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the research literature on online learning in higher education to identify instructional practices associated with effective learning, student support, faculty pedagogy, engagement, and success. The authors explicitly narrowed the review to empirical studies published from 2013–2019, focusing on undergraduate and graduate learners and studies with sufficient methodological detail to assess verifiability.

The review synthesizes 104 studies and organizes them into five themes: course design factors, student support, faculty pedagogy, student engagement, and student success factors. Across these studies, the authors report that many commonly used online practices are associated with student satisfaction, persistence, or achievement, including instructor feedback, high instructor presence, orientation to online learning, and supportive learning environments. However, they conclude that rigorous causal evidence is limited, no intervention besides faculty feedback could be confidently identified as evidence-based, and few studies support claims that specific online practices are research-based in the stronger sense.

For the sub-questions most relevant to formative assessment and broader outcomes, the review finds that feedback and support can improve motivation, self-reflection, self-regulation, and achievement, but the evidence is mostly correlational or small experimental work rather than strong causal studies. The paper also highlights that many studies rely on course grades or immediate performance measures, with relatively little direct evidence on long-term retention, transfer, or durable learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed online-learning studies, course design and pedagogy interventions were usually associated with immediate course achievement or performance, but results were inconsistent across modalities and tools. The review reports no significant differences in learning between fully online, blended, and face-to-face modalities in many studies, and many conclusions are based on course grades, exams, or other short-term achievement measures rather than transfer or retention outcomes.
finding.measure: course grades, end-of-term tests, course performance

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature linked online instruction features to motivation, engagement, satisfaction, persistence, and self-efficacy. Examples cited in the review include higher motivation from instructor presence and feedback, improved engagement from supportive structures and interactive tools, and associations between online success and self-regulation-related variables; however, much of this evidence is correlational and measures are often self-report surveys.
finding.measure: motivation scales, engagement surveys, self-regulated learning questionnaires, satisfaction surveys, persistence/retention indicators
finding.study_size: varies across studies; corpus n=104 studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies several studies suggesting that online instructional supports can improve durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, and critical thinking. For example, metacognitive support within flipped learning was associated with higher forethought, self-regulation, and self-reflection scores, and some course-design studies found that critical-thinking promotion and collaborative structures were related to student collaboration and knowledge building.
finding.measure: metacognitive/self-regulation scales, collaboration indicators, discussion/forum participation, knowledge-building measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper has an institutional-level contribution in that it synthesizes evidence to inform higher-education online-learning practice and identifies which practices are promising versus evidence-based. Its main institutional conclusion is that, because rigorous causal studies are scarce, institutions should be cautious in claiming effectiveness for most online practices; the review singles out faculty feedback as the only clearly evidence-based practice among the studies examined.
finding.measure: evidence synthesis across 104 studies; methodological appraisal of online-learning research

paper_profiles.title: Educational Games – Are They Worth The Effort? A literature survey of the effectiveness of serious games
paper_profiles.venue: Games and Virtual Worlds for Serious Applications (VS-GAMES), 2013 5th International Conference on
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Secondary School, High School, Higher Education, Preschool
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys empirical research on the educational effectiveness of serious games in formal school contexts. The authors ask not only whether games improve learning, but also what kinds of studies have been conducted, what outcomes have been measured, and whether evaluation results differ when the evaluator is a stakeholder in the game’s development. The review is limited to journal articles published between 2002 and the first half of 2012 that report empirical evidence on learning effects.

Using multiple databases and a structured screening process, the authors identified 40 papers covering a wide range of topics, including mathematics, language, geography, science, problem solving, software development, and surgery. Across the included studies, most reported positive effects, though results were mixed in some domains and the paper notes a tendency for more positive findings when developers were involved in evaluation. The review also highlights a lack of longitudinal evidence and calls for more research on actual classroom use, user acceptance, curricular fit, and longer-term effects such as retention and sustained transfer.

Although the paper is framed around learning effectiveness broadly, it does not directly synthesize formative assessment specifically. Its main contribution is a structured overview of the evidence base for serious games in education and the methodological patterns in that literature, rather than a single intervention effect estimate.

finding.finding_summary: Across the mathematics studies (13/40 papers), the review reports mixed results: 7/12 evaluations were positive, 5/12 neutral, and 1/12 negative. The paper also notes that motivational gains were often positive, but achievement effects varied by context and student subgroup; for example, Kim and Chang (2010) found lower mathematics achievement for English-speaking fourth graders who played computer math games every day, while some language-minority boys showed higher performance.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests and motivational outcomes in game-based learning studies
finding.study_size: Multiple studies; mathematics subset n=13 papers / 12 evaluations reported

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several language-learning studies and highlights one qualitative study of two 13-year-old Finnish boys over 13 hours of gameplay that showed rich opportunities for reading, speaking, and using English in interaction. However, the paper explicitly cautions that this evidence does not establish longitudinal gains in language expertise, so the finding concerns in-game language use and situated learning rather than durable proficiency.
finding.measure: Observed interaction, dialogue transcripts, and language use during gameplay
finding.study_size: n=2 focal participants; 13 hours of interaction data

finding.finding_summary: The review covers multiple non-math subjects including geography, history, science, computer science, and surgery, and reports that most included studies found positive learning outcomes. For example, geography and natural science studies are described as especially promising, and the surgery studies are highlighted as useful training tools that may correlate with real-world performance, though the paper does not aggregate effect sizes across these topics.
finding.measure: Subject-specific learning outcomes across multiple domains (e.g., geography achievement, history learning, surgical simulator performance, computer science learning)

finding.finding_summary: Motivation is one of the most consistently positive outcomes in the review. Several studies reported improved student motivation from game-based learning, including Yang (2012), where a quasi-experiment over 23 weeks with 44 ninth-grade students found better learning motivation in the game-based group than in the traditional-learning control group.
finding.measure: Motivation scales / motivational outcomes
finding.study_size: n=44 in the Yang (2012) quasi-experiment; multiple other studies in review

finding.finding_summary: The review explicitly includes studies on problem solving, collaboration, argumentation, and deep learning strategies, which it treats as higher-order skills. In Yang (2012), a quasi-experiment with 44 ninth-grade students found that the digital game-based learning group significantly improved problem-solving skills while the control group did not, suggesting benefits beyond immediate factual achievement.
finding.measure: Problem-solving test (finding causes, solutions, and avoiding problems); deep learning strategy use; collaborative argumentation
finding.study_size: n=44 in a semester-long quasi-experiment; other studies summarized qualitatively

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly study efficiency in terms of teacher workload or productivity, but it does discuss training tools such as surgical simulators as potentially useful because they can save money and reduce patient risk, and it notes that games can serve as effective assessment/training tools. These are discussed as practical advantages rather than measured efficiency outcomes, so the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing Large Language Models to Enhance Self-Regulated Learning via Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, can be used to deliver formative feedback that supports self-regulated learning (SRL). The authors argue that merely giving students access to a chatbot is not enough; instead, prompts should be carefully designed from theory to elicit feedback that stimulates cognition, metacognition, and motivation.

The paper introduces LEAP, an open-access web platform that allows teachers to create physics tasks and configure prompt templates for LLM-generated feedback without programming. The prompt framework is organized into three parts: a condition specifying when feedback should be given, a consequence that elicits a targeted scaffold (e.g., sense-making, elaboration, self-explanation, partial solutions, metacognitive or motivational scaffolds), and a refinement that prevents giving the full correct answer. The implementation is demonstrated with a Newton’s cradle physics task and example prompts that produce different kinds of feedback.

The intended context is secondary-school physics learning, with teachers using the system to support students’ problem solving and self-regulation. However, the paper is primarily a systems/design and theory paper rather than an empirical evaluation of student learning outcomes. Its main conclusion is that theoretically grounded prompt engineering can make LLMs more useful for formative feedback and SRL support, but the paper does not provide experimental evidence that LEAP improves retention, transfer, motivation, or self-regulated learning outcomes beyond illustrative examples of generated feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report empirical outcomes on scientific reasoning; it only demonstrates how the platform can generate physics feedback for a Newton’s cradle task. The example is illustrative, not a measured student outcome, so no effect size, confidence interval, or sample-based inference is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper theorizes that LEAP-generated feedback could support motivation and self-regulated learning, but it does not measure student motivation, persistence, engagement, or SRL. The only evidence is a set of example prompts and generated responses, so no empirical effect is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The central theoretical focus is on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and related cognitive scaffolds such as sense-making, elaboration, and self-explanation. Despite this strong conceptual emphasis, the paper does not evaluate whether these prompts improved metacognitive skill, transfer, or retention in learners.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LEAP may reduce teacher workload by allowing educators to create prompt-based formative feedback without programming and by streamlining task creation and answer-feedback handling. This is a functional/design claim rather than a measured productivity outcome; no sample size or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / task-creation workflow

paper_profiles.title: Irec: A Metacognitive Scaffolding for Self-Regulated Learning through Just-in-Time Insight Recall: A Conceptual Framework and System Prototype
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that current digital learning tools do not adequately support metacognitive reflection and self-regulated learning (SRL). The authors argue that spaced repetition systems emphasize de-contextualized fact review, while personal knowledge management tools impose high manual maintenance costs and still fail to surface learners’ past problem-solving insights at the moment they are most useful.

To address this, the paper proposes “Insight Recall,” a conceptual learning paradigm in which a system retrieves a learner’s own prior insights in response to a new problem context. The authors formalize the idea with a Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention (JITAI) framework and implement a prototype called Irec, which uses a Neo4j knowledge graph, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and an optional guided-inquiry LLM module. The system is designed for students working in knowledge-intensive domains such as calculus, but the paper only demonstrates the concept through an illustrative scenario rather than a user study.

The paper’s central contribution is theoretical and technical: it provides a framework and prototype for context-triggered, human-AI collaborative metacognitive support. The authors explicitly state that the manuscript does not yet validate learning outcomes empirically. Instead, it positions Irec as a foundation for future controlled longitudinal studies on retention, transfer, and SRL. Because there is no experimental evaluation, the paper offers no measured evidence of impact on achievement, motivation, or self-regulation beyond conceptual claims and a worked example.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not empirically test whether Irec improves motivation, engagement, or self-regulation. It only claims conceptually that the system is intended to promote metacognitive reflection as part of SRL and states that rigorous validation is still needed.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on metacognition and self-regulated learning as the central rationale for the system, but it provides no empirical evidence of improvement. The illustrative scenario suggests that context-triggered recall could prompt comparison, abstraction, and self-explanation, yet these are not measured outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce manual maintenance and cognitive burden in knowledge management workflows, but the paper does not report empirical productivity or workload outcomes. Claims about lowering user effort are architectural and conceptual rather than measured.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Metacognition and self-regulated learning in manipulative robotic problem-solving task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines creative problem solving (CPS) with unfamiliar modular robotic technologies through a metacognitive and interactionist lens. Rather than testing a formal intervention, the authors use the CreaCube task to analyze how a learner monitors, interprets, and regulates problem-solving actions while assembling and testing robot cubes to move autonomously from a start point to a goal point.

The chapter is framed around the question of how metacognition supports CPS in ill-defined tasks, especially when learners must build technological knowledge from interaction with the materials. The task requires participants to explore individual cubes, infer their affordances, recombine them into different configurations, and revise prior ideas based on feedback. The authors distinguish unitary-level and system-level technological knowledge and argue that these forms of knowledge emerge through exploration, trial and error, and metacognitive regulation.

The evidence comes from a single one-hour case study with one adult participant in the CreaCube session, recorded on audio and video and analyzed qualitatively using iterative coding and triangulation. The discussion emphasizes the role of prior knowledge, affordance perception, divergent and convergent thinking, and the regulation of creative behavior during the task. The main conclusion is conceptual rather than causal: modular robotics can surface metacognitive processes and support analysis of how learners construct knowledge during creative problem solving, but the chapter does not provide experimental evidence that this approach improves retention, transfer, or motivation.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter centrally analyzes metacognition, self-regulation, and creative problem-solving processes during the CreaCube task. The evidence is a qualitative single-case study (n=1 adult) showing that the participant used exploration, trial-and-error, and metacognitive monitoring to revise prior knowledge and narrow the solution space, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Video/audio-coded metacognitive and problem-solving behaviors during a modular robotics task

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses motivation, volitional orientation, and perseverance as parts of creative behavior regulation in CPS, but these are conceptualized rather than experimentally measured. The single case suggests the learner persisted through repeated exploration and testing, yet the paper reports no standardized motivation or engagement outcomes and no inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Observed persistence/volitional orientation during the CreaCube task

paper_profiles.title: Process Mining for self-regulated learning assessment in eLearning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing self-regulated learning (SRL) in e-learning environments, where students’ learning behaviors are only visible through platform traces rather than direct classroom observation. The authors argue that most prior distance-learning research has focused on achievement outcomes, while less is known about how to assess process-oriented skills such as planning, monitoring, review, and collaborative forum use.

To study this, the authors applied Educational Process Mining with the Inductive Miner algorithm to Moodle log data from 101 Spanish university students taking a one-semester online course. The course embedded weekly learning activities aligned to SRL phases (theory, practice, and forum discussion), and the logs were preprocessed into high-level SRL action categories. The dataset was analyzed as all-students combined, then split by pass/fail status and by unit to examine whether finer-grained logs produced more interpretable models and better fitness.

The main conclusion is that process mining can reveal meaningful differences in students’ SRL-related behavior patterns, especially when logs are segmented by unit. The discovered models suggested that passing students followed a more coherent SRL-like workflow, including more forum-supported collaborative learning actions, whereas failing students showed less organized paths and more deviation from the instructor’s suggested sequence. However, the paper does not test an intervention or report causal effects on retention, transfer, motivation, or SRL growth; it is primarily a descriptive modeling study of trace data and model quality (fitness).

finding.finding_summary: Using Moodle trace data from n=101 undergraduates (21,629 events), the Inductive Miner produced SRL process models that were more interpretable and better fitting when logs were split by unit rather than analyzed at the whole-course level. The authors conclude that passing students exhibited a more meaningful self-regulated learning workflow (e.g., comprehension/learning actions followed by execution and review), while failing students showed less coherent patterns and less alignment with the suggested learning path.
finding.measure: Process-mined SRL behavior models and fitness of discovered process models from Moodle event logs

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on SRL as a socio-cognitive learning skill and finds that the passing group’s traces reflected stronger self-regulatory behavior than the failing group’s traces. Although no direct motivation or self-report measure was used, the course design and log patterns indicate greater engagement with the planned learning sequence and forum-supported collaborative activity among successful students.
finding.measure: Logged SRL-related actions, including planning, learning, executing, review, and forum peer learning

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education, 2005
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines whether formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform and whether students perceive it as beneficial. The authors argue that formative assessment should support learning through frequent low-stakes testing and timely feedback, rather than serving only as a summative grading mechanism.

The intervention concept is a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests delivered through Blackboard Learning System, with immediate score reporting and detailed feedback after each attempt. The paper describes how Blackboard test tools could be used for open-book or structured online quizzes, and it emphasizes the role of feedback, reflection, and scaffolding in helping students identify strengths and weaknesses and keep up with the subject throughout the semester.

The empirical component is a student questionnaire survey at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) involving students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams. The study reports that a majority supported frequent internal assessments and preferred Blackboard tests over classroom tests because of immediate feedback, flexibility, and the ability to study topics in smaller chunks. Students also believed the approach would help their summative exam performance, though some worried that too many tests could create stress and overemphasize learning over grades. Overall, the paper concludes that Blackboard-supported formative assessment is workable and perceived positively, but the evidence is based on student perceptions rather than measured learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, and kept them on track through the semester. The paper does not report an experimental effect size; the evidence comes from questionnaire responses, including a majority favoring frequent internal assessments and 60% preferring good learning and more marks over less learning and more marks.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents formative assessment as supporting metacognition and learning-to-learn processes, especially through reflection on feedback and progressive topic-by-topic study. Students indicated that the approach helped them learn individual topics progressively and understand how to correct mistakes, but no direct performance measure of metacognition or self-regulated learning was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reflection, self-monitoring, and progressive learning

paper_profiles.title: Designing Theory-Driven Analytics-Enhanced Self-Regulated Learning Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses the problem that many learning analytics (LA) dashboards and indicators intended to support self-regulated learning (SRL) are not grounded in learning theory, human-computer interaction (HCI), or information visualization (InfoVis), and are often designed without meaningful learner involvement. The authors argue that this limits whether dashboards actually help learners plan, monitor, reflect, seek help, and regulate motivation during learning.

To address this, the paper proposes the Student-Centered Learning Analytics-enhanced Self-Regulated Learning (SCLA-SRL) methodology. The methodology has two cyclical parts: an 'Understand' phase that uses SRL theory to structure qualitative interviews and co-generate indicator requirements, and an 'Empower' phase that uses a human-centered indicator design (HCID) process to co-design, prototype, and test dashboard indicators with learners. The methodology integrates SRL models with HCI and InfoVis design guidance, including goal/question definition, ideation with indicator specification cards, prototyping, and testing.

The chapter then illustrates the methodology with a case study in an introductory Python programming course at a German university. The authors conducted interviews with students (n=5 to validate scenarios; n=11 to elicit indicator requirements) and co-design workshops with students (n=6) to develop feedforward and feedback indicators for novice programmers. The resulting prototype dashboard included indicators for help seeking, planning, learning success, learning difficulties, and motivation, arranged to support learning before, during, and after tasks. The main conclusion is methodological rather than outcome-based: the paper argues that theory-driven, learner-centered design can produce more useful LA indicators for SRL, but it does not evaluate learning gains or other student outcomes experimentally.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter does not report an outcome effect on motivation, engagement, or self-regulation; instead, it proposes and designs indicators intended to support these processes. In the case study, students identified and co-designed indicators related to motivation, help seeking, learning success, and learning difficulties, but no post-intervention measurement of motivation or SRL change was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interviews, co-design workshop feedback, and prototype preference/usefulness judgments

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on self-regulated learning processes and related learner skills such as planning, monitoring, reflection, and help seeking. However, the evidence presented is design-oriented and qualitative; it does not quantify improvement in metacognition, time management, or other durable skills after using the system.
finding.measure: Interviews and co-design sessions about SRL scenarios and indicator needs

paper_profiles.title: Fine-Tuned Large Language Model for Visualization System: A Study on Self-Regulated Learning in Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate students; AI beginners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how fine-tuned large language models can be integrated into visualization systems to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in education, rather than functioning only as generic chatbots. The authors argue that effective educational use of LLMs requires alignment across three areas: domain knowledge, visualization design, and user interaction. They propose a conceptual framework and an application workflow for adapting LLMs to domain-specific visualization tasks.

To demonstrate the framework, they develop Tailor-Mind, an interactive system for AI beginners that combines a fine-tuned LLM with multiple visualization views, including a chat view, file preview, knowledge mind map, learning path, question recommendation, and note-taking tools. The system is built around Zimmerman’s SRL phases: forethought, performance, and self-reflection. The model is fine-tuned on 74,932 instruction examples for tasks such as open-ended QA, relation extraction, question recommendation, and tests-and-answers.

The study includes a model performance evaluation, two usage scenarios, and an in-person comparative user study with 24 computer science participants split between Tailor-Mind and GPT-4. Results suggest the system improves the SRL experience by producing clearer, more structured responses, supporting deeper questioning, and encouraging more organized learning and self-reflection. The findings are mainly about usability, engagement, and learning process support rather than long-term retention or transfer outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Tailor-Mind was reported to improve the self-regulated learning experience by helping beginners stay engaged, maintain motivation, and structure their study process. In a comparative in-person study with n=24 (12 Tailor-Mind, 12 GPT-4), participants using Tailor-Mind showed better study habits, more engagement in self-reflection, and greater willingness to follow a learning plan, based on observation and interview data rather than standardized effect-size testing.
finding.measure: Observational metrics, post-task objective questions, and semi-structured interviews focusing on SRL behaviors (study plan adoption, completion, self-reflection, engagement)

finding.finding_summary: The system supported metacognitive and learning-strategy skills by helping participants organize knowledge, link concepts, and reflect on their understanding. The study reports that Tailor-Mind encouraged deeper questioning, improved hierarchical understanding of the Transformer material, and helped learners integrate fragmented knowledge into a more coherent knowledge network.
finding.measure: Observed question depth/level, learning-path use, knowledge mind-map interactions, and interview comments about understanding and reflection

finding.finding_summary: Although the topic is AI rather than a scientific experiment, the paper substantively evaluates domain learning and conceptual understanding of the Transformer and reinforcement learning. In the user study (n=24), Tailor-Mind participants answered objective questions better than the GPT-4 control group and reported better comprehension of complex model relationships, but no numerical learning gain statistics are provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Objective questions on Transformer-model understanding and AI domain concepts

paper_profiles.title: ‘I Spend All My Energy Preparing’: Balancing AI Automation and Agency for Self-Regulated Learning in SmartFlash
paper_profiles.venue: International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) Annual Meeting 2026
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a central tension in AI-supported learning tools: although automation can reduce the time and effort students spend preparing study materials, it may also undermine the learner agency and metacognitive engagement needed for self-regulated learning. The authors ask how higher-education learners experience this balance in authentic study contexts, and what design principles should guide AI tools intended to support study rather than replace it.

The study uses a formative design research approach around SmartFlash, an AI flashcard prototype. The researchers first used GPT-5 to generate hypotheses about user needs and pain points, then validated the prototype with two cognitive walkthroughs and six recorded student sessions. Participants were graduate and senior undergraduate students from several disciplines at a large public university in the southeastern United States. Sessions combined semi-structured interviews about study practices with think-aloud tasks using students’ own materials.

Findings from reflexive thematic analysis showed that students strongly valued automation for reducing overwhelming preparation burden, but wanted transparent, editable outputs so they could verify and own the content. They also endorsed metacognitive scaffolds such as study-path recommendations, as long as the system did not prescribe choices. Motivational features such as gamification produced divergent reactions: some students found them motivating, while others experienced anxiety or demotivation. The paper concludes that effective educational AI should balance automation with agency, preserving active engagement and cognitive ownership to support self-regulated learning.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI-supported motivational features and reduced preparation burden elicited mixed emotional responses among six higher-education students (n=6). Automation was widely experienced as helpful and stress-reducing, but gamification features such as leaderboards and competition were motivating for some participants and anxiety-provoking or demotivating for others.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews and think-aloud reactions to SmartFlash features; thematic analysis of reported motivation, anxiety, overwhelm, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly focused on metacognition and self-regulated learning. Across six participants, students valued features like 'Smart Study Path' and 'Suggested Next Step' because they helped clarify study direction, while also insisting on editability and transparency to preserve cognitive ownership and active monitoring. The authors conclude that automation can support rather than undermine metacognitive development when it preserves learner agency; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interviews and think-aloud tasks assessing metacognitive uncertainty, verification, editing, and study-direction support

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported that automating flashcard preparation reduced a major time burden and made studying feel more manageable. Thematic analysis of six student sessions found that preparation itself had been so time-consuming that it displaced actual review, with participants describing automation as a 'life-saver' and 'really helpful'; however, this was a qualitative usability finding rather than a measured productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Perceived preparation burden, usability reactions, and reported time savings during flashcard creation

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Effects of Perceived Technology-enhanced Environment on Self-regulated Learning: Beyond P-values
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks which factors in a technology-enhanced learning environment are associated with students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) after an intervention, and whether web-based self-assessment tools contribute beyond simple access to ICT. The paper is framed around the idea that formative self-assessment may matter more for SRL than merely giving students devices and internet access, and it also examines whether Bayesian structural equation modeling can reveal effects that conventional p-values might miss.

The intervention involved 262 eighth-grade students in northern Taiwan participating in eight socio-scientific issues and argumentation lessons over two months. Students used tablets and Google to search for evidence, and they also used web-based self-assessment tools/standards to evaluate the quality of their decision-making and argumentation. The authors measured pre- and post-intervention SRL, self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use using adapted self-report questionnaires, then analyzed relationships with maximum likelihood SEM and Bayesian SEM.

The main conclusion is that post-intervention SRL was predicted most strongly by initial SRL and by students’ perceptions of the web-based self-assessment tools, especially perceived usefulness of the self-assessment standards. ICT access/search tools by themselves did not significantly predict post-SRL. Self-efficacy influenced post-SRL only indirectly, largely through pre-SRL and perceptions of self-assessment tools, suggesting that technology features designed for monitoring and reflection matter more than generic access to technology. The study also argues that Bayesian estimation can surface a marginal positive effect (for perceived ease of use of self-assessment) that would be less visible in p-value-only analysis.

finding.finding_summary: Web-based self-assessment standards were associated with stronger post-intervention self-regulation. In the structural model, perceived usefulness of self-assessment standards predicted post-SRL (ML-SEM coefficient=.62, p<.001; B-SEM median=.58, 95% CI [.37, .80]), and perceived ease of use showed a smaller positive relationship in Bayesian estimation (median=.18, 95% CI [-.03, .40]).
finding.measure: Metacognitive self-regulation / self-regulation questionnaire (MSLQ-adapted), pre- and post-intervention
finding.confidence_interval: [.37, .80] for SASPU → PostSR; [-.03, .40] for SASPEU → PostSR

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined metacognitive self-regulation and related monitoring processes as outcomes of the intervention. Post-SR was strongly explained by pre-SR and the perceptions of self-assessment tools, with the full model explaining 82% of variance in post-SR (R2=.82).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning / metacognitive self-regulation, including monitoring and self-evaluation

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Computational Thinking in Early Ages
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of research on computational thinking (CT) in early childhood, with a specific focus on kindergarten and children ages roughly 2–5. The authors ask which tools and strategies have been used to support CT development at early ages, and they survey work from 2010 to 2020 across Scopus, ACM, IEEE, and Web of Science.

The review synthesizes 34 selected papers after screening an initial pool of 72 records. The paper organizes the literature into three major categories—tools, curriculum, and review—and proposes a taxonomy that distinguishes block-based, robot-based, block-and-robot, and prototype solutions, with tangible and web-based variants. Common tools discussed include Bee-Bot, KIBO, ScratchJr, Happy Maps, Blue-Bot, and related programming/robotics activities.

The review concludes that early CT interventions are growing rapidly and are often validated through case studies, surveys, and pretest-posttest designs. It argues that these initiatives can support young children’s computational thinking and related classroom skills, but it also emphasizes that many studies focus on short-term learning or immediate validation rather than long-term impact. The authors call for more rigorous experiments and evaluations that examine lasting effects and broader educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies multiple early-childhood CT interventions that used programming and robotics to support mathematical learning, especially spatial thinking and problem solving. For example, Palmer (2017) reported a 4-month intervention with 8 preschoolers (3-4.5 years old) using programming to facilitate mathematics learning, and Nam et al. (2019) found that an 8-week card-coded robotics curriculum improved sequencing and mathematical problem-solving among 53 kindergarteners.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning, spatial thinking, sequencing, and mathematical problem-solving assessments
finding.study_size: multiple studies; notable samples include n=8 and n=53

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies reported improved motivation, engagement, and interest when young children used CT tools such as ScratchJr and robots. For instance, Papadakis et al. (2016) found that ScratchJr made learning fun and increased engagement among 43 preschool children, and Urlings et al. (2019) reported a significant increase in motivation among 65 kindergarteners completing Bee-Bot maze tasks.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest, motivation, and enjoyment observations/reports
finding.study_size: multiple studies; notable samples include n=43 and n=65

finding.finding_summary: This review centrally examines computational thinking as a durable skill, and the included studies generally report gains in sequencing, problem solving, collaboration, and creativity. Examples include Munoz-Repiso et al. (2019), a quasi-experimental study with 131 children showing better CT and programming skills after educational robotics activities, and Bers et al. (2019), where a coding-as-playground intervention with 172 preschoolers promoted communication, collaboration, and creativity.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, programming skills, sequencing, problem solving, collaboration, creativity
finding.study_size: multiple studies; notable samples include n=131 and n=172

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that early CT interventions can support general programming knowledge and related literacy-like competencies beyond math. For example, Papadakis et al. (2016) found that ScratchJr helped preschool children master new vocabulary and programming concepts, and Strawhacker et al. (2018) investigated retention of programming content among 222 children in relation to teachers’ instructional styles.
finding.measure: Programming concepts, programming knowledge, retention of programming content, vocabulary related to coding
finding.study_size: multiple studies; notable sample includes n=222

finding.finding_summary: The paper itself is not an operational-efficiency study, but it summarizes evidence that CT tools can be integrated into classroom practice and teacher preparation, potentially making instruction more feasible. For example, studies in the review describe pre-service teacher training with Scratch and classroom implementation of robotics activities, though the review does not quantify workload or productivity effects.
finding.measure: Teacher implementation/feasibility and classroom integration

paper_profiles.title: MOLAM: A Mobile Multimodal Learning Analytics Conceptual Framework to Support Student Self-Regulated Learning
paper_profiles.venue: In P. Prinsloo, S. Slade, & M. Khalil (Eds.), Learning analytics in open and distributed learning: Potentials and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter addresses the challenge of supporting student self-regulated learning (SRL) in online, open, distance, and mobile learning contexts. The author argues that learners increasingly move across formal, non-formal, and informal settings and use multiple mobile devices, yet existing learning analytics approaches are often web-based and insufficient for capturing the continuous, contextual, and multimodal nature of SRL.

The chapter proposes MOLAM (Mobile Multimodal Learning Analytics), a conceptual framework that combines learning analytics, mobile learning, and SRL theory. MOLAM is intended to guide the design of apps, dashboards, and analytics pipelines that can continuously collect learner activity data and other multimodal signals, analyze SRL processes, and provide in-time support to learners, teachers, and researchers.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; it is a conceptual/theoretical chapter grounded in prior literature and design frameworks. Its main contribution is a model for how mobile multimodal data could be used to measure and foster SRL across contexts, with attention to privacy, ethics, and implementation. The chapter concludes that such an approach may help make SRL visible, support transferable SRL skills, and improve academic success, but it does not present original outcome data or causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: This chapter does not report empirical effects of MOLAM or any intervention on motivation, engagement, persistence, or self-regulated learning. Instead, it argues conceptually that mobile multimodal learning analytics could be used to measure and support SRL processes such as planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation, but no original data, sample, or effect size is presented.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses self-regulated learning as a durable skill and frames MOLAM as a way to make SRL processes visible and support development over time. However, the chapter is conceptual only and reports no empirical measurement of metacognition, SRL, or related durable skills.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses potential implications for educational design, dashboards, privacy governance, and institutional support for learning analytics, but it does not evaluate any institutional policy or system-level outcome. No empirical evidence is provided regarding adoption, governance, or institutional impact.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Large Scale Randomized Controlled Trial on Herding in Peer-Review Discussions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether the order in which reviewers begin peer-review discussions causally influences final paper decisions in a large academic conference setting. The authors focus on the possibility of herding behavior in peer review: if the first commenter’s opinion disproportionately shapes later discussion, then assigning a positive versus negative discussion initiator could shift acceptance outcomes.

To test this, the authors ran a large randomized controlled field experiment during ICML 2020. They selected 1,544 borderline papers (755 in the positive-initiator condition and 789 in the negative-initiator condition) and used a two-part discussion-management strategy: one condition asked the most positive reviewer to initiate discussion first, while the other asked the most negative reviewer first, followed by a balancing request to the opposite-extreme reviewer. The design was intended to keep the set of discussion participants comparable across conditions while varying only the order of initiation.

The intervention successfully changed who initiated discussions: initiators in the positive condition had much higher initial scores than initiators in the negative condition (difference 1.27 points, 95% CI [1.15, 1.39], p < .001). However, this did not translate into a statistically significant difference in acceptance rates (0.21 vs 0.25, difference -0.04, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.01], p = .122), nor into meaningful differences in score updates across groups. The authors conclude that they find no evidence of herding in the ICML 2020 discussion phase, while noting caveats about the specific initiator manipulation and the borderline-paper selection procedure.

finding.finding_summary: The randomized discussion-initiation strategy changed who started peer-review discussions, but it did not produce a statistically significant difference in the final institutional outcome of papers. Acceptance rate was 0.21 in the positive-initiator group (M+) and 0.25 in the negative-initiator group (M−), a difference of -0.04 with 95% CI [-0.08, 0.01] (p = .122).
finding.measure: Paper acceptance rate in ICML 2020 final decision

finding.finding_summary: The intervention effectively altered discussion initiation behavior, showing that the experimental procedure can steer the order in which reviewers join peer-review discussions. In the full sample, the fraction of discussions initiated by the most positive reviewer was 0.53 in M+ versus 0.09 in M−, while the fraction initiated by the most negative reviewer was 0.15 in M+ versus 0.59 in M− (both p < .001), indicating strong operational control over discussion start order.
finding.measure: Fraction of discussions initiated by designated extreme reviewers (R+ or R−) and initial score of initiator
finding.study_size: n=1544 papers; n=1140 papers for initiator-score analysis
finding.effect_size: 0.44 (difference in fraction initiated by R+ between conditions); 1.27 (difference in mean initial score of initiator)

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI-powered mobile app, Flourish, can proactively improve college students’ mental well-being through brief, personalized, strengths-based support. The authors motivate the study as a response to rising mental health challenges among young adults and the limits of reactive, deficit-based mental health services.

The intervention is a six-week mobile app trial run across three U.S. institutions (Chapman University, University of Washington, and Foothill College) with 486 undergraduates randomized to app access or waitlist control. The app combines an AI chatbot, science-based well-being activities, gamified reminders, and weekly insight summaries intended to boost positive emotions, resilience, mindfulness, belonging, and social connection. Outcomes were measured longitudinally with validated psychological scales at baseline, weeks 2, 4, and 6.

Results showed significant improvements in positive affect, loneliness, belonging, closeness to school, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing, with small effect sizes and mixed boosting/buffering patterns over time. Negative affect, depression, anxiety, stress, and academic self-efficacy did not show significant effects. Overall, the paper concludes that a purpose-built generative AI intervention can produce measurable short-term well-being benefits at scale, though the authors note the lack of an active control and the short duration as important limitations.

finding.finding_summary: In this 6-week RCT with 486 undergraduates, the Flourish app improved several social-emotional outcomes relative to waitlist control. Positive affect increased more in the treatment group by Week 4 and Week 6 (Week 6: d=0.33), and the intervention also reduced loneliness (b=-0.05, p=.038) while improving belonging and closeness to school.
finding.measure: Subcomponents of Affect Scale positive affect; UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale; Perceived Cohesion Scale single-item belonging; Inclusion of Other in the Self scale closeness to school

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced small but significant improvements in resilience and mindfulness, both of which are durable self-management capacities relevant to coping and self-regulation. In the mixed-effects models, resilience increased relative to control (b=0.11, p=.047; β=0.04) and mindfulness remained stable while declining in the control group (b=0.19, p=.045; β=0.05).
finding.measure: Brief Resilience Scale; state version of Mindful Attention Awareness Scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper included academic self-efficacy as an additional outcome, but it did not improve significantly in the intervention group. The authors report no statistically significant changes for academic self-efficacy (p≥.462), suggesting no detectable short-term academic benefit from the app in this sample and timeframe.
finding.measure: Academic self-efficacy

paper_profiles.title: Covariate Ordered Systematic Sampling as an Improvement to Randomized Controlled Trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in online experimentation: how to improve the sensitivity and variance reduction of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) without changing the target metric. The authors propose Covariate Ordered Systematic Sampling (COSS), a deterministic assignment strategy that first sorts units by a pre-experiment covariate and then alternates treatment and control assignment.

The method is presented as an alternative to post-experiment variance-reduction approaches such as CUPED. The paper develops theoretical arguments showing that the bias introduced by COSS is small and diminishes quickly with sample size, while variance reduction can be substantial when the ordering covariate is informative. The authors test COSS in simulations and in several large-scale online marketing campaigns at a C2C marketplace with millions of users.

Across simulations and online A/B tests, COSS generally outperforms standard RCT assignment and is often comparable to or better than CUPED, especially when the relationship between the covariate and outcome is nonlinear. The paper also reports that COSS improves decision power and does not materially increase false positives in AA tests. Overall, the conclusion is that COSS can be a practical, easy-to-implement alternative for reducing variance in randomized experiments, though the work is in an industry marketing context rather than education.

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on student self-assessment, with a particular emphasis on how the concept should be defined and operationalized as a formative feedback practice rather than a summative judgment. The review argues that self-assessment is most useful when students use criteria, standards, or rubrics to monitor their own work, generate feedback, and make revisions that deepen learning.

The article synthesizes 76 empirical studies published largely between 2013 and 2018, drawing on additional earlier studies and recent meta-analyses. It organizes the literature around four main topics: consistency of self-assessment with external judgments, relationships with achievement, student perceptions, and connections with self-regulated learning (SRL). The author concludes that formative self-assessment is associated with better achievement and stronger SRL, while summative self-assessment is more often inconsistent with external ratings and is less educationally valuable.

The review also highlights important design and measurement issues. It argues that much prior work overemphasized accuracy/consistency at the expense of learning-oriented outcomes such as revision, task selection, metacognitive monitoring, motivation, and self-regulation. The paper calls for future research on the cognitive and affective mechanisms of self-assessment, as well as more precise studies of how criteria, scaffolding, and task type shape its effects.

finding.finding_summary: Across 20 non-meta-analytic studies plus two meta-analyses, formative self-assessment was associated with improved writing outcomes. The review reports that a meta-analysis by Graham et al. (10 studies) found an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality, and Sanchez et al. found students who engaged in self-grading performed better on subsequent tests (g = 0.34).
finding.measure: Writing quality, written assignment scores, subsequent test performance
finding.study_size: Multiple studies; meta-analysis included n=10 studies (Graham et al.) and 44 effect sizes (Sanchez et al.)

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive associations between formative self-assessment and achievement across a wide range of academic tasks beyond literacy, including exams, map-making, dart-throwing, speaking English, and vocational task performance. Most of these were quasi-experimental or experimental studies, and the review characterizes the treatment groups as outperforming comparison/control groups.
finding.measure: Task performance, exam scores, discipline-specific achievement measures
finding.study_size: 25 studies total on achievement; 20 clearly formative plus 2 meta-analyses

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies in which self-assessment was linked to improved speaking English outcomes, indicating benefits for language performance in higher education or classroom settings. The paper does not report a pooled effect size for language fluency specifically, but treats it as one of several academic achievement domains improved by formative self-assessment.
finding.measure: Speaking English performance

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses self-assessment in math-related contexts, including estimating correct answers and mathematics word problems, and notes that guided self-assessment according to criteria improved performance. Specific evidence cited includes a study in which more structured self-assessment produced better outcomes on writing and other tasks, but the review does not provide a math-specific pooled estimate.
finding.measure: Math word problem performance and related numeracy tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review cites self-assessment studies in science contexts, including science reports and science concept understanding, and argues that criteria-based formative self-assessment supports learning. For example, it notes that guided self-assessment and revision processes improved performance, though no science-only effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Science report quality, science concept understanding

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that formative self-assessment is associated with stronger self-regulated learning, motivation, self-efficacy, self-satisfaction, and awareness of learning progress. In one cited study on dart throwing, students with graduated standards surpassed those with absolute or no standards on motivational beliefs, and the correlation between self-evaluation and performance was very high (r = 0.94).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires, think-aloud protocols, motivational beliefs (self-efficacy, attributions, self-satisfaction)
finding.study_size: 12 SRL studies in the review; one cited study had n=70

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the paper: self-assessment is framed as a metacognitive, criteria-referenced process that supports self-regulation, monitoring, and reflection. Studies using rubrics/scripts showed small-to-moderate gains in self-regulation (η2 = 0.06–0.42), and one study reported associations across all three SRL phases—forethought, performance, and reflection.
finding.measure: Self-regulation questionnaires, think-aloud protocols, metacognitive monitoring, SRL phases
finding.study_size: 12 studies focused on SRL; one cited study specifically examined rubric-referenced self-assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses assessment practice and pedagogy at the classroom and instructional level, arguing for clearer operational definitions and more formative use of self-assessment. However, it does not evaluate institutional policy or governance outcomes empirically, so the evidence here is indirect and conceptual rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Envisioning the use of online tests in assessing twenty-first century learning: a literature review
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of online tests in higher education and asks whether they are being used in ways that support twenty-first century learning rather than only efficient grading of low-level knowledge. The authors review literature on online tests, online quizzes, and e-assessment to examine their rationale, cognitive demands, feedback practices, student attitudes, and limitations such as cheating, publisher test banks, and accessibility concerns.

The review is based on English-language academic papers and research reports published since 2000 and spans a range of higher-education disciplines, with many examples from large first-year and other undergraduate contexts. The paper argues that online tests are most effective when used formatively, at low stakes, with immediate and corrective feedback, multiple attempts, and alignment to learning outcomes. It also highlights that these tools can support learner engagement, self-assessment, and self-regulation, but that they are often underused for higher-order or authentic assessment and are frequently limited by poor design and overreliance on recall-level multiple-choice questions.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes prior studies to propose principles for better online-test design using an assessment design framework. Its main conclusion is that online tests are not inherently limited to shallow learning; when thoughtfully integrated with other assessment methods and feedback processes, they can contribute to learning, efficiency, and assessment of twenty-first century competencies. However, the paper also emphasizes important gaps in the literature, especially around humanistic knowledge, diverse student cohorts, and practical validation of the proposed principles.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, online tests were found to support student learning when used formatively, aligned with other assessments, and designed beyond simple recall. The review concludes that such tests can improve learning outcomes, particularly when they assess foundational knowledge and are integrated with case-based or higher-cognitive questions, but they are often limited by overuse of low-level MCQs and narrow content coverage.
finding.measure: Summative exam performance, learning outcomes, performance on case-based versus non-case-based MCQs

finding.finding_summary: The literature reviewed indicates that formative online tests can enhance motivation, confidence, and engagement, especially when students receive multiple attempts, low-stakes credit, and immediate feedback. The paper also notes that students tend to respond positively to features such as convenience, multiple attempts, and feedback, which can support persistence in assessment tasks.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, motivation, confidence, engagement, participation in formative tests
