The theoretical contribution is a set of conditions under which encoder-decoder causal models can recover latent exogenous noise and bound counterfactual error by reconstruction error, though the assumptions are acknowledged to be restrictive.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies causal reasoning itself: how well diffusion-based causal models answer observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries. On synthetic benchmarks, DCM substantially improves causal-query estimation over prior methods, with counterfactual MSE as low as 3.42×10−2 on the ladder NLIN graph and 4.28×10−2 on the ladder NADD graph (values reported ×100), compared with much larger errors for VACA and CAREFL.
finding.measure: Accuracy of observational/interventional distribution matching (MMD) and counterfactual estimation error (MSE) on synthetic causal graphs; absolute prediction error on fMRI intervention data
finding.study_size: n=5000 per synthetic simulation; 20 random initializations; fMRI sample n=14 patients
finding.std_deviation: Reported as mean±standard deviation in tables (e.g., CF MSE 3.42±1.67 ×10−2 on ladder NLIN)

finding.finding_summary: The proposed node-wise diffusion approach is reported to be computationally more efficient than competing deep causal baselines. In one experimental setup, the authors state that DCM trained roughly 7 times faster than CAREFL and 9 times faster than VACA, indicating a clear efficiency advantage in model training.
finding.measure: Training time / computational efficiency compared with CAREFL and VACA

paper_profiles.title: Learning Causal Models Online
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (machine learning / algorithmic study; no human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of learning predictive models that generalize beyond the distribution they were trained on, especially when training data contains spurious correlations that make models brittle. The authors argue that causal structure can improve generalization, but directly learning causal structure is difficult in online and continual-learning settings, particularly when interventions are unknown or temporally distant.

To address this, the paper proposes an online method that estimates feature spuriousness by tracking the running variance of feature weights over time. Features whose association with the target changes across time are treated as spurious and downweighted or removed. The paper first evaluates this idea on an online Colored MNIST benchmark framed as an MDP, showing that the proposed variance metric can identify spurious color features without needing explicit intervention labels and that it generalizes well to unseen environments.

The paper then extends the method to learn features directly from raw images using Perturbations with Backtracking (PwB), a weakly directed search procedure that perturbs representation-learning weights and keeps changes only when they improve predictive loss or reduce the variance metric. Across the image-based Colored MNIST experiments, the online method and its offline variant outperform standard online learning and online IRM baselines on the unseen environment, demonstrating that the approach can learn representations that ignore spurious correlations. The study is methodological and algorithmic, focused on generalization under distribution shift rather than education outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Defining a Strategic Action Plan for AI in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how higher education institutions should respond strategically to the rapid spread of artificial intelligence in teaching, learning, assessment, and governance. Rather than testing a specific AI tool or intervention, it reviews normative guidance from international organizations and prior policy literature to identify the main challenges AI poses in higher education, especially around fairness and inclusion, privacy and data use, transparency and agency, accountability, and academic integrity.

The paper proposes a CASD framework: Challenges, Actions, Stakeholders, and Deployment. It maps five strategic actions—revising curriculum, reforming pedagogy, training educators, supporting local content, and establishing policy/governance—to five stakeholder groups: students, educators, institutions, policymakers, and technology providers. It also discusses deployment considerations such as institutional culture, rules, access, familiarity, and trust, drawing on related framework work to suggest how AI strategies can be implemented in practice.

The context is postsecondary education, with emphasis on institutional policy and leadership rather than classroom-level student outcomes. The paper cites examples such as AI-resistant assessments, AI literacy, and local-language content, and concludes that higher education systems need flexible, inclusive, ethically grounded AI strategies. It calls for future work on institutional readiness, piloting policy innovations, and sharing good practices, but it does not report original empirical data or causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual and policy-oriented paper proposing a strategic framework for AI adoption in higher education, not an empirical evaluation. It synthesizes existing guidance and literature to outline institutional actions and deployment considerations, but reports no original sample, no measured institutional outcomes, and no effect sizes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Quantitative probing: Validating causal models with quantitative domain knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in causal inference: how to validate causal models when the usual train/test split used for predictive models does not transfer to intervention-based reasoning. The authors argue that because interventions change the data-generating process, causal models cannot be validated solely by withholding observational data, and they review existing approaches such as sensitivity analysis, simulation-based benchmarking, and refutation tests as partial solutions.

To address this gap, the paper proposes "quantitative probing," a model-agnostic validation framework that uses known non-target causal effects as quantitative expectations. In a causal end-to-end analysis pipeline, users can combine qualitative domain knowledge, causal discovery, do-calculus, and estimation; quantitative probes are then checked after model fitting, and successful recovery of expected effects increases confidence in the target causal estimate. The paper illustrates the idea with Pearl’s sprinkler example and evaluates it in a large simulation study using random DAGs, random binary CPDs, causal discovery via fast greedy equivalence search, and linear regression estimation.

The study is not an education study and does not involve students, classrooms, or educational interventions. Its population is essentially methodological/technical and the context is simulation plus a toy causal example. The main conclusion is that higher probe hit rates are generally associated with better recovery of the causal graph and lower target-effect error, but the relationship is imperfect: disconnected graphs, insufficient probe coverage, and overly coarse probe tolerances can allow incorrect models to pass validation. The authors conclude that quantitative probing is promising as a way to incorporate quantitative domain knowledge into causal model validation, while noting several open theoretical and practical questions.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the pedagogical rationale for formative assessment and asks how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes testing with immediate, detailed feedback can support learning better than relying only on end-of-semester summative assessment.

The implementation described is a proposed series of weekly or fortnightly Blackboard online tests, including multiple-choice and true/false items, with automated score display and teacher feedback. The study context is Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus), and the paper reports student survey responses about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option. Students generally favored the approach because it broke content into smaller units, provided immediate feedback, and made it easier to monitor learning progress.

Methodologically, the paper is not a causal evaluation of learning outcomes. It is primarily a conceptual/practice paper supplemented by a questionnaire survey of student perceptions, with some subgroup comparisons across Business, Engineering, and IT students. The main conclusion is that formative assessment delivered through Blackboard is seen as workable and appealing to students, and the authors suggest it may help improve engagement and possibly summative grades, but they do not directly test achievement effects with an explicit counterfactual.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported strong support for frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based tests because they provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and a sense of continuous progress. The paper also notes concerns about stress from too many tests, but overall student attitudes toward formative assessment were favorable.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test option

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses and track whether they are 'on track.' Students also stated that splitting work into smaller topic assessments helped them learn progressively and keep up with the subject throughout the semester.
finding.measure: Survey items on self-monitoring, perceived learning progress, and usefulness of feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on assessment practices in undergraduate business, engineering, and IT courses and reports that students preferred weekly or fortnightly Blackboard tests over classroom tests. Students valued small-topic assessments and immediate teacher feedback as helpful for understanding course content and preparing for semester exams.
finding.measure: Survey responses on preferred assessment format and perceived usefulness for subject learning

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Annual Conference & Exposition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the pedagogical role of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms and argues that technology has made real-time collection and analysis of student responses easier to implement. The central question is not the effectiveness of one new intervention under controlled conditions, but how formative assessment can be used more effectively in engineering education, especially when combined with clickers, mobile polling, and open-format response tools.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and practitioner-oriented overview, drawing on prior literature and the authors' classroom observations. It contrasts multiple-choice clicker questions with open-format questions submitted via Tablet PCs and InkSurvey, emphasizing that open responses reveal student thinking more clearly and can guide instructors' next instructional steps. The paper includes illustrative examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course with 60 third-year engineering physics majors, but it does not report a controlled comparison, effect estimates, or counterfactual design.

The main conclusion is that embedded formative assessment can support active learning, metacognition, and improved instruction in undergraduate engineering, but its benefits depend on instructors responding to student feedback and asking questions that reveal reasoning rather than only final answers. The paper also notes that technology reduces clerical burden and enables real-time assessment at scale, though it warns that using technology merely for attendance or superficial checking limits educational value. Overall, the paper is an argument for broader and more thoughtful use of technology-assisted formative assessment in postsecondary STEM teaching.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment, especially through open-format questions, can improve students' understanding of scientific and engineering concepts by making their reasoning visible and allowing instructors to respond to misconceptions in real time. The evidence presented is illustrative rather than causal; one example comes from an undergraduate electromagnetics class with 60 students, where responses revealed difficulties with Gauss's law, limits, symmetry, and dot products, but no effect size or pre/post outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Student written solutions and sketches on electromagnetics concept/derivation questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that embedded formative assessment promotes metacognition, critical thinking, and students' ability to reason from principles rather than chase quick answers. In the open-format examples, student work exposed gaps in conceptual understanding and problem-solving processes, but the paper does not quantify changes in durable skills or report any controlled effect estimates.
finding.measure: Observed quality of student reasoning, metacognitive awareness, and problem-solving approaches in response artifacts

finding.finding_summary: A major claim of the paper is that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces instructors' clerical burden and enables real-time collection and rapid analysis of student responses. The paper describes clickers, texting, online tools, and InkSurvey as ways to streamline implementation, but it provides no quantitative workload measure, effect size, or controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Instructor burden / speed and feasibility of collecting and reviewing student responses

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether pre-existing social relationships between students affect the fairness, accuracy, and perceived value of peer assessment in an e-learning course. The authors are motivated by prior mixed evidence on anonymity and by the concern that friendship or dislike may bias peer grading, especially in courses where students know each other from prior in-person or blended learning contexts.

To study this, they built a Moodle plugin called PeerForum and deployed it in a Master’s-level course in Multimedia Content Production at Instituto Superior Técnico. Students first completed relationship nominations (most liked / least liked peers) and then peer-assessed course submissions under a single-anonymized design, with reviewer assignment partially tailored to include peers with different relationship statuses. Faculty provided rubrics and training pages before students could assess, and the analysis compared peer grades against professor ratings as well as against relationship categories (like, dislike, neutral).

The study finds that peer assessment was generally reliable and accurate when posts received at least three peer assessments: inter-rater agreement was moderate to good at the average-score level, and peer grades correlated significantly with professor grades (e.g., Spearman rs=.49 for rounded final peer grade; rs=.56 for average peer grades, n=588 posts). Students’ peer grades were slightly higher than professors’ on average, but the difference was small. Relationship bias was present—students who liked authors tended to grade them higher and those who disliked them lower—but the magnitude was small and did not materially change final aggregate peer grades under the reviewer-tailoring scheme. Student questionnaire responses were broadly positive, with many students reporting that peer assessment was fair, useful, and helped them learn and engage in the course.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment produced grades that were broadly aligned with instructor grading in a graduate multimedia production course. For posts with at least three peer assessments, the final peer grade correlated moderately with professor ratings (Spearman rs=.49, p<.001; average peer grades rs=.56, p<.001; n=588 posts), suggesting students can evaluate non-reading course work with reasonable accuracy after training and rubric support.
finding.measure: Peer grades versus professor ratings on skill-tree submissions
finding.study_size: n=588 posts (accuracy analysis); n=64 students in final analytic sample
finding.effect_size: rs=.49 (final peer grade vs professor); rs=.56 (average peer grades vs professor)
finding.std_deviation: Professor rating SD=.92; final peer grade SD=.61; average peer grade SD=.57

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable perceptions of peer assessment, including greater perceived usefulness and fairness after the course. Among questionnaire respondents (n=53 peer-graders), 54.7% agreed peer assessment was helpful after the course, 52.8% agreed it was fair, and many reported that peer assessment helped them learn, improve their work, and stay engaged.
finding.measure: End-of-semester questionnaire on usefulness, fairness, difficulty, and perceived learning/engagement
finding.study_size: n=53 questionnaire respondents who had peer-graded

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests peer assessment supported feedback-related and reflective skills, though these were measured mainly through student perceptions rather than direct skill tests. Students reported that giving feedback helped them learn the course material, understand expectations, and improve their submissions; open-ended responses emphasized learning through grading and responding to feedback.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire and open-ended comments about learning, feedback quality, and improvement
finding.study_size: n=53 questionnaire respondents (open-ended and Likert items)

finding.finding_summary: The peer assessment system was presented as a scalable replacement for some instructor grading burden, and the authors conclude it can replace traditional evaluation in this setting. Although they did not directly quantify teacher time saved, the platform automated reviewer assignment and used peer grading to support assessment of 863 posts, indicating potential efficiency gains in course administration.
finding.measure: Implementation of Moodle-based peer assessment workflow for grading student submissions
finding.study_size: 863 posts with at least one peer assessment; 625 posts with at least three peer assessments

paper_profiles.title: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Modern Digital Forensics and Incident Response
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in modern digital forensics and incident response (DFIR). It is framed around the growing volume, variety, and complexity of digital evidence, and asks how AI/ML methods can help investigators process, classify, retrieve, and analyze evidence more efficiently and accurately.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it conducts a systematic literature review of prior work on AI/ML applications in DFIR. It surveys approaches such as big-data forensic frameworks, volatile memory extraction, file-type identification, neural-network-based event reconstruction, incident response models, automated artefact relevancy ranking, large-scale email graph analysis, metadata clustering, chain-of-custody visualization, and malware detection/classification.

The context is professional digital forensics and incident response, not an educational setting. The authors conclude that AI/ML can improve speed, scalability, and some aspects of accuracy in forensic workflows, but that the field still faces major challenges, including data validity, bias, interpretability, privacy/security, generalization across devices and datasets, and lack of standards. Overall, the paper argues that AI/ML is promising for DFIR but remains underdeveloped and requires more rigorous, diverse, and legally robust research.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed DFIR literature, AI/ML methods are repeatedly described as improving speed, scalability, and automation in forensic workflows. Examples include reducing manual review burden, accelerating file and email analysis, and helping investigators prioritize relevant artefacts; however, the paper is a review and does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Forensic task efficiency, processing speed, automation, and reduced manual workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI/ML could materially affect digital forensics practice by improving evidence handling, chain of custody, and investigative workflows, but it also highlights institutional barriers such as privacy, admissibility, interpretability, and lack of standards. Because this is a narrative/systematic review, these are synthesized claims rather than direct measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Governance, admissibility, chain-of-custody practices, and legal/ethical robustness of DFIR systems

paper_profiles.title: Characterizing College Science Assessments: The Three-Dimensional Learning Assessment Protocol
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a problem in college science education: most assessments in introductory biology, chemistry, and physics emphasize factual recall and procedural problem solving rather than the kinds of scientific reasoning and application envisioned by contemporary science education reform. The authors argue that if gateway science courses are being transformed toward three-dimensional learning, then assessments must also be transformed so they can elicit evidence of scientific practices, crosscutting concepts, and core ideas.

To address this, the paper introduces the Three-Dimensional Learning Assessment Protocol (3D-LAP), a coding protocol developed by an interdisciplinary team at Michigan State University. The protocol provides criteria for determining whether a task in biology, chemistry, or physics can potentially elicit evidence of three-dimensional learning, with separate handling for constructed-response and selected-response items for scientific practices, and descriptive coding for crosscutting concepts and core ideas.

The study is not an intervention on student learning; rather, it is a method-development and validation paper that applies the protocol to representative exams from introductory gateway courses. The authors compare exams from traditional and research-based curricula, showing that the protocol distinguishes assessments with few opportunities for three-dimensional learning from those with substantially more. They report face/content validity evidence from expert negotiation and inter-rater agreement values that are generally high across disciplines, concluding that the 3D-LAP can be used to characterize assessments, support faculty development, and evaluate course transformation efforts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily develops and validates a protocol for identifying whether college science assessment tasks can elicit scientific practices, crosscutting concepts, and core ideas. Applied to representative exams in biology, chemistry, and physics, the protocol distinguished traditional exams with few three-dimensional tasks from research-based exams with more such tasks; for example, the B exams had at least 40% of points on three-dimensional tasks, whereas the A exams had few. No student learning effect size was reported because the study analyzes assessments rather than student outcomes.
finding.measure: Assessment task coding for potential to elicit scientific practices, crosscutting concepts, and core ideas

paper_profiles.title: Integrated Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) Education through Active Experience of Designing Technical Toys in Vietnamese Schools
paper_profiles.venue: British Journal of Education, Society & Behavioural Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how STEM education might be integrated into Vietnamese middle-school technology teaching through creative, experiential activities. The authors argue that Vietnamese schools need more practical, interdisciplinary learning opportunities because students are often passive learners and have limited problem-solving and technical experience.

The paper proposes a five-step procedure for teachers to design and implement technical-toy projects as a way to integrate technology, mathematics, and physics content. It then illustrates the approach with a classroom activity for 8th-grade students designing a mini-racing car, mapping the activity to curriculum competencies in technology, math, and physics and emphasizing active, hands-on learning, collaboration, and iterative design.

The study is not an experimental evaluation of student outcomes; rather, it is a qualitative, design-oriented paper that presents a framework and an illustrative example. The main conclusion is that integrated STEM education through technical-toy design is feasible in the Vietnamese secondary context, and that such activities may support competency development, though the authors note that stronger curriculum integration and further investigation are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the mini-racing car design activity directly engages 8th-grade students in mathematical competencies such as measuring wheelbase lengths, calculating transmission ratios, calculating areas, and evaluating component dimensions. No empirical pre/post scores are reported; the finding is based on curriculum alignment and the authors' analysis of the task rather than measured effect sizes.
finding.measure: Curriculum-mapped mathematical competencies (measurement, ratio, geometry, area calculation) in a technical-toy design task

finding.finding_summary: The activity is presented as supporting physics/science competencies including understanding motion, friction, speed, force, and energy transfer from electrical to mechanical energy. The paper does not report experimental outcomes or effect sizes; instead, it provides a conceptual mapping showing that the toy-design task can require scientific reasoning in a real-world engineering context.
finding.measure: Curriculum-mapped physics/science competencies (motion, friction, force, energy transfer)

finding.finding_summary: The authors repeatedly frame technical-toy design as fostering problem solving, creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and iterative design/revision. The paper's evidence is descriptive and theoretical rather than statistical, so no effect size is reported; the finding is inferred from the task structure and the competency tables.
finding.measure: Observed/claimed competencies in problem solving, creativity, collaboration, and iterative engineering design

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that hands-on toy design can increase student motivation, interest in STEM, enthusiasm, and pride in their products. These outcomes are discussed as expected benefits of active learning and experiential activity, but the article provides no direct survey or behavioral data and no effect sizes.
finding.measure: Motivation, interest, enthusiasm, and pride in STEM/technical toy design activities

paper_profiles.title: An Anarchist Approach to the Undergraduate Mathematics Curriculum
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective piece arguing that the undergraduate mathematics curriculum is in tension with the values many mathematicians and educators claim to hold. The authors frame this as a form of cognitive dissonance: mathematics is treated as open-ended, creative, communal, and process-based, yet undergraduate teaching is often organized around hierarchical instruction, fixed learning outcomes, and summative grading.

Rather than reporting a study of a specific intervention, the paper develops anarchism as a philosophical framework for rethinking curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment in undergraduate mathematics. The authors propose shifting from content to skills, from outcomes to process, and from hierarchical to horizontal teaching structures; they also discuss alternatives such as ungrading, self-assessment, portfolios, oral exams, dialogue-based instruction, and question-centered courses. The target context is undergraduate mathematics in North American higher education, and the recommendations are presented as possibilities for individual instructors and institutions.

The main conclusion is normative rather than empirical: if mathematics educators want their teaching to align with values such as autonomy, diversity, cooperation, and open-ended inquiry, then course design and assessment should be reorganized around those principles. The paper does not test these ideas experimentally, and it does not present causal evidence about student outcomes. It is primarily a conceptual essay intended to provoke reflection and guide future practice.

paper_profiles.title: Higher education assessment practice in the era of generative AI tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools, specifically ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard (Gemini), perform on assessment tasks in higher education. The authors are concerned with how these tools may affect assessment validity, academic integrity, and student learning, especially in STEM-related disciplines where AI-generated answers could potentially be used unethically.

To investigate this, the authors created three master’s-level case study assessments drawn from data science, data analytics, and construction management. They asked ChatGPT-4 and Bard to complete the tasks, then had the outputs graded using a criterion-referenced rubric and moderated by academic tutors. The study did not compare human learners against an intervention; rather, it evaluated the capabilities and limitations of GenAI as a solution generator within authentic assessment contexts.

The main conclusion is that GenAI tools can demonstrate strong subject knowledge, problem-solving, analytical ability, and some critical thinking/presentation skills, but performance varies by discipline and task structure. The tools did better on data analytics and data science tasks than on the more project-based construction management task, suggesting that well-designed assessments can expose model limitations. The paper recommends redesigning assessments for the GenAI era, using AI detectors alongside plagiarism tools, and incorporating more contextualized, reflective, discussion-based, and presentation-based assessment approaches.

finding.finding_summary: Across three master’s-level assessment case studies, the authors found that ChatGPT-4 and Bard demonstrated subject knowledge, problem-solving, analytical ability, and some discipline-dependent critical thinking and presentation skills. However, performance was uneven: the tools handled data analytics and data science tasks more successfully than the more complex construction management task, indicating limits in higher-order reasoning on less structured problems.
finding.measure: Performance on three criterion-referenced assessment case studies evaluating problem-solving, analysis, comprehension, critical thinking, discussion, and presentation quality
finding.study_size: n=3 assessment cases; two GenAI tools (ChatGPT-4 and Bard)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates AI performance on disciplinary higher-education assessments in data science, data analytics, and construction management. Results were positive for the more data-intensive tasks, where both tools produced largely coherent solutions, but negative for the construction management task, where key contextual and design elements were missed.
finding.measure: Grades and qualitative rubric-based evaluation of AI-generated solutions to discipline-specific higher-education assessment tasks
finding.study_size: n=3 assessment cases; two GenAI tools

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that GenAI meaningfully affects higher-education assessment policy and institutional practice because existing assessment designs can be vulnerable to AI-generated work. The authors recommend redesigning assessments, integrating AI detectors with plagiarism tools, and using more contextualized and reflective assessment formats to protect academic integrity and better evidence learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Assessment-design implications and institutional recommendations derived from rubric-based analysis of GenAI outputs

paper_profiles.title: DisasterM3: A Remote Sensing Vision-Language Dataset for Disaster Damage Assessment and Response
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces DisasterM3, a new remote sensing vision-language dataset designed for disaster damage assessment and response. The dataset contains 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123,010 instruction pairs drawn from 36 historical disaster events across five continents, with both optical and SAR imagery and nine tasks spanning recognition, counting, segmentation, relational reasoning, and report generation.

The main contribution is dataset construction and benchmarking rather than an educational intervention. The authors evaluate 14 generic and remote-sensing vision-language models on the benchmark, showing that existing models struggle in disaster contexts because of domain gaps, cross-sensor mismatch, and weak object counting. They then fine-tune several models on DisasterM3 and report improved performance, including gains of up to 10.4% on QA tasks, 2.1 points on report generation, and 40.8% on referring segmentation.

The paper is positioned in Earth vision and emergency response, not in schooling or instructional settings. It provides a large, curated resource and baseline results for disaster-focused multimodal AI, with conclusions centered on model limitations, the value of disaster-specific training data, and the challenges of optical-SAR generalization and counting robustness.

finding.finding_summary: The dataset and fine-tuned models improve disaster-response task performance, which the authors frame as supporting rescuers and planning personnel. Fine-tuning four VLMs on DisasterM3 led to stable improvements across QA, report generation, and referring segmentation, with gains up to 10.4% on QA, 2.1 points on report generation, and 40.8% on referring segmentation.
finding.measure: Task accuracy / GPT-scored report quality / referring segmentation IoU
finding.study_size: n=14 models benchmarked; n=4 models fine-tuned
finding.effect_size: 10.4% QA gain; 2.1 report points; 40.8% referring segmentation gain

paper_profiles.title: The Quantitative Reasoning for College Science (QuaRCS) Assessment, 1: Development and Validation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a valid, non-proprietary assessment of quantitative literacy for college students, especially those in general education science courses. The authors argue that science courses are an important venue for advancing numeracy, but that instructors lack an assessment tool aligned to the kinds of quantitative skills students actually need in science literacy and everyday life.

To meet this need, the paper reports the development and validation of the Quantitative Reasoning for College Science (QuaRCS) assessment. The instrument was refined over eight semesters, with expert educator surveys used to select skills, free-response piloting to improve question wording and distractors, and item-analysis work to examine difficulty, discrimination, reliability, and alignment of items to ten quantitative skill categories. The assessment was administered primarily to undergraduate general education science students at a large research university in the southwestern U.S., with additional validation data from a STEM major course.

The main conclusions are that QuaRCS can distinguish levels of quantitative literacy, has acceptable item statistics for many items, and appears valid for both general education science students and a STEM-major comparison group. The paper also finds wide variation in student effort, confidence, and calculator use, and notes that these factors can affect observed performance. Although the paper is not an intervention study and does not test learning gains from formative assessment, it establishes an assessment tool intended for future pre/post studies of numeracy interventions in college science courses.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an instructional intervention, but it provides strong validation evidence for a numeracy assessment instrument. The final QuaRCS instrument was administered to nearly 2,000 students in 2015 and over 4,000 students across eight semesters, and it showed the ability to distinguish varying levels of quantitative literacy with item difficulties spanning roughly 0.22-0.80 across skills and acceptable discrimination for many items.
finding.measure: Quantitative literacy / numeracy performance on the QuaRCS assessment (item difficulty, discrimination, and total scores)
finding.study_size: n=1480 for the main general-education sample; nearly 2000 in validation administrations; over 4000 across development
finding.std_deviation: SD=5.3 for Spring 2015 pre-semester total score distribution

finding.finding_summary: The instrument was explicitly designed around quantitative skills relevant to science literacy, and expert educators judged the assessed skills to align with science literacy and educated citizenship. The paper reports that the QuaRCS is valid for college general-education science students and can distinguish science-relevant quantitative reasoning skills across contexts.
finding.measure: Science-literacy-relevant quantitative skill alignment and assessment validity
finding.study_size: n=48 educators in the ranking survey; n=1480 student sample for main validation

finding.finding_summary: The paper measures student confidence, effort, and persistence while taking the assessment. More than half of students who answered incorrectly still reported being confident or very confident, and 25-40% of students across administrations reported quitting midway, indicating substantial variation in self-regulation and motivation during low-stakes assessment.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence, effort, and completion behavior on the QuaRCS
finding.study_size: n=1480 for Spring 2015 cohort; similar patterns reported across earlier administrations

paper_profiles.title: Equity in College Physics Student Learning: a Critical Quantitative Intersectionality Investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether student learning gains in introductory college physics differ across intersecting identities of race/ethnicity and gender, and whether those differences vary between lecture-based and collaborative courses. The authors frame the work as a critical quantitative intersectionality investigation, explicitly problematizing how “equity” is defined and measured in physics education research.

The analysis uses nationally aggregated LASSO data from 13,857 students in 187 first-semester college physics courses across 31 institutions. Student conceptual learning was measured with pretest and posttest scores on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), analyzed with hierarchical linear models and multiple imputation. The paper compares two equity operationalizations: Equality of Learning (comparing gaps between demographic groups after controlling for pretest) and Equity of Individuality (whether collaborative instruction improves outcomes for marginalized groups).

Results show substantial inequities in both preparation and learning: White male students were predicted to have the highest pretest and gain scores, while Black female students had the lowest predicted pretest scores. After controlling for pretest, White and Hispanic women had significantly lower gains than their male peers, and most marginalized groups had lower gains than White men in both lecture and collaborative settings. Collaborative courses produced higher gains for all groups, but did not reduce group-to-group gaps, so Equality of Learning was not achieved. However, because collaborative instruction improved gains for marginalized students relative to lecture, the authors conclude that Equity of Individuality was achieved.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measures conceptual learning in introductory physics using pretest-to-posttest gains on validated concept inventories. In the aggregated model, collaborative instruction was associated with larger gains overall (about +3.06 percentage points relative to lecture), but White male students still had the largest adjusted gains and most marginalized groups had lower gains after controlling for pretest scores. The direction is therefore mixed: positive for overall learning, but inequitable across demographic groups.
finding.measure: Physics conceptual learning gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE), analyzed as posttest minus pretest percentage correct

finding.finding_summary: The study assesses how instructional context at the course level—lecture versus collaborative learning—relates to equity in student outcomes across race/ethnicity and gender. Collaborative courses increased predicted gains for all groups by about 3.06 percentage points and were judged to achieve Equity of Individuality, but they did not reduce demographic gaps in learning and therefore did not achieve Equality of Learning.
finding.measure: Course-type effects on predicted learning gains and equity operationalizations across lecture-based versus collaborative introductory physics courses
finding.effect_size: 3.06 percentage point gain increase in collaborative courses

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines the value of formative assessment and how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university context. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to improve learning through frequent testing, immediate feedback, and ongoing teacher support, contrasting it with end-of-semester summative testing.

The paper describes a proposed implementation of weekly or fortnightly online quizzes on Blackboard, with detailed feedback after each attempt. The discussion emphasizes that such assessments can help students monitor their progress, identify weaknesses, and prepare better for summative exams. The authors also connect the approach to prior theory and reviews on formative assessment, arguing that feedback, scaffolding, and metacognitive reflection are central to its effectiveness.

Empirically, the paper reports a questionnaire survey of university students about continuous assessment and Blackboard testing. Students generally favored frequent online assessments and immediate feedback, and the only subgroup comparison reported was a statistically significant difference across Business, Engineering, and IT streams in attitudes toward open-book continuous assessment and Blackboard test ratings. The paper concludes that technology-supported formative assessment is well received by students and may support better learning, though the study does not measure actual achievement gains from the intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable attitudes toward frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based testing, largely because they perceived immediate feedback, flexibility, and reduced pressure from smaller topic-based assessments. Open-ended responses also suggested that the approach helped them stay engaged with the subject throughout the semester, though some students worried about stress from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and learning how to learn by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses, reflect on feedback, and progressively master individual topics. However, these claims are based on student perceptions and literature review rather than direct measurement of durable-skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and conceptual/theoretical discussion of metacognition and self-monitoring

finding.finding_summary: Students viewed the Blackboard formative assessment approach as helpful for learning course content in smaller steps and believed it would support performance on semester examinations. The paper reports no direct achievement test outcomes, but it does document strong perceived usefulness of the assessment format for subject learning.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and preparation for summative semester examinations

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that Blackboard can be used institutionally to implement frequent formative assessment and strengthen assessment practice within a university course. The paper is focused on the feasibility and acceptability of this assessment model within the campus learning environment, rather than on policy or governance outcomes.
finding.measure: Feasibility/acceptability of Blackboard implementation for formative assessment at the course level

paper_profiles.title: Work from Home and Job Satisfaction: Differences by Disability Status among Healthcare Workers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the option to work from home is associated with better job satisfaction and workplace experiences, and whether those associations differ by disability status. The authors focus on a practical equity question: whether remote work can help reduce disability-related gaps in work experience among healthcare employees.

Using an original survey of 1,405 employees from a large university-affiliated healthcare system administered in mid-2023, the authors analyze 993 complete responses. They compare workers with and without disabilities on job satisfaction, turnover intentions, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, workplace inclusion, treatment of people with disabilities, and manager/coworker relations. They then estimate multivariable regressions with interaction terms between disability status and frequency of working from home.

The results show that workers with disabilities report substantially less favorable workplace experiences than workers without disabilities on most measures, even after adjusting for demographics and job characteristics. Work from home is generally associated with more positive job experiences for all workers, especially for those working from home three or more days per week. However, these benefits are often smaller for workers with disabilities, meaning remote work does not narrow disability gaps in workplace experiences; in some cases, remote work is associated with especially weak manager and coworker relations for workers with disabilities. The authors conclude that remote-work policies alone are unlikely to close disability inequities and should be paired with additional, disability-targeted supports that reduce isolation and improve inclusion.

finding.finding_summary: Work from home is associated with better work-related functioning and lower turnover intentions for the full sample. For example, working from home 3+ days/week was associated with higher job satisfaction (b=0.195) and lower turnover intentions (b=-0.162), with the analyses based on n=993 healthcare workers.
finding.measure: Job satisfaction; turnover intentions; job autonomy; organizational commitment; perceived organizational support; workplace inclusion; manager/coworker relations

finding.finding_summary: Remote work improved several workplace-experience indicators related to engagement and belonging, but workers with disabilities reported weaker baseline experiences overall. The strongest positive association for job satisfaction was for 3+ days/week of work from home (b=0.195), while several interaction terms showed smaller gains for workers with disabilities.
finding.measure: Job satisfaction; turnover intentions; organizational commitment; perceived organizational support; climate for inclusion

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is that workplace accommodation through remote work does not eliminate disability inequities in job-related experiences. Although work from home benefited both groups, the gains were often larger for workers without disabilities, and disability gaps remained for organizational commitment, inclusion, support, and manager/coworker relations.
finding.measure: Regression-adjusted disability gaps and disability-by-work-from-home interactions across workplace experience indices

paper_profiles.title: Differentially Private Algorithms for 2020 Census Detailed DHC Race & Ethnicity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to release detailed race and ethnicity tabulations from the 2020 U.S. Census while protecting individual privacy. The authors focus on the Census Bureau’s Detailed Demographic and Housing Characteristics (DHC) Race & Ethnicity product and propose a candidate algorithm, SafeTab, that adds either two-sided geometric noise or discrete Gaussian noise to tabulated counts under differential privacy.

The algorithm is designed for population-group tabulations across multiple geographic levels (nation, state, county, AIANNH) and two statistic types: total counts and sex-by-age marginals. For non-total-only groups, SafeTab adaptively chooses coarser or finer age bins based on a noisy total count, using a two-stage privacy budget split. The paper provides formal privacy proofs for pure DP, zCDP, and RDP, along with error analyses calibrated to Census margin-of-error targets.

The population and context are the entire U.S. population as represented in Census microdata, but the paper is methodological rather than a human-subjects study. Its main conclusion is that SafeTab can satisfy the Census’s privacy and utility requirements, and that the discrete Gaussian and geometric variants offer different privacy-utility tradeoffs, with the discrete Gaussian achieving slightly smaller approximate-DP loss in their comparisons. The paper does not study educational outcomes, but instead addresses institutional data-release policy and privacy-preserving statistical computation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and formally analyzes SafeTab, a differentially private algorithm for releasing 2020 Census detailed race and ethnicity tabulations while meeting Census Bureau privacy, accuracy, integrality, and non-consistency requirements. It shows that the algorithm can be calibrated to target 95% margins of error across multiple population-group levels (e.g., nation, state, county, AIANNH) and provides privacy guarantees under pure DP, zCDP, and RDP.
finding.measure: Differential privacy guarantees and target 95% margin-of-error calibration for Census tabulations

paper_profiles.title: Moderator: Moderating Text-to-Image Diffusion Models through Fine-grained Context-based Policies
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of moderating harmful or policy-violating outputs from text-to-image diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion and SDXL. The authors argue that existing moderation approaches are too coarse and often fail to account for context, leading either to overblocking or to easy circumvention. To address this, they propose Moderator, a policy-based model management system that lets administrators specify fine-grained content policies describing what to moderate, in what context, how to moderate it, and why the moderation is needed.

Moderator works by generating self-sourced examples from the base model, fine-tuning on those examples, extracting task vectors, and then subtracting or composing those vectors to reduce the model’s ability to generate moderated content. The system supports remove, replace, and mosaic operations, plus policy expansion to cover synonyms, sub-concepts, and descriptive prompts. The paper evaluates the system on harmful prompts, policy interference, adversarial bypass prompts, and policy-author usability. It finds that Moderator substantially lowers CLIP similarity for moderated content while preserving unrelated content reasonably well, outperforms several baseline moderation methods against adversarial prompts, and remains usable for administrators in a small study.

The population studied is adults in two roles: 14 adult participants acting as administrators in a usability study, and 32 adult Stable Diffusion users in a moderation effectiveness experiment. The context is content moderation for generative AI systems, not classroom learning. Overall, the paper concludes that fine-grained, policy-based moderation of text-to-image models is feasible and can be implemented with relatively low effort, though policy interactions can affect non-target content and the approach is primarily a systems/security contribution rather than an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Moderator improved administrator efficiency in authoring and debugging moderation policies. In the usability study with n=14 adult participants, authors report an average of 2.29 policy iterations and 2.11 minutes to create a policy that passed all unit tests, with a mean SUS score of 80.71 (reported elsewhere as ~81), indicating relatively efficient policy creation and high usability.
finding.measure: Policy authoring iterations, task completion time, System Usability Scale (SUS)

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates a policy-governance mechanism for controlling model behavior at the institutional level. In experiments with n=32 Stable Diffusion users, Moderator prevented 65% of users from generating moderated content within 15 attempts and required the remaining users an average of 8.3 times more attempts to generate undesired content, indicating strong moderation/management impact on model access and governance.
finding.measure: Bypass success rate / number of attempts required to generate moderated content

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Moderation on Online Mental Health Conversations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether human moderation changes the quality and outcomes of online mental health conversations. The authors ask whether the presence and activity level of a moderator affect engagement, civility, linguistic coordination, conversational focus, and users’ psychological perspective in peer-support chats.

To study this, they analyze a natural experiment from an online mental health mobile application that replaced an unmoderated chat platform (NOMOD) with a nearly identical moderated platform (MOD). The dataset includes about 200,000 messages from 7,000 conversations across both conditions, with moderators who were psychology students trained in peer support facilitation. The study compares moderated and unmoderated conversations using psycholinguistic methods (LIWC), toxicity detection, and topic/coordination measures, and also examines variation in moderator activity.

The main findings are that moderated conversations had higher user engagement, substantially lower toxic and abusive language, greater linguistic coordination, and stronger positive changes in users’ psychological perspective over the course of conversations. Moderation also helped conversations stay on topic, especially when moderators were more active. The authors conclude that moderation can meaningfully improve the safety and effectiveness of online mental health support spaces, though they note this is an observational study and not a randomized trial.

finding.finding_summary: Moderation was associated with better engagement and more positive psychological perspective in online mental health conversations. Users in moderated discussions wrote about twice as many messages on average, and moderated users showed the largest improvement in future-focus and positive sentiment across conversation thirds (e.g., future-focus increased by 0.13 ± 0.06; sentiment increased by 0.22 ± 0.05).
finding.measure: User engagement (messages per participant) and psycholinguistic perspective measures from LIWC: future-focus, self-focus, and sentiment
finding.study_size: n=7,079 conversations (NOMOD) and n=317 conversations (MOD); perspective analysis restricted to 2,541 NOMOD and 219 MOD conversations with at least 20 user messages

finding.finding_summary: Moderation increased linguistic coordination between users, suggesting stronger trust-building and group cohesion. Peer users in MOD coordinated significantly more than users in NOMOD (mean=0.05, med=0.01, sd=0.13 vs. mean=0.01, med=0, sd=0.07; U=433419, p<0.01), and active moderation also helped keep conversations more on topic.
finding.measure: Linguistic coordination (Convokit) and topic stability via cosine distance between first and second halves of conversations
finding.study_size: n=7,079 conversations (NOMOD) and n=317 conversations (MOD) for topic/coordination analyses
finding.std_deviation: NOMOD sd=0.07; MOD sd=0.13 for coordination

finding.finding_summary: Moderation was associated with more sustained participation, suggesting more efficient and effective conversation flow. Users in moderated conversations sent roughly twice as many messages per conversation as those in unmoderated conversations, indicating higher engagement rather than early dropout.
finding.measure: Messages per chat participant and tokens per message

finding.finding_summary: At the platform level, moderation substantially reduced harmful behavior and improved conversation safety and coherence. Toxic language fell from 5.2% of messages in NOMOD to 1.0% in MOD, and moderate-to-active moderators were especially effective at keeping discussions on topic, indicating that moderation policies and staffing can materially shape institutional platform outcomes.
finding.measure: Toxicity/incivility rates and cosine distance for topic coherence
finding.study_size: n=183,570 NOMOD messages and n=14,985 MOD messages (user messages analyzed for toxicity)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Moderation in Online Social Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of toxicity diffusion in online social networks and asks how moderation strategies can alter the spread and persistence of toxic behavior. The authors argue that classical epidemic-style diffusion models such as SEIZ are too simplistic because they do not account for active moderation or individual differences among users.

To study this, they develop two simulation-based extensions of SEIZ: SEIZ-BasicModerator, which applies uniform generic moderator interventions, and SEIZ-SmartModerator, which uses user-specific psychological profiles based on the Dark Triad traits (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy) to trigger personalized, threshold-based moderation. The system is implemented as an agent-based simulator over synthetic Erdős–Rényi networks, with experiments varying intervention rate, intervention threshold, message volume, and toxicity classification threshold.

The study population is not a human sample but simulated adult social network users in an online platform context. Across simulation runs, the personalized SEIZ-SmartModerator generally outperforms the generic moderator by reducing infected/toxic users more effectively, slowing spread, and increasing recovery to less toxic states. The paper concludes that moderation effectiveness depends strongly on timing, thresholding, and personalization, and that profile-aware interventions are more resilient than one-size-fits-all moderation.

Because this is a simulation study without real-world educational outcomes, it does not provide evidence about student learning or formative assessment. Its main contribution is to systems design and governance for online moderation rather than K-12 instructional impact.

finding.finding_summary: The simulation results indicate that personalized, threshold-driven moderation is more effective than uniform moderation at reducing the spread and persistence of toxic behavior in online social networks. Across parameter sweeps, the SmartModerator consistently lowers infected-user prevalence and improves recovery to less toxic states, though the paper reports no human-subject effect sizes because the study is entirely simulated.
finding.measure: Simulated prevalence of user states in an agent-based SEIZ model (susceptible, exposed, infected, skeptic) under different moderation parameter settings

paper_profiles.title: Hybrid moderation in the newsroom: Recommending featured posts to content moderators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping online news moderators choose which user comments should be featured at the top of a discussion thread. Because featured-post selection is time-consuming and partly subjective, the authors propose a machine-learning recommender system that ranks comments by their probability of being featured, with the goal of supporting rather than replacing human moderators.

The approach is evaluated on a large Dutch news-comment dataset from NU.nl/NUjij containing 821,408 posts across 2,952 articles, with 8,262 featured posts. The authors compare several models: a threshold baseline, a random forest using moderator-available non-text features, a Dutch transformer (RobBERT) using text only, and hybrid models combining text and non-text features via embeddings or bag-of-words. They evaluate both classification performance and ranking quality on unseen articles using F1 and NDCG, then conduct an expert evaluation with four current moderators.

The best results came from the random forest with bag-of-words features (F1=0.41 on the test set; NDCG@5=0.87 on unseen articles), slightly outperforming the non-text random forest (F1=0.44; NDCG@5=0.86) and clearly beating the text-only transformer. In moderator review, the system produced suitable featured candidates for all but one of 30 sampled articles, with NDCG=0.83 and moderate inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha=0.62). The paper concludes that historical moderation signals are highly predictive, but also warns that the system may reinforce prior featuring patterns and bias toward users who were featured before or comments with higher respect counts.

finding.finding_summary: The recommender is designed to support and speed up the moderator’s task of selecting featured comments. On unseen articles, the best hybrid model (RF_BoW) achieved NDCG@5=0.87 and the plain RF achieved NDCG@5=0.86, indicating that moderators can be presented with high-quality candidate comments near the top of the ranking. In expert review with four moderators over 30 articles, the system produced suitable featured comments in all but one article (NDCG=0.83), suggesting practical usefulness for reducing curation effort.
finding.measure: Classification F1 and ranking quality (NDCG@3, NDCG@5, NDCG@10); moderator expert evaluation of recommended comment sets
finding.study_size: n=821,408 posts across 2,952 articles; expert evaluation n=4 moderators, 30 articles

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid human-AI moderation workflow intended to improve newsroom governance rather than user learning outcomes. The system aligns with editorial moderation practices by ranking featured-comment candidates for human decision-making, and the moderators judged the recommendations usable in most articles. However, the error analysis also shows institutional risk: the model is biased toward comments from users with prior featured history and higher respect counts, which may reinforce existing moderation patterns.
finding.measure: NDCG on unseen articles; moderator assessment; feature-based error analysis of false positives/negatives
finding.study_size: n=821,408 posts; n=4 moderators in expert evaluation

paper_profiles.title: LIONGUARD 2: Building Lightweight, Data-Efficient & Localised Multilingual Content Moderators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of multilingual content moderation in low-resource, code-mixed settings, with a specific focus on Singaporean English, Chinese, Malay, and partial Tamil. The authors argue that mainstream moderation systems often underperform on localized language use such as Singlish, creating safety gaps in real deployments.

The paper presents LIONGUARD 2, a lightweight moderation classifier built on frozen OpenAI embeddings with a trainable multi-head ordinal classifier. The system is trained on a curated mix of Singaporean forum comments, synthetic query rewrites, and selected English safety datasets, with an emphasis on language-aware curation and a small CPU-deployable model footprint.

Evaluation is conducted on 17 benchmarks, including Singapore-localized and general English safety datasets, plus a native-speaker red-teaming set of 391 multilingual cases. The model outperforms or matches several commercial and open-source moderation systems on Singlish, Chinese, and Malay benchmarks, but shows weaker performance on Tamil. The authors conclude that high-quality local data and strong multilingual embeddings can outperform much larger models for localized safety filtering, while also noting remaining gaps and potential bias in underrepresented linguistic communities.

finding.finding_summary: LIONGUARD 2 is designed and evaluated as a lightweight, CPU-deployable moderation system that can be retrained in under two minutes and processes text at roughly 300 tokens/s end-to-end. The classifier contains only 0.85M parameters (3.2 MB on disk), and the authors report performance comparable to or better than much larger moderation systems on several benchmarks while using far less compute.
finding.measure: Deployment latency, throughput, model size, and benchmark F1 for moderation performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that LIONGUARD 2 is actively deployed on the Singapore Government’s AI Guardian platform as a safety module for internal services, indicating direct institutional use. The authors frame the work as a practical case study for localized moderation infrastructure and argue that the model improves governance of text-centric AI services in multilingual public-sector settings.
finding.measure: Operational deployment in the Singapore Government’s AI Guardian platform and benchmarked moderation performance

paper_profiles.title: A tutorial for propensity score weighting for moderation analysis: An application examining smoking disparities among sexual minority adults
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a methods tutorial on how to estimate moderation effects using propensity score weighting in observational data. The authors focus on a practical five-step workflow: checking covariate overlap within moderator strata, estimating propensity score weights separately within each moderator level, evaluating balance, estimating moderated treatment effects, and conducting sensitivity analyses for unobserved confounding.

The illustrative case study uses data from 41,832 adults in the 2019 National Survey on Drug Use and Health to examine whether gender moderates the association between sexual minority status (LGB identity) and past-month cigarette smoking. The paper shows how to implement the approach in R and Stata, reporting that weighting achieved good covariate balance within gender groups and that LGB status was associated with higher smoking prevalence in both men and women, with a larger effect for women (risk difference 0.15, 95% CI 0.08, 0.18) than men (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.00, 0.10). The tutorial concludes that propensity score weighting within moderator strata can reduce bias in subgroup effect estimates and that sensitivity analyses are important because findings may differ in robustness across subgroups.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not study social-emotional skills directly; it uses past-month smoking as the outcome and discusses minority stress. There is no empirical measure of engagement, self-regulation, or persistence.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: This paper directly studies a methodological approach for improving estimation of moderated effects in observational data, which is an analytical/institutional contribution rather than a participant outcome. In the case study, propensity score weighting improved covariate balance within gender strata and supported more credible subgroup inference (all absolute SMDs and KS statistics < 0.10 after weighting).
finding.measure: covariate balance diagnostics (standardized mean differences, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics)

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (theory/review paper; no single empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework for formative assessment, arguing that existing definitions and classroom practices need a clearer conceptual basis. Black and Wiliam position formative assessment as evidence about student achievement being elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or peers to make better-founded instructional decisions. They aim to connect formative assessment to broader theories of pedagogy, self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment.

The paper is not an intervention trial; instead, it is a conceptual and literature-based analysis that synthesizes prior research and examples from classroom practice. The authors organize formative assessment into five strategies: clarifying learning intentions and success criteria, engineering effective discussions and tasks, providing feedback that moves learners forward, activating students as instructional resources for one another, and activating students as owners of their own learning. They then examine how these strategies relate to models of learner cognition and to the teacher’s diagnostic and prognostic decisions during classroom interaction.

The central conclusion is that formative assessment should be understood as contingent, dialogic, and grounded in teachers’ models of student thinking, rather than as a checklist of techniques. The paper argues that effective formative practice depends on interpreting student responses through robust theories of learning and on aligning feedback with instructional goals. Because the article is theoretical rather than empirical, it does not report original effect sizes or subgroup analyses, but it offers a framework intended to improve future research and classroom implementation.

paper_profiles.title: Examining the use of Kahoot to support digital game-based formative assessments in UAE higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how the digital game-based learning platform Kahoot can support formative assessment in a highly incentivized higher-education context in the United Arab Emirates. The authors are particularly interested in the tension between students’ motivation to protect GPA-linked outcomes and the pedagogical goal of using formative quizzes to promote engagement, feedback, and deeper learning.

The study was conducted in an all-female second-year undergraduate paramedic program. Students experienced both Kahoot quizzes and conventional paper-based formative assessments in a paramedic-pharmacology module, after which the researchers interviewed participants using an activity-theory framework and Mwanza’s eight-step model to elicit perceptions of the tool and to identify contradictions within the assessment activity system.

Findings suggest that Kahoot made formative assessment feel less stressful, more fun, and more collaborative, and students reported better knowledge retention and greater satisfaction with the course and teacher. However, Kahoot did not increase students’ motivation to study outside class; in this setting, paper-based quizzes were seen as more serious and more closely tied to GPA-related consequences. The authors conclude that Kahoot can transform classroom interaction and reduce anxiety, but its effectiveness is strongly shaped by the socio-economic and cultural context of the UAE and by existing assessment norms.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that Kahoot made formative assessment feel "less stressful" and "fun," and the authors interpret this as a reduction in test anxiety relative to paper-based quizzes. All 10 interview participants described the Kahoot sessions positively in affective terms, with repeated references to lowered stress and greater comfort during assessment.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of stress, anxiety, enjoyment, and satisfaction during formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Kahoot encouraged greater collaboration, peer discussion, and collective knowledge-building during in-class formative assessment. Students said they could hear and challenge one another’s answers, which made feedback more interactive and helped them construct understanding together, although this came with opportunities for collusion/cheating.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview accounts of collaboration, discussion, and peer feedback during formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: Students said Kahoot helped them retain knowledge and recall information, and they felt they learned more from Kahoot than from paper-based formative assessments. However, the study did not report test-score gains or other standardized academic performance metrics; the evidence is based on qualitative perceptions of knowledge retention and understanding.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of knowledge retention and recall during module formative assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Kahoot shifted classroom norms and assessment interactions, but it did not displace the wider GPA-centered incentive structure of the UAE higher-education context. Students continued to prioritize GPA maintenance and viewed paper-based quizzes as more consequential for academic progression and bursary-linked outcomes, indicating that institutional rules and socio-economic pressures remained dominant.
finding.measure: Interview evidence about GPA pressure, institutional rules, assessment norms, and perceived consequences of failure

paper_profiles.title: Beyond feedback: Developing student capability in complex appraisal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual article addresses a practical problem in higher education assessment: teachers often provide detailed feedback, yet students frequently do not improve because they cannot adequately interpret or use the comments. Sadler argues that the limitation is not simply the quality of feedback, but students’ lack of the background knowledge needed to decode evaluative statements and connect them to their own work.

The paper proposes an alternative pedagogical approach built around purposeful peer assessment. Rather than relying primarily on teacher-generated feedforward and feedback, students should be inducted into appraisal practice so they learn to make and justify judgments about complex work. The approach emphasizes three core concepts—task compliance, quality, and criteria—along with tacit knowledge developed through repeated evaluative experience.

The population and context are higher education students, especially undergraduates and postgraduates completing complex, open-ended assessment tasks across disciplines. The article is not an empirical intervention study; it is a theoretical argument supported by references to prior empirical work on feedback, assessment criteria, and peer assessment. Its main conclusion is that improving learning in complex assessment depends less on more detailed telling and more on structured opportunities for students to practice appraisal, thereby building durable evaluative capability.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that purposeful peer assessment and repeated appraisal practice can develop students’ evaluative judgment, critical reasoning, and ability to explain and justify judgments about quality. No direct effect sizes or sample sizes are reported because this is a conceptual/theoretical paper rather than a primary empirical study.
finding.measure: Development of appraisal capability, evaluative judgment, and understanding of task compliance, quality, and criteria

finding.finding_summary: The paper asserts that structured peer assessment can deepen student engagement with content and promote self-regulated learning by helping students monitor the quality of their own work during production. These claims are theoretical and grounded in prior literature rather than tested in a new empirical sample.
finding.measure: Student engagement and self-regulated learning (theoretical claims, not newly measured in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: Sadler notes that structured mechanisms such as rubrics, templates, and databases of feedback sentences can reduce the labor and cognitive demands of producing feedback, but the paper’s main thrust is that these efficiencies are secondary to developing student appraisal capability. No empirical estimate of workload reduction is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload and efficiency of feedback production (discussed conceptually)

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.population: Kindergarten through university students and teachers in educational contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the evidence base on educational feedback by conducting a large meta-analysis of primary studies rather than relying on prior meta-syntheses. The authors ask two main questions: what is the overall effect of feedback on student learning, and which feedback characteristics moderate that effect. They also compare their results with the influential Visible Learning syntheses by Hattie and colleagues.

The review integrates 994 effect sizes from 435 studies, covering more than 61,000 participants across kindergarten, primary, secondary, and higher education contexts. Eligible studies compared a feedback intervention with a control or pre-post design and reported learning-related outcomes. The authors code moderators including research design, publication type, outcome type, feedback type, feedback channel, and feedback direction, and analyze the data with random-effects models and robust variance estimation when needed.
