The main conclusion is that feedback has a positive overall effect on student learning, but the effect is smaller than in earlier meta-syntheses and highly heterogeneous. After removing extreme outliers, the overall effect is d=0.48 (95% CI 0.44–0.51). Effects are stronger for cognitive and physical outcomes than for motivational and behavioral outcomes, stronger for high-information feedback than for corrective feedback or reinforcement/punishment, and stronger for teacher-to-student and especially student-to-student feedback than for student-to-teacher feedback. The paper emphasizes that feedback is not a single uniform treatment and that its effectiveness depends heavily on the information content and form of the feedback.

Although the paper includes moderators such as research design and participant context, it does not report subgroup evidence on equity variables such as disability status, multilingual learners, socioeconomic status, race, or ethnicity. Its relevance to the retrieval question is primarily in providing a broad, high-quality synthesis of feedback effects and some moderator evidence by study design and outcome type.

finding.finding_summary: Across 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000), feedback produced a positive overall effect on student learning. After excluding 35 extreme outliers, the random-effects mean effect was d=0.48 (95% CI 0.44–0.51), indicating a medium-to-large benefit on learning outcomes overall.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes/achievement-related outcomes across educational feedback studies

finding.finding_summary: Feedback effects were smaller for motivational outcomes than for cognitive outcomes. For motivational measures such as intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, and persistence, the pooled effect was d=0.33 (95% CI 0.23–0.42), and 21% of motivational effect sizes were negative, especially when feedback was uninformative rewards or punishments.
finding.measure: Motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found that feedback had a positive effect on cognitive outcomes, which the authors frame as including student achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance. The pooled effect for cognitive outcomes was d=0.51 (95% CI 0.46–0.55), and effects were strongest when feedback contained more information about task, process, and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes, including achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics outcomes are included within the paper's broader cognitive/physical learning effects and are explicitly mentioned in examples and moderator interpretation, but mathematics is not isolated as a separate main outcome category. The review reports that feedback benefits learning overall and gives examples of studies with math-test outcomes, but a distinct pooled math effect is not reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics test performance (within broader cognitive/physical outcomes)

paper_profiles.title: Affective Teacher–Student Relationships and Students’ Engagement and Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Update and Test of the Mediating Role of Engagement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether the quality of affective teacher–student relationships is associated with students’ engagement and achievement, and whether engagement helps explain that association. The authors update an earlier meta-analysis with newer studies and use meta-analytic structural equation modeling to test a mediation model across positive relationship aspects (such as closeness, support, warmth) and negative relationship aspects (such as conflict and rejection).

The sample includes 189 studies published from 1990 to 2016, covering 249,198 students from preschool through high school. The authors also test whether the pattern differs by school level (primary vs. secondary) and whether it holds in a longitudinal subsample. They analyze correlations among teacher–student relationships, engagement, and achievement rather than an intervention.

Results show that positive relationships are associated with higher engagement and achievement, while negative relationships are associated with lower engagement and achievement. Engagement partially mediates both the positive and negative relationship–achievement links in the full sample, in primary and secondary school separately, and in the longitudinal subsample. The only notable subgroup difference is that the positive relationship–engagement association is stronger in secondary school than in primary school. Overall, the paper concludes that affective teacher–student relationships matter for academic outcomes partly because they shape student engagement, but also through direct effects on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Across 189 studies (N=249,198), positive teacher–student relationships were associated with higher student engagement (β=.29, 95% CI [.25, .32]), while negative relationships were associated with lower engagement (β=-.19, 95% CI [-.24, -.15]). In the longitudinal subsample (k=52), the pattern persisted (positive→engagement β=.16; negative→engagement β=-.23), and engagement partially mediated relationship quality’s association with achievement.
finding.measure: Student engagement (multidimensional; behavioral/emotional/cognitive indicators such as effort, persistence, school liking, participation, and engagement/disaffection measures)
finding.effect_size: β=.29; β=-.19; indirect β=.07 and β=-.05 (overall)

finding.finding_summary: Teacher–student relationship quality was positively associated with academic achievement, with positive relationships showing a small direct effect (β=.07, 95% CI [.04, .11]) and negative relationships showing a small negative direct effect (β=-.07, 95% CI [-.11, -.02]). Engagement also predicted achievement (β=.24, 95% CI [.18, .30]), and the indirect effects through engagement were significant (positive→achievement β=.07; negative→achievement β=-.05), indicating partial mediation.
finding.measure: Academic achievement/performance (grades, test scores, and other academic performance indicators across subjects)
finding.effect_size: β=.07; β=-.07; indirect β=.07; β=-.05; total effect positive=.14; total effect negative=-.12

paper_profiles.title: The role of peer feedback in oral communicative tasks for young adult learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This action research study examines whether peer feedback can improve young adult English learners’ oral communicative performance, specifically lexical variety in speaking. The author frames the problem as a classroom need to move beyond teacher-centered correction, which can interrupt fluency development, and to find a feedback strategy that more actively involves learners in assessing and improving their own speaking.

The intervention used peer feedback rubrics during a semester-long series of oral communicative tasks with a group of university learners at La Sabana University in Colombia. Students were trained to give and receive feedback on one another’s speaking performances, and the study collected data from a diagnostic speaking test, a final speaking test, surveys, students’ logs, focus groups, and recordings/transcriptions of oral tasks. The design is best characterized as mixed-methods action research because it combines qualitative reflections and perceptions with comparison of speaking performances over time.

The participants were 23 pre-intermediate university students aged 17–19, though the abstract reports 16 learners and the body describes a larger class with implementation data gathered across the group. The main conclusions are that peer feedback can support oral communication and is especially understandable and useful when peers share a similar language level. However, the study also finds that low self-efficacy and limited confidence can make learners reluctant to give effective feedback, indicating that peer feedback works best when students are trained and actively engaged in the process.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that peer feedback supported learners’ oral communicative performance, especially lexical variety, and helped them become more active and independent in speaking tasks. At the same time, students’ low self-efficacy limited their confidence in giving feedback, so the overall effect on speaking development was positive but conditional on learner readiness and training.
finding.measure: Diagnostic speaking test, final speaking test, audio recordings/transcriptions of oral tasks, surveys, students’ logs, focus groups

paper_profiles.title: Indeterminacy in the use of preset criteria for assessment and grading in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the theoretical and practical problems that arise when university teachers use preset criteria, rubrics, and additive scoring schemes to assess complex student work. Sadler argues that although these systems are widely promoted as transparent, objective, and reliable, they often fail to capture the full nature of quality in divergent tasks such as essays, projects, performances, and design products.

The article is not an intervention study but a conceptual and practice-based critique grounded in published research on judgment, tacit knowledge, and expert appraisal, along with the author’s observations and conversations with academics. It identifies six recurring anomalies in analytic grading, including discrepancies between holistic and analytic judgments, emergence of criteria not included on preset lists, blurred criterion boundaries, variation in criterion sets across teachers, and disagreement over criterion-level interpretations. The central conclusion is that analytic grading systems have structural indeterminacies that limit their validity for complex higher-education assessment, and that holistic judgment may better represent overall quality in many cases.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that analytic grading systems are often labor-intensive and cognitively convoluted in practice, because teachers do not usually score each criterion independently in a neat linear sequence. Instead, assessors often run dual agendas and may retrospectively assign criterion scores after forming an overall judgment, which undermines the practical efficiency promised by rubrics and matrix scoring.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading process efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article concludes that fixed-criteria grading schemes and additive rubrics have a weak theoretical foundation for complex higher-education assessment and can produce distorted grading decisions. Across the paper’s six observations, the author argues that these systems systematically misrepresent quality, limit valid feedback, and create ethical and institutional tensions around transparency and consistency.
finding.measure: validity of grading systems / institutional assessment practice

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.venue: WIPTTE 2013 (Working paper / conference proceedings; arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment on pen-enabled mobile devices, appears effective across a range of educational settings. The core problem is that while formative assessment is widely theorized to improve learning, instructors need a practical classroom method for collecting open-ended student responses quickly and using them to adjust instruction.

The paper presents seven illustrative vignettes from diverse contexts, including high school algebra, undergraduate physics, engineering physics, chemical engineering, food science, and graduate courses in the United States and Mexico. Across these settings, instructors report using InkSurvey to reveal misconceptions, guide discussion, tailor instruction, and increase student engagement and participation. Evidence is drawn from a mix of classroom observations, anonymous student surveys, summative assessment comparisons, and reported changes in quiz/problem-solving performance, but the paper is not a controlled study of causal effects.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey is a flexible and promising pedagogical tool for real-time formative assessment in varied educational environments. The paper suggests positive learning gains and improved student metacognition, with some indication that female students in one high school algebra context may have benefited more than males. However, the evidence is largely illustrative and heterogeneous, so the findings should be interpreted as indications of effectiveness rather than definitive causal proof.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I context, students exposed to regular real-time formative assessment with InkSurvey showed greater mastery of fundamental concepts than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper reports that female students in particular demonstrated much greater learning gains than the control group, but it does not provide an effect size for this subgroup comparison.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments in Algebra I; student responses to a survey item about understanding

finding.finding_summary: Across several physics and engineering contexts, InkSurvey was associated with improved performance on conceptual and problem-solving tasks. Examples include a Calculus III misconception nearly disappearing on a summative assessment two weeks later (1/87 students vs 12/103 in a comparison lecture section), steady improvement in upper-level engineering physics problem-solving across the semester, and chemical engineering students increasing average competence from about 1.8 to about 3.1 on a 4-point scale after instructor-guided use of simulations plus InkSurvey.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions on triple integrals; problem-solving skill scores; 4-point competence ratings on chemical engineering concepts

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward InkSurvey were generally favorable, with many students reporting increased engagement, motivation, and participation. In one undergraduate survey, 54 of 63 students (86%) said their responses gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 48 of 63 (76%) said creating responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did not understand.
finding.measure: Anonymous student surveys; focus group comments; agreement with attitudinal statements
finding.study_size: n=63 (survey subset described in one course)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that InkSurvey helped students improve metacognition and self-assessment by making their thinking visible and prompting them to reflect on what they knew and did not know. Student survey responses indicate that the tool supported immediate feedback, reflection, and deeper thinking rather than passive note-taking, and instructors observed that it helped diagnose misconceptions and guide subsequent discussion.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about understanding and metacognition; instructor observations of problem-solving and thinking processes
finding.study_size: n=63 for one metacognition survey; other contexts not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Instructors reported that InkSurvey made it easier to obtain immediate information about student thinking and to adjust instruction in real time. The paper emphasizes gains in instructional efficiency such as quickly identifying common difficulties, tailoring feedback, and using the same class period to repair misconceptions before they become entrenched, though these are descriptive rather than experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Instructor reports of real-time feedback use and instructional adjustment; classroom process descriptions

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether learning gains produced by a classroom model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment differ by students’ learning styles. The motivation is to see whether a visually rich, hands-on, feedback-rich instructional approach is especially effective for some learners and less effective for others.

The intervention, called the Coupled Model, uses one pen-enabled mobile device per student (Tablet PCs in this study) so that students can interact with simulations and answer open-format InkSurvey questions in real time. The paper focuses on an undergraduate engineering physics course (Advanced Physics Laboratory I) taught in two sections with a total of 41 students. Learning was measured with pre-tests and end-of-semester summative assessments across five simulations (circuits, Fourier analysis, diffraction, standard deviation mean, and least squares), and learning styles were measured with the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles.

Results show statistically significant learning gains for all five simulations, but little to no relationship between learning gains and any of the four learning-style dimensions. Pearson correlations between learning gain and learning style were all close to zero (e.g., ACT-REF r=0.02 for circuits; VIS-VRB r=0.10 for diffraction; most others between -0.28 and 0.25), indicating no meaningful moderation by learning style. The authors conclude that the coupled simulation-plus-formative-assessment approach is broadly effective across learning styles rather than preferentially benefiting particular learner types.

finding.finding_summary: Students achieved statistically significant learning gains on all five simulation-based content areas after using the coupled model of interactive simulations plus real-time formative assessment. Across the five simulations, average normalized gains ranged from 60% to 75% (e.g., circuits 63%, Fourier 67%, diffraction 60%, standard deviation mean 75%, least squares 61%), with paired tests reported as p<0.001.
finding.measure: Pre-test vs. summative assessment scores on simulation-based physics/statistics concept questions scored with a rubric
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; simulation-specific n ranged from 30 to 41

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically tests whether the instructional model’s effectiveness varies by learning style, which is treated as a learner characteristic related to how students process information. Correlations between learning gain and learning-style dimensions were near zero across all five simulations (e.g., ACT-REF r=0.02, SEN-INT r=0.02, VIS-VRB r=-0.04, SEQ-GLO r=-0.12 for circuits), and the authors conclude there was no statistically significant relationship.
finding.measure: Pearson correlations between normalized learning gains and Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles dimensions
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; simulation-specific n ranged from 30 to 41
finding.effect_size: r values ranged approximately from -0.28 to 0.25 depending on simulation and learning-style pair
finding.confidence_interval: 95% confidence ranges reported in table; for example circuits ACT-REF -0.28 to 0.32, SEN-INT -0.28 to 0.32, VIS-VRB -0.34 to 0.26, SEQ-GLO -0.41 to 0.19

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for collecting real-time formative assessment responses using pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors argue that open-format, digital-ink responses let instructors see student thinking more directly than multiple-choice clicker questions and respond immediately to misconceptions during class.

Rather than reporting a controlled study, the paper presents seven vignettes from different educational settings: university calculus and physics, high school algebra, community college biology, and upper-level undergraduate/graduate food chemistry and physics courses in the United States and Mexico. Across these cases, instructors used InkSurvey to ask open-ended questions, project anonymized student work, and adjust instruction in real time.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey is broadly applicable across subjects, device types, and educational environments, and that it can support active learning, reveal misconceptions, and help instructors scaffold understanding more effectively. The paper does not provide a rigorous comparative effectiveness analysis; it mainly offers illustrative implementation examples and practitioner observations.

finding.finding_summary: In the University Honors Calculus III vignette (n=87 first-term college students), InkSurvey was used to elicit open-format responses on triple integrals and regions of integration. After in-class discussion of responses, the share of students showing the specific misconception of all constant bounds dropped from 32 of 83 responses on Q4 to 0 students on the follow-up Q6, while all students responded to the second prompt.
finding.measure: Accuracy of open-ended calculus responses on defining inequalities for triple integrals / regions of integration

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, biology, and food chemistry vignettes, InkSurvey was used to probe student reasoning in real time, reveal misconceptions, and support immediate instructional adjustment. In the introductory physics example, open-format responses exposed cases where students reached the right answer with faulty reasoning; in the community college biology and food chemistry examples, the tool was used to scaffold conceptual understanding and connect prior knowledge to new scientific ideas.
finding.measure: Quality of student explanations, conceptual understanding, and misconception diagnosis in science/STEM tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that InkSurvey increased active engagement and participation in class discussions, especially when students submitted responses anonymously and could see a range of peer ideas. In the community college biology vignette, students were described as motivated to participate and engaged in interspersed discussions; in the creativity-in-physics vignette, anonymity was said to reduce evaluation apprehension and encourage participation.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement, participation, and willingness to contribute in class discussions

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that InkSurvey supports metacognition, critical thinking, and collaborative idea development. For example, open-ended questions required students to explain reasoning rather than select an option, and the creativity-in-physics vignette used structured brainstorming and critical-comment cycles to generate and refine ideas; the authors explicitly state that the tool enhances metacognition and helps students attend to the ideas of others.
finding.measure: Observed use of open-ended reasoning, metacognitive reflection, brainstorming, and peer critique

finding.finding_summary: The tool is presented as reducing the delay and burden of formative assessment by allowing instructors to collect and scan all student work quickly during class. In the high school algebra vignette, the teacher could review all 25 students' solutions and address misconceptions before students left class; similarly, the paper argues that real-time collection is less cumbersome than traditional formative assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Instructor ability to review student work and respond to misconceptions in real time

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper asks whether student-produced videos can function as a useful formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that traditional tests and questionnaires capture only a narrow slice of understanding, whereas making and discussing videos may reveal students’ conceptual misunderstandings, reasoning processes, and collaborative skills.

The approach was implemented in a Brazilian high school (Colégio Pedro II, Rio de Janeiro) with students across grades 1–3 of high school (ages roughly 14–17). After regular physics instruction, students worked in self-selected groups of up to five to produce short videos on topics studied that term, along with a short written explanation. The teacher reviewed the videos and texts, gave feedback, and then led class discussions to use the videos as part of assessment and instruction.

The paper reports descriptive analysis of 55 videos produced by 232 students in 2011. The authors found that many videos were at least partially correct conceptually, most had coherent structure, and technical quality was strongly correlated with conceptual quality. The paper concludes that student video production can be a reliable formative assessment tool in high school physics because it reveals student thinking, supports teacher feedback, and encourages planning, collaboration, and meaningful learning. The paper does not report subgroup or equity moderation analyses.

finding.finding_summary: In the analysis of 55 student-produced physics videos (n=232 students), 35% were judged physically correct and 45% partially correct, while 47% presented the physics ideas clearly. The authors conclude that the videos revealed both correct understanding and misconceptions, and that they can diagnose where learning succeeded or failed.
finding.measure: Teacher/content analysis of physics correctness, clarity, and fit to the assigned topic in student-produced videos

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that video production required students to plan, replan, collaborate, and reflect on their own work, indicating metacognitive and collaborative skill use. Although no standardized scale was used, the analysis reports that 87% of videos had a logical sequence and that higher technical quality was associated with better conceptual quality, suggesting substantial student effort and planning.
finding.measure: Observed planning/organization, logical sequence of videos, and group production process

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe the activity as engaging and motivating: students used age-appropriate humor, music, and creative formats, and almost all videos (84%) used music. The paper presents the activity as supporting participation and interest, but it does not include direct survey measures of engagement or motivation.
finding.measure: Observed student participation and qualitative features of video production/discussion

finding.finding_summary: The authors present student video production as a practical formative assessment method that lets teachers identify misconceptions during the term and adapt instruction in time. The main evidence is descriptive: the teacher analyzed all 55 videos and used them to guide feedback and classroom discussion, suggesting the approach provided actionable assessment information beyond traditional tests.
finding.measure: Teacher use of video artifacts for formative feedback and instructional adjustment

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Curiosity Using Interactive Simulations Combined with Real-Time Formative Assessment Facilitated by Open-Format Questions on Tablet Computers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether real-time formative assessment delivered through pen-enabled tablet computers can reveal and enhance student curiosity in an undergraduate engineering physics course. The authors argue that in lecture settings students often appear passive and inquisitive behavior is hard to observe, so they used open-format questions to prompt students to describe what they observed, learned, and wondered about while interacting with simulations.

The approach used InkSurvey, a web-based tool for collecting free-response answers in real time, alongside interactive physics simulations on tablet computers. Students in a junior-level electromagnetics course submitted questions and comments after working through four simulations (induced charge, moving charge, inductance calculator, and quantum harmonic oscillator). The authors then categorized the questions into curiosity types such as congruous, incongruous, modifying, generalizing/analogy, causal/creative, and informational.

The population was undergraduate engineering physics students, and the study context was a junior-level electromagnetics course with a concurrent quantum physics class. Results showed that students produced many questions without extrinsic incentives, most often questions aimed at understanding how the models and simulations worked (especially congruous questions), with smaller numbers of modifying, analogy-based, or creative questions. The authors conclude that the combination of interactive simulations and real-time open-response formative assessment can make student curiosity visible, stimulate deeper engagement, and provide instructors with useful springboards for discussion and conceptual clarification. Because the paper is primarily descriptive and does not report controlled outcome comparisons, it does not provide subgroup moderation evidence about equity-related differences in formative-assessment effects.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appeared to increase and surface student curiosity and engagement during learning activities. Across four simulations, students submitted many open-ended questions without extrinsic incentives (e.g., 68 questions from 40 students on the induced-charge simulation; 53 questions from 31 students on the moving-charge simulation; 35 comments from 35 students on the inductance calculator; 32 questions from 31 students on the quantum harmonic oscillator), suggesting heightened intrinsic motivation and willingness to participate.
finding.measure: Student curiosity/question generation and qualitative engagement in response to interactive simulations and open-format prompts
finding.study_size: n=40, n=31, n=35, and n=31 across the four simulations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the activity supported metacognition, question generation, and critical thinking by asking students to explain observations, identify incongruities, and consider modifications or analogies. The authors report that students used the prompts to practice asking questions, connect concepts across contexts, and evaluate limitations of the simulations and models.
finding.measure: Categorized student questions and comments reflecting metacognition, critical thinking, analogy-making, and model evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Integrating LLMs for Grading and Appeal Resolution in Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to grade computer science exams and resolve student grade appeals in an undergraduate object-oriented programming course. The authors introduce AI-PAT, a Python-based assessment workflow that transcribes handwritten answers into digital form, checks for discrepancies, applies rubric-based LLM grading, generates feedback, and supports an appeal mechanism where students can challenge grades and receive LLM-assisted responses.

The study was conducted in a second-year undergraduate computer science course at Gebze Technical University in Fall 2024. It analyzed more than 850 exam submissions, including quizzes, a midterm, and a final exam, and processed 185 appeals. The authors compared ChatGPT and Gemini grading outputs, compared LLM and human grader reliability, and examined student perceptions through surveys. They found strong correlations between LLMs but also meaningful variability across prompts and settings, substantial disagreement among human graders, and that 74% of appeals resulted in grade changes.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can improve grading speed and provide detailed formative feedback, but their use requires transparent rubrics, human oversight, and appeal mechanisms to support fairness and trust. Student feedback was mixed to negative: many valued the speed and detail of AI feedback, but they expressed strong concerns about fairness, interpretability, and willingness to use the system for future assessment.

finding.finding_summary: AI-PAT automated grading and appeal handling for more than 850 exam submissions and 185 appeals, substantially reducing manual grading and review workload. The authors argue the system improved efficiency by generating grades, detailed feedback, and appeal responses at scale, though the paper does not report a formal time-savings effect size.
finding.measure: Volume of exam submissions and appeals processed through the AI-assisted grading workflow

finding.finding_summary: Across final exam grading, ChatGPT and Gemini showed strong agreement but different score distributions: Gemini’s mean score was 43.59 versus ChatGPT’s 36.11 (n=73), and the total-score correlation was high (Pearson r=0.909, Spearman=0.920). However, the paper also reports substantial variability by prompt/model configuration and notable disagreement between human graders, indicating that rubric-based AI grading is promising but not yet fully stable for programming assessment.
finding.measure: Final exam grades and per-question grading correlations across LLMs and human graders
finding.study_size: n=73 final-exam papers for LLM comparison; n=30 sampled papers and 2 human graders for human reliability analysis
finding.effect_size: r=0.909 for total score agreement between ChatGPT and Gemini
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total score SD=17.22; Gemini total score SD=12.81

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses suggest that AI-PAT’s feedback was seen as helpful by some students, but overall satisfaction and trust were low. Among 49 respondents, 22 (45%) agreed or strongly agreed the feedback helped learning, while 43 (88%) opposed future use and zero students expressed confidence in the fairness of AI-PAT, indicating concerns about trust and acceptance despite perceived utility.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of satisfaction, trust, and usefulness of AI-generated feedback and grading

finding.finding_summary: The appeal mechanism materially affected grading outcomes: 137 of 185 appeals (74%) led to a grade change, with mean normalized grades rising from 21.59 to 34.37 overall. This indicates the AI-assisted grading system had consequential institutional effects on assessment outcomes and suggests that transparent appeal processes can alter final grades substantially.
finding.measure: Appeal outcomes and changes in original versus revised grades
finding.std_deviation: Original grades SD=21.52; new grades SD=24.48

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on rubric-based evaluation of students’ written explanations, object-oriented programming solutions, and appeal justifications, which require reasoning, explanation, and self-advocacy. While no formal durable-skills outcome was isolated, the study suggests AI-PAT may support structured reflection during appeal resolution, but the evidence is indirect and based on grading/feedback analyses rather than a dedicated assessment of metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Student written exam responses and appeal justifications

paper_profiles.title: Combining Log Data and Collaborative Dialogue Features to Predict Project Quality in Middle School AI Education
paper_profiles.venue: CSEDM’25: 9th Educational Data Mining in Computer Science Education (CSEDM) Workshop
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether two types of process data—student dialogue transcripts and system interaction logs—can predict the quality of chatbot training phrases produced during collaborative AI learning. The authors focus on an open-ended project-based learning environment where middle school students work in pairs to design and iteratively improve conversational agents in a science class. The central question is whether multimodal feature fusion improves prediction of three project-quality proxies: training phrase count, lexical density, and lexical variation.

The study was conducted in a public middle school science classroom in the southeastern United States during a 10-hour AI learning module. Data came from 47 student pairs (94 students) across 121 collaborative sessions, with audio/video transcribed and synchronized to 23 types of interaction logs from the AMBY chatbot-building environment. The authors trained feedforward neural network models using log-only, dialogue-only, and combined features, evaluating performance with held-out AUC and cross-validation.

Results show that log data better predicts productivity-related outcomes, especially training phrase count, while dialogue features better predict linguistic richness, especially lexical density. Multimodal fusion improved prediction for training phrase count and slightly for lexical variation, but did not improve lexical density. Overall, the paper concludes that the usefulness of combining logs and dialogue depends on the specific learning outcome being predicted, and it highlights the promise and limitations of multimodal learning analytics in K-12 AI education. The paper does not examine subgroup moderation, equity, or differential effects across demographics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper models the quality of student-created chatbot training phrases in a K-12 AI learning environment and finds that multimodal features can predict these project-quality proxies with moderate accuracy. The best result was for training phrase count, where combined log+dialogue features achieved AUC=0.8301 (95% CI [0.7732, 0.8822]) on the held-out test set, compared with 0.8053 for log-only and 0.5971 for dialogue-only.
finding.measure: Prediction of training phrase quality proxies: training phrase count, lexical density, and lexical variation

finding.finding_summary: The strongest substantive outcome is productivity in the chatbot-building process, operationalized as the number of training phrases students entered. Log-based features predicted this best (AUC=0.8053, 95% CI [0.7470, 0.8604]), and early fusion improved performance further to AUC=0.8301 (95% CI [0.7732, 0.8822]). This suggests system interaction logs can serve as indicators of task progress and productive effort during collaborative development.
finding.measure: Training phrase count as a proxy for productivity/engagement during chatbot development

finding.finding_summary: The study also examines collaboration-related linguistic richness in student dialogue and its relationship to the diversity and richness of chatbot training phrases. Dialogue-only features predicted lexical density better than logs (AUC=0.6551, 95% CI [0.5920, 0.7168]), and combined features did not improve on this (AUC=0.5700, 95% CI [0.5042, 0.6352]). Although not a direct measure of collaboration quality, the paper treats dialogue as a marker of collaborative reasoning and joint meaning-making in pair programming.
finding.measure: Lexical density and lexical variation of training phrases predicted from collaborative dialogue and logs

paper_profiles.title: Human-Robot Mutual Learning through Affective-Linguistic Interaction and Differential Outcomes Training
paper_profiles.venue: Pre-print / conference paper accepted for publication (conference name not reported)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether differential outcomes training (DOT), implemented through a robot’s affective-linguistic responses, improves mutual learning in a human-robot interaction task. The authors compare DOT versus non-DOT feedback, and also compare two robot reinforcement-learning policies: greedy and epsilon-greedy exploration-exploitation.

The study uses a simulated Reachy robot that communicates three internal homeostatic needs (thirst, hunger, curiosity) through three babbling sounds, while human participants infer the need and select the corresponding object. Participants from the University of Gothenburg campus (n=28, ages 21-66) completed all four within-subject conditions in a language acquisition-style task; the main quantitative outcome was Reachy’s mean reward, interpreted as mutual learning, and a post-task interview was analyzed thematically.

Results showed that DOT improved terminal accuracy, with higher final-block mean reward in DOT conditions than Non-DOT, and that learning rate improved over time in DOT+greedy and DOT+epsilon-greedy conditions. The robot’s reinforcement-learning policy did not show a significant main effect on terminal accuracy, though epsilon-greedy sometimes supported learning over blocks. Interview data indicated that many participants found the task confusing or frustrating, suggesting interface and wording issues that may have affected performance. The paper concludes that affective, differential outcomes can support mutual learning in human-robot interaction and may be useful for long-term assistive or educational applications.

finding.finding_summary: The task was explicitly a language acquisition / communication-learning interaction in which humans learned to interpret the robot’s babbled utterances and select the correct object. DOT conditions produced significantly higher terminal mutual-learning performance than Non-DOT, with a main effect of Human Training Type on final-block mean reward (F(3,108)=0.488, p=.017, partial η2=.194).
finding.measure: Mutual learning performance in a language acquisition-style human-robot task, operationalized as Reachy’s mean reward when the human selected the object corresponding to the robot’s communicated need

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines whether affective-linguistic robot responses and differential outcomes improve engagement-like mutual learning in a socially interactive task. Learning improved over blocks in the DOT conditions, and thematic analysis found both positive affect (fun, interesting, achievement) and negative affect (confusing, frustrating), indicating that the interaction influenced participants’ emotional experience alongside performance.
finding.measure: Participant affective interview responses; learning performance in a socially interactive human-robot task
finding.effect_size: partial η2=0.396 (DOT+greedy block-to-block learning rate); partial η2=0.336 (DOT+epsilon-greedy block-to-block learning rate)

finding.finding_summary: The study frames mutual learning as a two-way learning process requiring humans and robots to adapt to each other, which aligns most closely with collaboration and adaptive learning skills. DOT conditions significantly improved learning rate over successive blocks, suggesting better sustained adaptation in the joint task, although the study did not directly measure collaboration skills with a validated durable-skills instrument.
finding.measure: Change in mean reward across blocks as a proxy for mutual learning and adaptation
finding.effect_size: partial η2=0.396 and 0.336 for block effects in DOT conditions

paper_profiles.title: Graduate teaching assistants use different criteria when grading introductory physics vs. quantum mechanics problems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether graduate teaching assistants (TAs) apply different grading standards when evaluating student solutions in introductory physics versus upper-level quantum mechanics (QM). The central question is whether TAs reward reasoning and explicit problem-solving steps more in QM than in introductory physics, and why those differences occur. The authors frame grading as potentially serving a formative assessment function, especially when it encourages students to explicate their reasoning rather than only provide final answers.

The study was conducted in a mandatory semester-long TA professional development course at a U.S. research university. Fifteen first-year physics graduate TAs graded paired student solutions to an introductory mechanics problem and a QM problem, each with a brief solution and an elaborated solution that showed reasoning more explicitly. The researchers analyzed TA score patterns, written justifications, class discussion, and follow-up interviews with seven volunteers. TAs more often rewarded explicit reasoning in the QM context than in the introductory context, and their explanations suggested that they viewed QM as more complex and expected advanced students to demonstrate understanding more explicitly.

The main conclusion is that many TAs graded more leniently on introductory physics solutions and more strictly on QM solutions because they treated grading primarily as summative rather than formative assessment and often judged introductory problems from their own expert perspective instead of from the perspective of novice learners. The paper argues that TA professional development should explicitly address grading as a formative tool and help TAs recognize that introductory students may also need credit for reasoning and problem-solving process, not just correct answers and formulas.

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on TA grading behavior and how TAs assign scores to student solutions, showing that grading criteria differed by context. TAs gave higher average scores to elaborated solutions than brief solutions in both contexts, with a larger difference in QM (brief M=6.57, SD=2.06; elaborated M=8.47, SD=1.55; p=0.008) than in introductory physics (brief M=7.07, SD=2.71; elaborated M=7.93, SD=1.24; p=0.274).
finding.measure: TA-assigned quiz scores to brief vs. elaborated student solutions in intro physics and QM
finding.std_deviation: Intro brief SD=2.71; intro elaborated SD=1.24; QM brief SD=2.06; QM elaborated SD=1.55

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies how graduate TAs evaluate reasoning, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving process, all of which relate to metacognition and critical thinking in assessment practices. TAs more often expected students to explicitly demonstrate understanding in QM than in introductory physics, and 40% said they would grade QM more on conceptual understanding while emphasizing equations, calculations, and final answers more in introductory physics.
finding.measure: TA written justifications and interview explanations about grading criteria

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates a TA professional development intervention intended to improve grading practices within a university teaching program. Findings suggest the activity can be used to surface and potentially reshape TA beliefs about grading, with the authors concluding that professional development should help TAs recognize grading as formative assessment and encourage more equitable grading practices across course levels.
finding.measure: TA responses in a mandatory semester-long professional development course, including worksheet responses, class discussion, and interviews

paper_profiles.title: Students’ interaction with and appreciation of automated informative tutoring feedback
paper_profiles.venue: FAME 1 – Feedback & Assessment in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how students interact with an automated formative assessment environment that delivers informative tutoring feedback (ITF) in mathematics. The central question is whether a balanced feedback strategy—one that initially withholds worked-out solutions, instead offering knowledge-of-results, error-specific feedback, try-again opportunities, subtasks, direct instruction videos, and later access to worked examples—supports productive student-environment interactions and whether students prefer this approach over immediate worked-out solutions.

The study was conducted with 25 Dutch senior general secondary school students aged 15–17 (10 tenth-graders and 15 eleventh-graders) working on linear and exponential extrapolation tasks. Data came from screen recordings and post-task interviews. The authors qualitatively coded students’ navigation and interview responses, finding that most feedback episodes led to improvement, with particularly strong improvement after direct instruction and subtasks. Students sometimes displayed self-guidance by checking intermediate results, though this was relatively uncommon.

In interviews, students generally preferred a combination of error-specific feedback first and worked-out solutions later. They valued specific feedback for pinpointing errors and helping them continue working, while worked examples were seen as useful for overview and confirmation, but sometimes encouraged passive memorization or premature closure. The chapter concludes that a balanced ITF strategy can support fruitful interactions and is appreciated by students, though the authors note limitations in generalizability because the sample was small and drawn from one school, and the study did not measure learning gains directly.

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on students’ work on linear and exponential extrapolation tasks in an automated formative assessment environment. Across 79 coded event sequences, 65 led to improvement or successful continuation, with especially strong improvement after direct instruction (13/14) and subtasks (7/7); error-specific feedback led to improvement in 14/29 cases. However, the study does not report standardized achievement gains or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Task performance and next-step improvement in linear and exponential extrapolation tasks; coded transitions after feedback (improvement, non-improvement, worked example, subtask, direct instruction, unable to continue)

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the feedback strategy helps manage cognitive load and uncertainty, which in turn supports engagement and persistence. In the coded interaction data, 6 of 79 episodes ended with students being unable to continue, and in interviews students sometimes reported that worked examples reduced effort but could also create a false sense of certainty; students also explicitly appreciated feedback that helped them stay engaged and proceed.
finding.measure: Observed continuation/disengagement in task episodes; interview themes about appreciation, uncertainty, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies self-guidance and self-checking as learners interacted with the formative feedback system. Five of 25 students showed self-guidance by testing whether intermediate results were correct, and interview/theoretical analysis suggested that room for exploration fostered this behavior; however, the authors also note that worked examples required self-explanation skills that some students lacked.
finding.measure: Self-guidance/self-check episodes coded from screen captures; interview reflections on understanding errors and worked examples

finding.finding_summary: The environment automated final-answer diagnosis, error-specific feedback, retry opportunities, and selection of subtasks, reducing the need for teacher intervention during task work. The paper does not measure teacher workload or time savings directly, but it does show that the system provided guidance and automatic subtask selection in a way intended to support students without direct teacher input.
finding.measure: Use of automated feedback, automated diagnosis, and automatically selected subtasks in the learning environment

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Love Edge Cases in Formative Math Assessment: Using the AMMORE Dataset and Chain-of-Thought Prompting to Improve Grading Accuracy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automatic short answer grading (ASAG) for open-response math questions in a real-world K-12 formative assessment setting. The authors introduce AMMORE, a dataset of 53,031 math student responses collected from 2,508 at-home users of Rori, an AI-powered WhatsApp math tutor used in several African countries, and use it to evaluate whether large language models can improve grading accuracy for difficult-to-score student answers.

The study runs two empirical experiments. In Experiment 1, the authors compare string matching, text processing, zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting using GPT-4o on a hard subset of 4,463 answers. CoT achieved the best performance, with 0.97 accuracy and 0.93 linear weighted kappa, improving overall grading accuracy and reducing false negatives on edge cases; however, it sometimes showed inconsistent or flawed reasoning and was slower than simpler methods. In Experiment 2, the authors feed different grading outputs into a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing model and show that grading accuracy materially changes estimates of student mastery: the worst method misestimated mastery for 6.9% of students, while CoT reduced this to 2.6%. The paper concludes that LLM-based grading may enable more reliable use of open-ended formative assessment in mathematics, especially in low-resource contexts, but it does not directly test learning gains from deployment.

finding.finding_summary: Chain-of-thought prompting produced the best grading performance on the hard math-answer subset, reaching 0.97 accuracy and 0.93 linear weighted kappa on 4,463 answers. Relative to naive string matching, it improved detection of difficult correct responses and raised overall grading accuracy from 0.79 to 0.97 on the binary correct/wrong task.
finding.measure: Automatic short-answer grading accuracy and agreement with human labels on open-response math questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM-based grading can reduce the burden of grading open-response math items and that better grading can improve downstream student mastery estimation. Chain-of-thought prompting took longer than text processing (average 2.79 seconds vs. 0.006 seconds), but it substantially improved grading quality, suggesting a tradeoff between speed and accuracy for operational use.
finding.measure: Answer-evaluation latency and grading performance for automated assessment workflows
finding.study_size: n=4,463 for grading evaluation; n=100 for reliability reruns

finding.finding_summary: Improved grading accuracy changed estimates of student mastery at the system level. Using human labels as the gold standard, naive string matching misestimated mastery for 6.9% of students (165/2,388), whereas chain-of-thought grading reduced this to 2.6% (61/2,388), implying that better grading can improve adaptive-learning decisions in tutoring systems.
finding.measure: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing mastery estimates derived from differently graded student responses

paper_profiles.title: Vernier caliper and micrometer computer models using Easy Java Simulation and its pedagogical design features—ideas for augmenting learning with real instruments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and classroom use of two Easy Java Simulation (EJS) computer models for teaching students how to read vernier calipers and micrometers, including the treatment of zero error. The authors argue that these tools complement real laboratory instruments by making the reading process more visible, offering hints and answers, supporting different scale versions, and providing automated assessment-for-learning feedback.

The study was conducted in a Singapore junior college physics context with students using a Google Site, the real instruments, and the simulations during lessons on measurement. The paper is primarily a design-and-implementation report rather than a controlled efficacy study: it presents student performance on seven formative multiple-choice items, survey responses, and informal interview excerpts. The reported results are positive, with students answering most items correctly and describing the lesson as engaging, useful, and helpful for understanding measurement procedures.

The authors conclude that the simulations can augment learning when used alongside real instruments and direct instruction, especially by supporting student-directed exploration and immediate feedback. No subgroup analyses or equity-related moderation evidence are reported, and the paper does not examine differences by prior attainment, disability, multilingual status, socioeconomic status, race, or ethnicity.

finding.finding_summary: Students using the vernier caliper and micrometer simulations performed well on formative measurement questions. Across 70 students, the average correct score on the seven multiple-choice items was reported as 88%, with 96% correct on the simplest vernier items (Q1–Q2), 81% correct on vernier zero-error items (Q3–Q4), 90% correct on the simpler micrometer items (Q5–Q6), and 77% correct on the micrometer zero-error item (Q7).
finding.measure: Performance on seven formative multiple-choice questions assessing reading of vernier calipers and micrometers, including zero-error correction

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative feedback indicated that students found the lesson fun, engaging, and helpful for remembering how to use the measurement tools. Interview excerpts suggest improved focus, enjoyment, and confidence in self-directed learning with hints, answers, and feedback, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and informal interview excerpts on engagement, enjoyment, and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The simulations were designed to support student-directed inquiry, self-assessment, and conceptual reasoning through hints, answer checks, and automated feedback. The paper reports that these features helped students think through measurement logic and identify errors on their own, but the evidence is qualitative and formative rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections and formative-question performance related to self-directed problem solving and self-assessment

paper_profiles.title: Модель використання системи комп’ютерного моделювання для формування компетентностей учнів з природничо-математичних предметів
paper_profiles.venue: Інформаційні технології і засоби навчання / Information Technologies and Learning Tools
paper_profiles.population: Secondary (general education students; grades not specified)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of weak methodological support and low teacher awareness of effective ICT-based teaching approaches, arguing that these gaps limit students’ ability to build individualized learning trajectories and develop competencies in natural and mathematical subjects. The author situates the problem in the context of declining achievement and broad policy goals for improving school STEM education in Ukraine.

The paper proposes a conceptual model for using computer modeling systems (СКМод) in general secondary education. Rather than evaluating a single implemented program, the article synthesizes literature and prior experience to define principles, selection criteria for computer modeling tools, pedagogical approaches (child-centered, systemic, activity-based, differentiated), and instructional uses such as cognitive tasks, reflection, formative assessment, and final assessment.

The population discussed is school students in general secondary education, with particular relevance to learners in natural and mathematical subjects. The paper also emphasizes teacher preparation and professional development as a necessary condition for implementation, including training future teachers to select, integrate, and assess computer modeling resources. The main conclusion is that computer modeling can diversify instruction, shift learning from passive to active, support individualized development, and strengthen subject competencies, but the article does not report an empirical classroom trial or measured student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that computer modeling supports students’ understanding of natural phenomena and scientific processes, development of research skills, and deeper subject comprehension. However, this is a conceptual/theoretical claim rather than a measured effect; no effect size, confidence interval, or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Computer modeling is presented as a tool for forming competencies in mathematics and other STEM subjects, including through cognitive tasks and interactive simulations. The paper cites prior work but does not present its own quantitative mathematics outcome data, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes development of cognitive tasks, problem solving, analysis, synthesis, generalization, and research-oriented thinking as outcomes of using computer modeling systems. These are discussed as intended benefits of the model, not as empirically measured gains, and no sample or effect estimate is given.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The author states that simulations, interactive exercises, animation, and formative assessment can increase students’ interest and allow them to learn with enthusiasm. This is a theoretical/argumentative claim about engagement and motivation, with no reported quantitative measure or effect size.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating GPT- and Reasoning-based Large Language Models on Physics Olympiad Problems: Surpassing Human Performance and Implications for Educational Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether modern large language models (LLMs) can solve advanced physics problems at the level of high-performing secondary students, and whether prompting strategies change performance. The authors compare GPT-4o under four prompting conditions (no prompt, general prompt, chain-of-thought, and single-shot chain-of-thought) with the reasoning model o1-preview and with students from the German Physics Olympiad.

The study uses six mechanics problems drawn from recent German Physics Olympiad stages. The authors generated 20 independent LLM solutions per problem per prompting condition (600 total), scored them using the official Olympiad rubrics, and compared the distributions to student solutions. They also examined problem-by-problem solution patterns and common errors in the generated responses.

Overall, both GPT-4o and especially o1-preview outperformed the Olympiad student benchmark on average, with o1-preview showing the strongest and most consistent performance. Prompting had little effect on GPT-4o, and the reasoning model generally worked best with straightforward prompting. The paper concludes that LLMs pose a challenge for unsupervised summative assessment because they can solve advanced physics problems at a level that exceeds top students, while also offering potential for formative assessment if used to help students evaluate their own solutions.

finding.finding_summary: Both GPT-4o and especially o1-preview solved advanced Olympiad-style physics problems at a level above the human Physics Olympiad benchmark. Across six mechanics problems, simulated exam scores showed that o1-preview consistently outperformed all GPT-4o prompting conditions and the student participants, with a very large to huge effect versus students (Cohen’s d=2.28).
finding.measure: Scores on six advanced Physics Olympiad mechanics problems, aggregated into simulated exam totals and problem-level rubric scores
finding.study_size: n=600 LLM-generated solutions; student solution set size varies by problem and was not reported as a single total
finding.effect_size: d=2.28 (o1-preview vs Physics Olympiad participants, overall aggregated score)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines multi-step physics problem solving, including problem representation, strategy selection, execution, and evaluation, which are core reasoning and metacognitive skills. GPT-4o prompting variations had little effect overall, while o1-preview more consistently produced complete solutions; however, both model types frequently omitted explicit solution evaluation steps.
finding.measure: Rubric-based scoring of solution process quality and completeness across four phases of physics problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that advanced LLMs threaten the authenticity of unsupervised summative assessment because they can solve Olympiad-level physics problems better than human participants. At the same time, they suggest a positive institutional role for formative assessment, where LLMs could help students inspect and improve their own solutions.
finding.measure: Comparison of LLM and student performance on high-stakes-style Olympiad assessment tasks; discussion of assessment implications

paper_profiles.title: Implementing Confidence Assessment in Low-Stakes, Formative Mathematics Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding confidence assessment (CA) to routine low-stakes formative mathematics quizzes improves students’ later mathematics attainment. In CA, students record a confidence rating alongside each answer, and their score rewards correct high-confidence responses while penalizing incorrect high-confidence responses, with the goal of encouraging truthful confidence judgments and better self-monitoring.

The study used a naturalistic quasi-experimental design in four secondary schools in England. Parallel classes were assigned either to CA or to business-as-usual formative assessment, while all schools continued using their own normal summative assessments as outcome measures. Across 475 students and intervention periods ranging from 3 weeks to one academic year, the study found no evidence that CA improved attainment relative to control. School-level effects varied in sign, but the pooled estimate was essentially zero (Cohen’s d = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.19]), and Bayesian meta-analysis provided substantial evidence for no difference (B01 = 8.48).

finding.finding_summary: Across four secondary-school mathematics trials (total N=475), confidence assessment in formative quizzes did not improve later summative mathematics attainment relative to business-as-usual control. The pooled meta-analytic effect on gain scores was essentially zero (Cohen’s d = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.19]), and Bayesian meta-analysis gave B01 = 8.48, providing substantial evidence for the null.
finding.measure: Gain in normal termly/half-termly summative mathematics assessment scores (pre-test to post-test, converted to percentages)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses possible effects of confidence assessment on student motivation, confidence, risk aversion, and self-reflection, and includes limited teacher comments suggesting students were intrigued and enjoyed the process. However, these outcomes were not measured directly with validated social-emotional instruments, so evidence here is indirect and not a central empirical focus.
finding.measure: Informal teacher comments / anecdotal student reactions to the confidence-scoring process

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is theorized to improve metacognition and calibration, but the study did not directly report a formal calibration outcome; instead, it tested whether the intervention improved downstream attainment. On that primary outcome, there was no detectable benefit (d = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.19]), so the paper does not provide evidence that repeated confidence assessment improved durable skills in a measurable way within this study.
finding.measure: Downstream attainment as a proxy for hypothesized metacognitive benefits; calibration discussed conceptually but not directly analyzed in the reported results

paper_profiles.title: The use of Moodle for Formative Assessment in Mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: Compass: Journal of Learning and Teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article discusses the use of Moodle’s multiple-choice quiz functionality for formative assessment, with a focus on mathematics. The author’s main question is whether randomly generated, non-assessed online quizzes can help students build understanding and confidence, while also noting the limitations of online assessment in mathematics compared with pen-and-paper work.

The paper describes how Moodle quizzes can randomize question order and question parameters, allowing students to receive different versions of the same concept each time they attempt a quiz. The discussion is largely practice-oriented and includes examples of how variables can be used to generate equivalent items, as well as caveats about Moodle’s limited mathematical functionality and lack of graphical randomization.

The only empirical evidence reported is a small trial in a Statistics course for Business and Information Technology students, where feedback from more than ten respondents was overwhelmingly positive. Students reported that the quizzes were especially useful for examination revision and appreciated getting different questions on repeated attempts; around 75% said this was their primary use. The article concludes that Moodle quizzes are a useful but limited formative-assessment tool, potentially transferable beyond mathematics to other subjects with quantitative content, but it does not provide a controlled comparison against an alternative baseline.

finding.finding_summary: In a small trial in a Statistics course for Business and Information Technology students (over ten responses), students reported that Moodle’s randomized multiple-choice quizzes were helpful for exam revision and understanding quantitative material. The paper does not report achievement test scores or an effect size, but it frames the quizzes as supporting formative understanding in mathematics/statistics contexts.
finding.measure: Student feedback on usefulness of Moodle quizzes for formative understanding/exam revision in a Statistics course

finding.finding_summary: Students’ feedback indicated that the quizzes helped them feel more confident and supported repetition for revision, with every respondent reporting it was helpful to have different questions each time they attempted the quiz. The article presents this as evidence that the tool supports confidence-building and engagement with revision, but without formal pre/post measurement.
finding.measure: Student self-reported helpfulness, revision use, and confidence-building related to quiz repetition

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions of objective formative assessment in language learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether undergraduate English learners perceive objective formative assessment as more supportive of language learning than objective summative assessment. The authors frame the problem as a tension between end-of-course testing and in-process assessment, arguing that quizzes, self-evaluations, exercises with scores, and mock exams may reduce stress and improve learning compared with high-stakes exams.

The study was conducted at the Language Center in Xalapa, Veracruz, Mexico, with a random sample of 117 undergraduate students drawn from a population of 500 English learners who had studied English for more than one year. Data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire asking students to rate perceptions of final exams, partial exams, quizzes/short exams, self-assessments, and scored exercises, and to rank these assessment types by preference.

Results were analyzed with descriptive frequency procedures using the median and mode. Students generally perceived final exams and partial exams as more negatively affecting learning, while quizzes, self-evaluations, and exercises with scores were seen as less stressful and more helpful for learning English. In the ranking task, formative-style activities were preferred over summative exams. The paper concludes that participants perceive objective formative assessment as a better support for language learning, while noting that the findings are specific to this context and do not definitively invalidate summative assessment as a testing approach.

finding.finding_summary: Undergraduate English learners perceived objective formative assessment activities as more helpful for language learning than objective summative exams. In a sample of n=117, respondents favored quizzes, self-evaluations, and exercises with scores over final and partial exams when asked which activities best supported learning English.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of assessment activities for learning English; ranking of assessment types

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that formative-style activities such as quizzes, self-assessments, and scored exercises were less stressful and did not negatively affect learning, whereas final and partial exams were more often perceived as producing negative effects. The study interprets these perceptions as indicating that formative assessment may lower stress and increase confidence in language learning.
finding.measure: Perceived negative affect/stress and confidence related to different assessment formats

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that formative assessment may better support learners' awareness of their own progress and learning through self-evaluations and practice exercises. This is based on participants' preference for self-assessment and scored practice over summative exams, which the authors interpret as aligning with self-awareness and learning-to-learn processes.
finding.measure: Perceptions of self-evaluations and practice exercises as learning supports

paper_profiles.title: Using paper-based, near-immediate feedback to support active learning in an introductory programming course
paper_profiles.venue: American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Annual Conference & Exposition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a paper-based automated grading system (AMC) that returns near-immediate feedback can support formative assessment and active learning in an introductory programming course. The author’s motivation is to reduce grading burden while increasing the frequency and timeliness of student feedback, especially in flipped or active-learning settings where students need quick checks on pre-class reading and in-class preparation.

The intervention was implemented in a sophomore-level introductory C programming course at a small undergraduate-only midwestern institution. In Fall 2017, the course used daily reading quizzes generated, scanned, auto-graded, and returned to students within about an hour; in Fall 2016, the same course did not use the daily quizzes and met more often with more lecture time. The study compares outcomes across these two course offerings, including in-class exam scores, final exam scores, and end-of-course self-reports, while also describing the instructor’s experience with AMC.

The main findings suggest higher performance in the quiz-supported offering, including a higher final exam mean (85.63% vs. 77.23%) and fewer low-performing students by course end (5% below 70% vs. 30% below 70% in the prior year). Students also reported greater confidence on most self-evaluation items and generally endorsed the daily quizzes as helpful. However, the paper explicitly notes that the causal contrast is not clean because the 2017 offering differed from 2016 in multiple ways, including class meeting frequency and time for in-class problem solving, so the effect of the quizzes/feedback cannot be isolated confidently.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports higher exam performance in the 2017 course offering that used daily quizzes with near-immediate feedback, but the contrast is confounded by simultaneous changes in weekly meeting structure and in-class problem-solving time. The final exam mean increased from 77.23% in 2016 to 85.63% in 2017, and the share of students below 70% fell from 30% to 5% by the end of the course.
finding.measure: Course exam scores (two mid-semester exams and cumulative final exam), especially final exam percentage scores

finding.finding_summary: End-of-course self-evaluation responses suggest students in the quiz-supported offering felt more confident about most programming skills, and 68% said the daily quizzes helped them learn the material (with the remaining 32% choosing the neutral option). However, response rates to the course evaluations were low, limiting confidence in the student-reported results.
finding.measure: Student self-efficacy/self-assessment items on end-of-course evaluations; one item asking whether daily quizzes helped learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AMC substantially reduced grading burden while increasing timely feedback, allowing the instructor to add 45 quiz opportunities across the semester without increasing workload substantially. Quizzes were typically returned the same day, and the system automated grading, compilation, emailing of corrected PDFs, and spreadsheet generation.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported grading time and workflow efficiency; return time for quizzes; number of assessments handled

paper_profiles.title: Procedural Generation of STEM Quizzes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a proof-of-concept Python API, QuizGen, for procedurally generating STEM quiz questions for learning management systems. The central problem is that GUI-based quiz authoring in systems like Moodle is slow and cumbersome for creating large banks of varied, reusable, and dynamically generated questions. The paper argues that script-based generation can improve authoring speed, support richer question types (including formulas, images, videos, and interactive 3D content), and simplify maintenance and collaboration through code-based question banks.

The approach is evaluated by comparing quiz-question editing and creation workflows in Moodle versus the proposed script-based method. The main empirical study uses five trained users to copy 20 text-based multiple-choice questions into Moodle and into the script-based workflow, finding that the script-based approach is consistently faster by about 49 seconds per question and that linear models fit completion time well for simple questions (R² > 0.94). The paper also reports creation times for several more complex example scripts and estimates Moodle-equivalent times, suggesting 2.4-6.3x speed-ups for those examples.

The population/context is STEM instructors, especially those with some programming familiarity, and the implementation is framed around undergraduate STEM quizzes and LMS workflows. The paper’s conclusions emphasize operational benefits: faster question creation, easier maintenance, and richer question content. It does not evaluate student learning outcomes from formative assessment itself; rather, it focuses on instructor productivity and quiz-authoring efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: In a user study with five trained users copying 20 text-based multiple-choice questions, the script-based workflow was about 49 seconds faster per question than Moodle’s GUI. The fitted time models explained most of the variance in completion time (R² > 0.94), with estimated per-question times of T = 0.19n + 61.3 s for Moodle and T = 0.197n + 12.5 s for the script-based approach, where n is question length in characters.
