This article examines blended learning in higher education, focusing on whether blended courses improve student access, success, withdrawal, and perceptions of instruction relative to online and face-to-face courses. The paper is framed as a broad discussion of blended learning’s role in the emerging digital/ICT environment, but its empirical evidence comes from institutional data at the University of Central Florida across several semesters.

The study compares blended, online, and face-to-face course outcomes from fall 2014 through fall 2015, and it further disaggregates success and withdrawal rates by minority versus non-minority status. It also analyzes end-of-course student ratings using a CART decision tree to identify which course/instructor rating items best predict an overall rating of “excellent.” The final model shows that three instructional items—helping students achieve course objectives, creating a learning environment, and communicating ideas/information—are the key predictors, while demographic and course-level variables do not contribute to the final rule.

Overall, the authors conclude that blended learning is at least competitive with, and often slightly better than, fully online and face-to-face formats on institutional measures of success and withdrawal. They report that these advantages hold for both minority and non-minority students, suggesting no obvious disadvantage for underrepresented groups in this dataset. They also argue that student perceptions of course excellence are driven primarily by core instructional behaviors rather than modality, grade expectations, or desire to take the course.

finding.finding_summary: Across fall 2014–fall 2015, blended courses had slightly higher success rates than online or face-to-face courses and slightly lower withdrawal rates. Success was reported as the proportion earning A, B, C, or S grades, with blended courses ranging from 91% to 95% across terms (e.g., n=17,954 in fall 2014; n=21,482 withdrawals table row n=19,831 reflects the enrollment for withdrawal calculations), compared with 87%–92% for face-to-face and 89%–92% for online courses. Minority and non-minority students showed similar patterns, with no evidence of a subgroup penalty for blended delivery in these institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Course success rate (A/B/C/S) and withdrawal rate by modality and minority status

finding.finding_summary: Student perceptions of the learning environment favored blended learning, and the study found robust if-then decision rules for assigning excellent course ratings. In the CART model (N=58,156), if students rated three items as excellent—helping achieve course objectives, creating an environment that helps students learn, and communicating ideas/information—the probability of an overall excellent rating was .99, and this rule held regardless of modality, expected grade, or desire to take the course.
finding.measure: End-of-course student perception of instruction / overall instructor rating; conditional excellent-rating decision rule

finding.finding_summary: The student rating model centered on items tied to course objectives, learning environment, and communication, which the authors interpret as formative, pedagogy-linked aspects of learning experience. However, the paper does not directly measure durable skills such as critical thinking or metacognition; therefore the evidence here is indirect and limited to instructional conditions associated with higher perceived course quality rather than demonstrated skill gains.
finding.measure: Student ratings of instructor effectiveness items related to achieving objectives, learning environment, and communication

paper_profiles.title: The Theory and Practice of Online Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is an edited volume that synthesizes theory, design, infrastructure, and support practices for online learning. The excerpted text introduces the second edition and argues that effective online learning depends less on the delivery technology itself than on instructional design, learner support, and the thoughtful integration of multiple learning theories, including behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, and connectivism.

Across the chapters summarized in the introduction, the book addresses issues such as how to design online materials, how to support learners at a distance, how to organize online course development, and how to use emerging technologies such as mobile tools and social software. The audience is primarily higher-education and distance-education practitioners, administrators, and educators rather than a specific student sample. Because the provided text is a conceptual/book overview rather than a single empirical study, it does not report original quantitative effects or subgroup analyses; instead, it offers practice-oriented arguments and examples about access, flexibility, quality, and learner support in online education.

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the question of how effective feedback is for student learning by conducting a large meta-analysis of educational feedback research. The authors aim to replicate and update the influential "Visible Learning" feedback synthesis, while addressing methodological concerns such as double-counting studies, differences in weighting, and heterogeneity across feedback forms and contexts.

The review integrates 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (over 61,000 participants) drawn from 32 prior meta-analyses. Studies had to involve an educational context and report outcomes related to learning, motivation, or behavior. The authors code and test several moderators, including research design, publication type, outcome type, feedback type, feedback channel, and feedback direction.

Overall, feedback shows a medium effect on student learning (d=0.55; 95% CI [0.48, 0.62]), which drops to d=0.48 after removing extreme outliers. Effects vary substantially by feedback characteristics: high-information feedback is strongest, corrective feedback is moderate, and reinforcement/punishment is weakest. Feedback is more effective for cognitive and physical outcomes than for motivational and behavioral outcomes, and feedback from teachers to students is generally stronger than feedback in other directions. The paper concludes that feedback is not a single uniform intervention and that its impact depends heavily on the information it conveys and the context in which it is delivered.

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found an overall positive effect of feedback on student learning across educational contexts. Using all 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000), the weighted mean effect was d=0.55 (95% CI [0.48, 0.62]); after removing 35 extreme outliers, the estimate was d=0.48 (95% CI [0.44, 0.51]). The main learning-related outcomes coded here included cognitive measures such as achievement, retention, and test performance.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes, including achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance

finding.finding_summary: Feedback had a smaller but still positive average effect on motivational outcomes, with substantial heterogeneity. For motivational measures including intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, and persistence, the subgroup effect was d=0.33 (95% CI [0.23, 0.42]) based on 109 effect sizes. The authors also note that 21% of motivational effect sizes were negative, particularly for uninformative feedback such as rewards or punishments.
finding.measure: Motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes self-regulation-related concepts in its moderator framework and defines high-information feedback as feedback that can include self-regulation information, but it does not present a separate pooled estimate for metacognition or collaboration. Because the review explicitly treats cognitive complexity/self-regulation as a meaningful feedback dimension, this is only a secondary but substantive durable-skills connection rather than a primary outcome.
finding.measure: Self-regulation-related aspects of feedback content

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education (HE) published from 2016 to 2022. The authors asked where AI in HE research was conducted, who conducted it, what populations and subject domains were studied, who the intended users were, and how AI was being used across the literature.

Using PRISMA procedures, the authors screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. The review found that most studies were conducted in Asia and North America, with China leading publication counts in the later years of the review period. Education departments were the most common first-author affiliation, undergraduate students were the most studied population, and language learning, computer science, and engineering were the most common subject domains.

Grounded coding produced five major use categories for AI in HE: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistant, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper does not report experimental effects on learner outcomes; instead, it maps trends and use cases in the literature. Its main conclusion is that AI in HE is rapidly expanding, but much of the work remains concentrated in a few countries, disciplines, and undergraduate settings, with a need for more research on graduate education, managerial uses, and unexplored affordances such as new generative tools.

finding.finding_summary: Across 138 studies, AI in higher education was most often used for assessment/evaluation, predicting, intelligent tutoring, and managing student learning rather than as an intervention with a single measured effect. The review reports descriptive counts only (e.g., assessment/evaluation was the most common use; predicting appeared in 21 studies; ITS in 18 studies) and does not synthesize causal effects on achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of AI use cases in higher education studies

finding.finding_summary: Some included studies used AI to assess or support emotions, persistence, and engagement-related behaviors, such as affect, student emotions toward learning, and motivation/persistence support in AI assistants. However, the paper only reports how often these constructs appeared in the reviewed literature and gives no pooled effect on social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of outcomes such as affect, student emotions, and persistence support

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that some studies assessed higher-order thinking, community identification, reflection, and self-regulated learning, and that AI systems were used to support diagnostic questioning and adaptive guidance. These are reported as use cases and outcome types in the literature, not as aggregated outcome effects.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of constructs including higher-order thinking, reflection, self-regulated learning, and diagnostic support

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature framed AI as improving efficiency, especially through automatic assessment, feedback generation, question creation, learning analytics, and instructional management. The review states that automatic assessment was the most common subcode within assessment/evaluation and that AI reduced instructor grading time, but it provides no pooled numerical effect size.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of efficiency-related uses such as automatic assessment, feedback, question generation, learning analytics, and curriculum/instructional management

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institutional uses of AI in higher education, including admissions prediction, student management, curriculum sequencing, quality assurance, and big-data-supported decision making. These are presented as emerging uses and gaps in the literature rather than measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of institutional applications such as admissions prediction, student management, and quality assurance

paper_profiles.title: Experiences of WNGER II Ph.D. Fellows During the COVID-19 Pandemic – A Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examined how Ph.D. fellows in the Western Norway Graduate School of Educational Research II (WNGER II) experienced the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular attention to how home office arrangements, digital teaching, and digital supervision affected their doctoral work. The paper is framed by frame factor theory and asks how the pandemic impeded doctoral fellows’ micro-level and meso-level conditions, including project progress, supervision, collaboration, wellbeing, and institutional support.

The study used a sequential mixed-methods design with a survey (N=62; 85% women), six semi-structured interviews, one focus group (n=11), field dialogs, online observations, and document analysis. Quantitative analyses were descriptive and correlational (Spearman’s rho), and qualitative analyses used thematic analysis. The context was doctoral education in Norway during March 2020–November 2021, when nearly all doctoral learning and supervision shifted online.

Findings indicate that many fellows experienced negative effects on doctoral progress: 50.0% reported the pandemic impeded their project, 56.5% reported their project was negatively influenced by working from home, and 30.7% changed data collection methods. Care responsibilities for children were associated with greater reported impediment, and less frequent supervisor communication was associated with worse project conditions. At the same time, many respondents remained satisfied with digital teaching and supervision, suggesting mixed experiences: institutional support and online supervision helped some fellows, but delays, altered research plans, and psychosocial strain were common. The paper concludes that pandemic-era doctoral regulations and support systems were often insufficiently adjusted to extraordinary conditions, especially for research progress and feasibility.

finding.finding_summary: The pandemic was associated with substantial disruption to doctoral productivity and progress. In the survey (n=62; correlation analyses n=61), 50.0% reported that COVID-19 impeded their doctoral project, 56.5% said working from home negatively influenced the project, and 30.7% reported changing data collection methods. The authors also report that project impediment correlated with altered data collection (rs=0.40, p<0.01) and making other project changes (rs=0.61, p<0.01), while being on track correlated negatively with impediment (rs=-0.35, p<0.01).
finding.measure: Survey items on project progress, home office influence, altered data collection, other project changes, and being on track with the Ph.D. project

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports both strain and resilience-related experiences. Many fellows experienced psychosocial challenges during the pandemic, but the quantitative survey also found that 82.2% were unlikely to leave their projects, and open-ended responses/interviews highlighted persistence, resilience, and emotional support as important coping resources. No standardized wellbeing scale or mean change score was reported; evidence is based on self-report survey items and qualitative themes.
finding.measure: Survey items on considering quitting and qualitative interview themes on emotional support, persistence, and resilience
finding.study_size: n=62 survey; n=6 interviews; n=11 focus group

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines institutional responsiveness, supervision structures, and doctoral regulations during the pandemic. It finds that existing Ph.D. guidelines, regulations, and assessment norms were largely unchanged despite extraordinary conditions, and that incremental supports were often insufficient. In the survey, many respondents rarely communicated with department heads (59.7%) or Ph.D. coordinators (66.1%), and 45% were dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with information about possible contract extensions, indicating institutional support gaps.
finding.measure: Survey items on communication with supervisor/coordinator/department head, satisfaction with supervision and extension information; qualitative data on regulations and support systems
finding.study_size: n=62 survey; n=6 interviews; n=11 focus group; N=15 documents

paper_profiles.title: LOFAR: The LOw-Frequency ARray
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a technical overview and reference description of the LOFAR radio telescope, a new-generation low-frequency interferometric array built in the Netherlands and across Europe. Its purpose is to explain the instrument’s science motivation, array layout, station hardware, digital signal processing, data transport network, and central processing infrastructure, with selected commissioning results used to illustrate performance.

The paper describes how LOFAR achieves wide-field, low-frequency observations through fixed antenna stations, digital beam-forming, a flexible correlator, and large-scale computing and storage systems. It emphasizes the system’s ability to support multiple observing modes, including standard imaging, high-time-resolution beam-formed studies, and transient buffering, as well as the technical challenges of radio-frequency interference, ionospheric calibration, and high data rates.

Because the article is focused on instrument design and capabilities rather than an educational intervention or human-subject study, it does not investigate learners, classrooms, or educational outcomes. Its main conclusions are that LOFAR is operational, scientifically versatile, and a pathfinder for future data-intensive radio astronomy facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array.

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews research on student self-assessment, focusing on studies published largely between 2013 and 2018, with some earlier foundational studies included for context. The central problem is definitional and empirical: what counts as self-assessment, how it should be operationalized, and whether it should be treated as a formative learning process rather than a summative judgment of ability.

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies and organizes them around four major topics: consistency with other judgments, student perceptions, achievement, and self-regulated learning. Andrade argues that formative self-assessment is most useful when it is guided by criteria, rubrics, scripts, feedback, and opportunities to revise work, whereas summative self-assessment tends to be inconsistent and can be distorted by incentives such as grade consequences.

Across the reviewed studies, formative self-assessment was generally associated with better academic outcomes and stronger self-regulated learning. The review highlights that students’ self-assessments are more useful when they are task-specific, scaffolded, and embedded in opportunities for improvement. The paper concludes by calling for more research on the cognitive and affective mechanisms of self-assessment, rather than further work narrowly focused on accuracy/consistency alone.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports consistently positive associations between formative self-assessment and writing outcomes. In the cited meta-analysis by Graham et al. (2015), 10 studies yielded an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality; the review also notes that quasi-experimental and experimental studies found treatment groups outperformed comparison groups on writing tasks.
finding.measure: Writing quality; scores on written assignments

finding.finding_summary: The review notes experimental and quasi-experimental studies in which formative self-assessment improved speaking English performance, but it does not report a pooled effect size for language fluency outcomes. These findings are described as part of a broader set of achievement gains across disciplines.
finding.measure: Speaking English performance

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics-related self-assessment tasks and reports improved performance in studies using math word problems and dart-throwing/motor-skill analogs tied to self-evaluative standards. However, it does not provide a pooled effect size specific to mathematics, so the finding is based on narrative synthesis rather than a meta-analytic estimate.
finding.measure: Math word problem performance; task performance on numeracy-related/self-evaluative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review describes self-assessment studies in science contexts, including elementary students improving science reports and self-regulated learning strategies in science-related tasks. Effects are presented narratively rather than with a pooled effect size, but the overall direction for formative self-assessment is positive.
finding.measure: Science reports; science concept understanding; self-regulated learning in science contexts

finding.finding_summary: Across non-writing academic tasks, formative self-assessment was associated with better performance in a wide variety of disciplines, including exams, map-making, and vocational tasks. The review states that nearly all non-meta-analytic achievement studies employing formative self-assessment found treatment groups outperformed controls, though specific pooled effects are not reported for this broad category.
finding.measure: Exams; map-making; vocational/task performance; assorted disciplinary outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that formative self-assessment is associated with stronger self-regulated learning, motivation, self-efficacy, and self-satisfaction. One cited study on darts reported that students with graduated self-evaluative standards outperformed those with absolute or no standards in motor skill and motivational beliefs, including self-efficacy, attributions, and self-satisfaction.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires; think-aloud protocols; motivational beliefs (self-efficacy, attributions, self-satisfaction)
finding.study_size: n=70 in Kitsantas and Zimmerman (2006); otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review’s strongest non-achievement emphasis is on metacognition and self-regulated learning processes. It reports that self-assessment using rubrics/scripts was associated with more self-regulated behavior, with effect sizes described as small to moderate (η²=0.06–0.42), and one study showed association across all three SRL phases: forethought, performance, and reflection.
finding.measure: Self-regulation questionnaires; think-aloud protocols; SRL phase measures

finding.finding_summary: A small subset of the reviewed work addresses task selection and study-time allocation, suggesting that self-assessment can improve learners’ subsequent learning-task choices and study behaviors. Evidence is largely narrative and based on laboratory or exploratory designs rather than direct measurement of classroom productivity, so this is a weaker but substantive fit for operational efficiency.
finding.measure: Task selection choices; study time allocation; restudy decisions
finding.study_size: n=15 in Nugteren et al. (2018); otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review is not primarily about policy or institutional change, and it does not report empirical institutional effects. It discusses classroom assessment practice and pedagogy rather than system-level outcomes, so this category is only marginally applicable and the empirical finding is effectively absent.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Adversarial Bandits with Multi-User Delayed Feedback: Theory and Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies an online learning problem in which a decision-maker must repeatedly choose among multiple arms while receiving feedback from multiple users after unknown, arbitrary delays. The motivation comes from real-world recommendation and resource-allocation settings, such as online advertising, caching, and traffic management, where feedback from different users arrives at different times and the underlying losses may change over time.

The authors propose two adversarial multi-armed bandit algorithms with delayed feedback: MUD-EXP3 for cases where the time horizon and delay bound are known, and AMUD-EXP3 for cases where they are unknown. Both methods use importance-weighted loss estimates and exponential weighting, and AMUD-EXP3 adds a doubling-trick style adaptive learning rate. The paper provides regret analyses showing sublinear regret under stated assumptions and evaluates the methods in simulation against delayed-UCB baselines and a random policy.

The experimental section uses synthetic stochastic and adversarial bandit environments with varying numbers of arms, users, delay bounds, and distribution-change frequencies. Results show that the proposed methods generally outperform delayed-UCB baselines in adversarial settings when delays are moderate and environmental change is not too frequent, while performance degrades as delays become large or the environment changes more rapidly. The paper does not study educational populations or learner subgroups; it is an algorithmic paper about delayed-feedback bandits in general application domains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is an online decision algorithm for delayed-feedback settings, and its empirical evaluation shows improved cumulative loss/regret versus delayed-UCB baselines in simulated adversarial environments. In the default adversarial setup (N=10, M=10, tran num=3), MUD-EXP3 and AMUD-EXP3 outperform DUCB and successive elimination, with the advantage most visible when the maximum delay is relatively small (e.g., 10 or 100 rounds).
finding.measure: Cumulative regret; cumulative loss in synthetic bandit simulations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the proposed multi-user delayed-feedback bandit framework better matches operational decision-making in applied systems such as caching optimization and traffic management. The main demonstrated impact is algorithmic/system-level: it provides a more realistic optimization method for settings where feedback is delayed and multiple users are involved, though the evidence is only from simulation rather than field deployment.
finding.measure: Theoretical regret bounds; simulated performance under varying system parameters

paper_profiles.title: Nusselt Number for Steady Periodically Developed Heat Transfer in Micro- and Mini-Channels with Arrays of Offset Strip Fins Subject to a Uniform Heat Flux
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates steady, periodically developed conjugate heat transfer in micro- and mini-channels containing arrays of offset strip fins under a uniform wall heat flux. The authors focus on the Nusselt number, which they define using a spatially constant, physically meaningful heat transfer coefficient based on the volume-averaged temperature difference between fluid and solid, rather than the approximate coefficients used in much of the earlier literature.

The study uses finite-element simulations on a unit cell of the fin array to examine how the Nusselt number changes with Reynolds number, fin geometry, Prandtl number, and thermal conductivity ratio. Across 197 geometries and more than 2,000 simulated data points, the authors show that prior empirical correlations—largely developed for larger conventional channels, transitional/turbulent flows, and often constant wall-temperature conditions—do not accurately predict the laminar micro-/mini-channel regime considered here.

The main conclusions are that, for the simulated conditions, the Nusselt number is well approximated by simple asymptotic forms in the geometric ratios and by a near-linear dependence on Reynolds number over substantial ranges. The paper proposes new correlations that better match the numerical data and highlights that flow-regime transitions in heat transfer align closely with previously identified weak/strong inertia flow regimes. This is a fluid mechanics/heat transfer paper and does not study educational outcomes, formative assessment, or learner subgroup effects.

paper_profiles.title: Transfer Learning between Motor Imagery Datasets using Deep Learning - Validation of Framework and Comparison of Datasets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies cross-dataset transfer learning for EEG-based motor imagery decoding in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). The authors ask which motor-imagery datasets are suitable as pretraining donors and which are easiest or hardest as receiver datasets when using a simple deep-learning transfer framework.

The approach uses EEGNet as a feature extractor. A model is first trained on one donor dataset, then its classification head is discarded and replaced with a newly trained linear classifier using a small number of calibration trials from a receiver dataset. The study evaluates 12 public motor-imagery EEG datasets from MOABB, examining three classification settings: right hand vs. feet (rh-f), left hand vs. right hand (lh-rh), and all available classes. Performance is measured mainly by ROC-AUC for the binary tasks and accuracy for the multiclass task.

The context is adult EEG/BCI research rather than classroom education. The main conclusion is that the simple transfer-learning framework can achieve decent cross-dataset decoding performance, but transfer quality depends strongly on the compatibility of donor and receiver datasets. Datasets such as Schirrmeister2017, Zhou2016, BNCI2014001, Lee2019 MI, and PhysionetMI are generally useful, while Ofner2017 is consistently near chance, reflecting a substantial distribution mismatch. The paper emphasizes operational efficiency and online feasibility, showing that only a lightweight linear layer must be trained on receiver data, but it does not study educational outcomes, delayed retention, or subgroup equity effects.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed transfer-learning pipeline reduced calibration burden by freezing the pretrained EEGNet embedding and training only a new linear classifier on a small number of receiver trials. The authors report that the approach remained viable with as few as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 calibration examples per class depending on dataset, and that the fine-tuning step could be completed in seconds on a CPU, supporting online use.
finding.measure: Cross-dataset motor-imagery classification performance under varying numbers of calibration examples; online feasibility / training time
finding.study_size: n=12 datasets; 871,488 classifier evaluations across folds, sessions, subjects, datasets, and pretrained models

paper_profiles.title: Transfer Representation Learning with TSK Fuzzy System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of transfer representation learning for unsupervised domain adaptation. The central question is how to learn a shared feature space that reduces distribution mismatch between a labeled source domain and an unlabeled target domain while preserving discriminative and geometric structure in the data. The authors argue that conventional kernel-based feature transformations are hard to interpret and difficult to select appropriately, especially for nonlinear mapping.

To solve this, the paper proposes TRL-TSK-FS, which uses a multi-output Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy system as the feature mapping. The antecedent part of the fuzzy system performs nonlinear transformation via fuzzy mapping, while the consequent part performs linear dimensionality reduction; the method also incorporates maximum mean discrepancy for marginal and conditional distribution matching, plus LDA/PCA-style terms to preserve class-separating and geometric information. Antecedent parameters are initialized with a deterministic Var-Part clustering procedure rather than fuzzy c-means, which the authors claim improves stability.

Experiments are conducted on two benchmark transfer-learning datasets: Office-Caltech (image domains) and NG20 (text/newsgroup domains). The method is compared against 1NN baselines, traditional TSK-FS, and several transfer representation learning methods including TCA, GFK, JDA, TJM, and SCA. The reported results show that TRL-TSK-FS achieves the best average accuracies across the tested transfer tasks, with especially strong gains on the Office-Caltech and NG20 benchmarks. The paper concludes that TSK fuzzy systems can be used effectively as interpretable feature learners for transfer representation learning, though the approach is framed for homogeneous transfer and still has scalability limitations.

finding.finding_summary: On benchmark transfer-learning classification tasks, TRL-TSK-FS outperformed competing methods on average. On Office-Caltech, the proposed method reached 54.29% average accuracy versus 46.33% for SCA and 46.31% for JDA; on NG20 with linear kernel settings, it reached 89.47% versus 87.69% for JDA and 86.12% for TJM.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy on transfer-learning benchmark tasks (Office-Caltech image domains; NG20 text domains)

paper_profiles.title: Communication-Efficient and Privacy-Preserving Feature-based Federated Transfer Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the communication bottleneck and privacy concerns in federated learning and federated transfer learning over wireless networks. The authors argue that standard federated learning requires repeated transmission of large model updates, which is costly for mobile and IoT devices with limited spectrum and power. They propose feature-based federated transfer learning (FbFTL), in which clients upload extracted intermediate features and labels once, rather than repeatedly uploading gradient or parameter updates.

The method uses a pretrained source model, splits the network at a cut layer, and keeps the feature-extraction sub-model fixed while training only the task-specific sub-model at the parameter server. A privacy-preserving random shuffling scheme is introduced so that uploaded outputs are detached from client identities, reducing the risk that labels reveal client information. The paper derives analytical payload formulas and privacy-leakage expressions, then evaluates the method on image classification (ImageNet to CIFAR-10) and a dry-bean classification task.

Across the experiments, FbFTL substantially reduces uplink communication compared with federated learning and conventional federated transfer learning, while achieving the same optimization trajectory as the corresponding task-specific transfer-learning variant. On CIFAR-10, the paper reports 6.6 Gb total uplink payload for FbFTL versus 599 Tb for task-specific FTL and 3216 Tb for FL, with test accuracy of 85.59% for FbFTL and task-specific FTL, compared with 89.1% for FL and 91.68% for full-model FTL. On the dry-bean dataset, FbFTL similarly lowers total uplink payload to 15.0 Mb, with test accuracy matching task-specific FTL at 98.06%.

finding.finding_summary: FbFTL greatly improves communication efficiency by replacing iterative gradient uploads with one-time uploads of extracted features and labels. On CIFAR-10, total uplink payload fell to 6.6 Gb versus 599 Tb for task-specific FTL and 3216 Tb for FL, and on the dry-bean task it fell to 15.0 Mb versus 15.2 Gb for task-specific FTL and 16.1 Gb for FL.
finding.measure: Uplink payload, downlink payload, number of upload batches, and upload parameters per batch
finding.study_size: CIFAR-10: n=50000 training images across U=6250 clients; dry beans: dataset size not_reported with U=1176 clients

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Modelling for Knowledge Transfer Across Engineering Fleets via Multitask Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses knowledge transfer for sparse predictive modeling in engineering fleets, where related subgroups have incomplete data and independent models perform poorly. The authors propose a hierarchical Bayesian multitask learning framework that shares information across related tasks while preserving interpretable, group-specific parameters and uncertainty estimates.

The approach is illustrated with two operational case studies: survival analysis for alternator and turbocharger components in a truck fleet, and power-curve prediction for turbines in a wind farm. In each setting, data are partitioned into subgroups (e.g., use-type, component, or operating condition), and the model learns both shared and subgroup-specific effects through hierarchical priors and mixed effects. The key claim is that sparse groups borrow statistical strength from data-rich groups, improving out-of-sample predictive log-likelihood and reducing posterior uncertainty compared with single-task learning, complete pooling, and a correlation-alignment domain adaptation baseline.

For the truck-fleet case, the model improves predictive performance for most subgroups, especially sparse ones, but also shows that inappropriate sharing can cause negative transfer; this is demonstrated when a naive extension across alternators and turbochargers performs poorly for some tasks. The wind-farm case similarly shows that tailoring shared structure to component type improves extrapolation and predictive fit. The paper’s main contribution is methodological rather than educational: it develops an interpretable Bayesian transfer-learning framework for engineering monitoring, with emphasis on subgroup structure, uncertainty quantification, and the risk of over-sharing information.

finding.finding_summary: The hierarchical Bayesian multitask model improved predictive accuracy for fleet-monitoring tasks relative to independent single-task learning, complete pooling, and correlation alignment. In the alternator case, the combined population log-likelihood increased from 355.47 (STL) to 409.57 (MTL) over 25% held-out test data across 8 sub-flleets (total n=437); in the extended alternator+turbocharger model it increased from 570.41 to 646.28 over 14 tasks (alternators n=437; turbochargers n=287).
finding.measure: Out-of-sample predictive log-likelihood for hazard/power regression tasks; posterior predictive distributions; standard deviation reductions in latent parameters
finding.study_size: n=437 (alternators), n=287 (turbochargers), with 25% test split; total task-wise samples across 14 tasks
finding.std_deviation: Average posterior SD reduction of 90% for slopes and 73% for intercepts in alternators; 51% for slopes and 67% for intercepts in turbochargers

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that hierarchical Bayesian transfer learning can support better fleet-level monitoring and decision-making by identifying which subgroups should share information and by quantifying uncertainty at multiple levels. It also demonstrates that the model can inform operational decisions such as servicing or component replacement, and can be used to evaluate when negative transfer may occur if subgroup structure is misspecified.
finding.measure: Posterior correlations, subgroup-level uncertainty, and predictive log-likelihood used to support fleet-management and decision-process implications

paper_profiles.title: Transfer Learning for Causal Effect Estimation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of causal effect estimation in settings where target-domain data are limited but related source-domain data are available. The authors propose Transfer Causal Learning (TCL), a framework that transfers information from a source domain to improve estimation of average causal effects (ACE) in the target domain when the two domains share the same covariates but differ in treatment assignment and/or outcome relationships.

The main method, called 8-TCL, uses a two-stage procedure: first, it fits nuisance models in the source domain to obtain a rough estimate; second, it applies 8 regularized bias correction on the target domain to estimate the sparse difference between source and target nuisance parameters. The corrected nuisance estimates are then plugged into inverse probability weighting (IPW), outcome regression (OR), or doubly robust (DR) estimators. The paper provides non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees under sparsity assumptions and shows through simulations that the approach improves ACE estimation accuracy relative to target-only and naive merge baselines.

The empirical application is a real-world observational study of vasopressor therapy for septic patients using in-hospital electronic medical records from two adjacent academic level-1 trauma centers in the southeastern United States. The outcome is 28-day mortality, and covariates include 34 vital-sign and laboratory variables. The paper reports that baseline methods produce implausible positive treatment effects, whereas 8-TCL yields an estimate consistent with prior medical literature: vasopressor therapy appears to reduce mortality. The paper also demonstrates a more general partition-then-transfer use case on the IHDP benchmark dataset for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, but this is still a causal inference / treatment-effect paper rather than an education study.

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive Feature Ranking for Unsupervised Transfer Learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (machine learning image datasets; no human learner population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine-learning transfer learning problem: how to rank and select hidden representations learned by a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) on a source dataset so that only the most useful features are transferred to a target dataset. The authors propose an adaptive feature ranking method based on minimizing information loss in the source RBM, then use the selected high-scoring sub-networks as fixed transferred parameters in a target RBM. They also compare this approach with standard self-taught learning and with transferring low-scored features.

The empirical work uses image datasets only: MNIST as the source domain and ICDAR/TiCC as targets, plus within-TiCC transfer experiments. The study evaluates feature quality through visual inspection, reconstruction behavior after pruning, and downstream classification accuracy using an SVM on learned RBM features. Reported results show that high-scoring features are more meaningful than low-scoring ones and that transferring high-scoring features can improve target classification accuracy in 3 of 4 MNIST-based transfer cases, with mixed results on TiCC transfers. The paper concludes that selective transfer can help unsupervised transfer learning, especially when source and target domains are related, but that too much transferred knowledge can hurt performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether adaptive feature ranking improves downstream classification performance after unsupervised transfer learning. Using MNIST as source and ICDAR/TiCC as targets, the proposed ASTL method achieved statistically significant gains over baseline RBM/self-taught learning in 3 of 4 MNIST-based transfer settings; for example, ASTL (α=1) reached 40.43% on MNIST30k→ICDARd versus 30.47% for RBM STL, and 77.56% on MNIST30k→TiCCw A versus 72.88% for RBM STL.
finding.measure: Predictive classification accuracy on target-domain test sets after RBM feature transfer; comparison with SVM, PCA STL, SC STL, RBM STL, RBM, and ASTL variants
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported for accuracies in tables, but not a standardized effect size; not_reported

gaps: The sweep has some relevant formative assessment items, but it is not yet covering the conceptual/definitional literature well enough to answer how formative assessment is defined and distinguished from summative, diagnostic, feedback, and classroom assessment.

There is little evidence of foundational syntheses/frameworks or widely cited definitional sources (e.g., review articles, handbooks, encyclopedias, classic chapters) that explicitly compare formative assessment with adjacent constructs.

The K–12 and postsecondary split is uneven: there are a few university and secondary/elementary items, but little on kindergarten/early childhood and no clear coverage of postsecondary conceptual treatments beyond isolated empirical studies.

The sweep appears to include noisy or tangential results (e.g., sports training, engineering taxonomy) and misses more precise terminology such as 'assessment for learning,' 'assessment as learning,' 'diagnostic assessment,' 'classroom assessment,' and 'feedback' as definitional contrasts.
The 403 error suggests the current search strategy is fragile; alternative sources/search terms are needed to fill the conceptual gap.

The sweep is heavily skewed toward general formative assessment studies and a few K-12/postsecondary items, but it does not yet surface the canonical definitional and conceptual literature that explicitly distinguishes formative assessment from summative assessment, diagnostic assessment, feedback, and classroom assessment.
